Bank Statement and Cash Analysis

Bank Statement and Cash Analysis
DisciplineForensic accounting; fraud examination
Core testsProof of cash; bank reconciliation review; deposit-in-transit and outstanding-check tests; kiting and lapping tests; check examination
Indirect methodsSource and application of funds; expenditures method
Typical inputsBank statements, check images, deposit slips, cash receipts journal, general ledger
Fraud-tree branchesSkimming; cash larceny; check tampering; fraudulent disbursements

Bank statement and cash analysis is the family of procedures a forensic accountant uses to test whether the cash an organization (or a person) reports agrees with what actually passed through its bank accounts. Because almost every asset-misappropriation scheme eventually touches cash, the bank is the one independent, third-party record that a fraudster cannot easily rewrite. This article is a working guide: it sets out step-by-step procedures, formulas and worked numeric examples, followed by the evidence each test produces and the pitfalls that commonly trap examiners. For the theory of why such schemes occur see Fraud Triangle; for the person-level equivalent of the indirect methods, see Net Worth Method.

1 Acquiring and preparing bank evidence

Every test below depends on a complete, authentic set of bank records, so acquisition comes first. The procedure is:

  1. Inventory every account. Request a list of all accounts, including dormant, payroll, sweep, petty-cash and savings accounts, from the bank (via the entity's signatory or by subpoena or document request in litigation). Omitted accounts are the commonest way a scheme escapes testing. Cross-check against signature cards, the general ledger chart of accounts and Forms 1099-INT.
  2. Obtain statements directly from the bank, not from the suspect or from the accounting department, wherever practicable. Statements held by the suspect may have been altered. Preserve the request, the transmission and the receipt under chain-of-custody discipline.
  3. Obtain images, not just totals. Request front-and-back images of every paid check and every deposit item, plus deposit slips. The back of a check (endorsements, bank stamps, the depositary institution) frequently contains the evidence.
  4. Cover a continuous period that includes at least one full month before the suspected start and the whole period to date, so that the first and last periods of each test have valid opening balances.
  5. Convert to a working dataset. Load transactions into a spreadsheet or database with one row per item: date, amount, check number, payee, depositor, account. Reconcile the total of the dataset to each statement's printed totals before analysing anything (a control total check).

Where records are voluminous, the same dataset supports the analytics described in Fraud Detection Analytics and Benford's Law testing of disbursement amounts.

2 Reviewing bank reconciliations for manipulation

A monthly bank reconciliation is the primary internal control over cash, and it is also the usual place where a custodian hides a theft. Review the reconciliations for the period under investigation against the bank statements, not against each other. Look for the following manipulation patterns:[1]

  • Reconciler is the custodian. The same person who handles receipts, writes checks and reconciles the bank account has the opportunity to conceal anything. Segregation-of-duties failure is a root red flag (see Red Flags).
  • Fictitious reconciling items. Deposits in transit that never clear, or outstanding checks that are not on the check register, used as plugs to force agreement.
  • Forced balances. An unexplained "adjustment" or "miscellaneous" line, or a book balance that was changed at the last minute to equal the bank balance.
  • Altered statements. The reconciler works from a photocopied, retyped or electronically edited statement. Compare the copy held internally with a statement obtained directly from the bank, checking balances, check numbers and fonts (see Document Examination).
  • Stale items carried forward. Outstanding checks or deposits in transit that remain open for many months (checks rarely stay uncashed beyond 90 to 180 days, and a deposit in transit should clear within one to three business days).
  • Reconciliations prepared late or unsigned, or reconciliations missing for specific months (often the months in which the scheme was most active).

The practical test: re-perform one month's reconciliation from scratch using the bank statement, the cash receipts journal and the check register. Then trace every reconciling item to a subsequent-period statement (see section 4).

3 The proof of cash

The proof of cash (four-column reconciliation) is the most powerful single test of bank-versus-book cash because it reconciles not only balances but also the receipts and disbursements that flow between them, which exposes both unrecorded transactions and cut-off errors. It uses four columns: the beginning balance, receipts, disbursements and the ending balance. The same adjusting items (deposits in transit and outstanding checks at both ends of the period) are carried across the columns.[1]

Procedure.

  1. Choose the period (usually one month; for investigations, test several months, including months you suspect and months you do not).
  2. Enter the balance per bank at the start and end of the period, and total deposits and total withdrawals per the bank statement.
  3. List deposits in transit (DIT) and outstanding checks (OC) at the beginning and at the end of the period.
  4. Adjust the receipts column: subtract beginning DIT (already counted by the bank this month but booked last month) and add ending DIT.
  5. Adjust the disbursements column: subtract beginning OC and add ending OC.
  6. Compare the adjusted bank totals to the book totals from the cash receipts and cash disbursements journals. Any difference is an unreconciled item to investigate.

Worked example. An illustrative nonprofit shows these figures for a month:

LineBeginning balanceReceiptsDisbursementsEnding balance
Per bank statement$40,000$300,000$290,000$50,000
Deposits in transit, beginning+5,000−5,000——
Deposits in transit, ending—+9,000—+9,000
Outstanding checks, beginning−8,000—−8,000—
Outstanding checks, ending——+12,000−12,000
Adjusted (true) cash$37,000$304,000$294,000$47,000
Per books (ledger)$37,000$296,500$294,000$39,500
Difference0$7,5000$7,500

Check: $37,000 + $304,000 − $294,000 = $47,000, so the adjusted bank columns foot across. The books, however, recorded $7,500 less in receipts than the bank actually received, leaving book cash $7,500 too low. In this fact pattern the discrepancy is in the books, not the bank, and it must be explained: unrecorded donations or loan proceeds, a transfer from another account, or a receipt that the bookkeeper recorded as a net amount after pulling cash. The inverse pattern, where book receipts exceed bank receipts, suggests fictitious entries or deposits that were never made; if the shortfall is concentrated in cash (currency) receipts, skimming or lapping becomes the leading hypothesis.

What the test cannot do. The proof of cash shows that recorded and banked amounts differ; it does not tell you whether revenue that was never recorded or banked (pure off-book skimming) exists. That requires the indirect methods in section 8 or comparison to independent sales evidence (see Analytical Methods).

4 Deposit-in-transit and outstanding-check tests

Both reconciling items rely on the reconciler's say-so, so test them directly against the following period's bank statement (a "subsequent clearing" test).

Deposit-in-transit test.

  1. List all DIT at period end from the reconciliation.
  2. Obtain the bank statement for the next month and the deposit slips.
  3. Confirm each DIT cleared the bank within the first one to three business days. Tolerate weekends and holidays, but flag any item that took longer.
  4. Confirm the DIT amount and the make-up of the deposit (cash versus checks) agree to the cash receipts journal and the deposit slip.
  5. Flag a DIT that does not clear, clears for a smaller amount, or clears in a differently composed deposit. A common concealment is to record a "deposit in transit" on the last day of the month that is later offset with the next month's receipts.

Outstanding-check test.

  1. List outstanding checks at period end from the reconciliation.
  2. Trace each to the check register and to the date and amount in the following statements.
  3. Flag outstanding checks that are listed on the reconciliation but are missing from the register, that have been outstanding more than six months, or that were issued for round amounts at the period end. A check recorded as outstanding but actually cashed (the paid check is in the next statement dated before the period end) shows a deliberately false reconciling item.
  4. Test the reverse: checks dated in the period that cleared in the first days of the next month but are not listed as outstanding. This understates outstanding checks and overstates cash, one signature of window dressing.

Cut-off arithmetic. Adjusted cash equals balance per bank + DIT − OC. If the entity delayed recording $25,000 of checks written in the last days of the month, the book cash balance is overstated by $25,000 at period end, which can hide a loan covenant breach or a negative working-capital position. The proof of cash catches this because the same $25,000 appears in the disbursements column of the following period.

5 Kiting

Check kiting exploits the float, the time between a check being deposited and the funds being collected from the drawee bank, to create a fictitious balance that does not exist. Typically two or more accounts at different banks are used: a check drawn on Account A is deposited in Account B, which is credited provisionally, and the funds are drawn out before the check clears; a check on Account B is then deposited back into Account A to cover the first overdraft, and the cycle repeats and grows. Each bank sees only its own side. A related variant, kiting with wire transfers, uses same-day wires in place of checks to move apparent funds between accounts.

A well-documented example is E.F. Hutton & Co., which in 1985 pleaded guilty to 2,000 counts of mail and wire fraud for a 1980–1982 scheme in which it deliberately overdrew accounts at many banks and covered the overdrafts with checks drawn on other banks, obtaining in effect interest-free loans. Hutton agreed to a $2 million fine and the costs of the investigation, and to restitution to the affected banks.[2] The case shows that kiting is not limited to small businesses; it is a form of unauthorized borrowing.

Detection procedure.

  1. Obtain statements for all accounts held by the entity and by related parties for at least a month on either side of the suspect period.
  2. Build a transfer schedule: list every deposit of a check drawn on another of the entity's accounts, and every check that clears an account and was deposited into another. Fields: drawn-on account, check number, amount, date written, date deposited, date cleared.
  3. Calculate the float days for each item (date cleared minus date deposited). Kites rely on a sustained gap of 2 to 5 days.
  4. Compute the kite balance: the total of items in float on each date. Compare it to the ledger balance of the accounts; a kite shows as a large "balance" supported by uncleared items.
  5. Run statistical screens: deposits and checks of near-equal amounts between the same accounts; check numbers that appear sequentially across the accounts; account balances that hover near zero with large gross activity ("high turnover, low balance"); total debits and credits that are many multiples of the real business revenue.
  6. Reconcile the schedule to the proof of cash. A kite appears as large reconciling items in both DIT and outstanding checks that net to a small number.

Worked example (illustrative). Account A at Bank 1 and Account B at Bank 2 each carry a true balance near $0. On day 1 the owner writes check #101 for $50,000 on A and deposits it in B; B shows $50,000 provisional. On day 2, he writes check #5001 for $50,000 on B (available because of the provisional credit) and deposits it into A so that check #101 clears. On day 3, #5001 clears at B only if another check covers it, and so a larger check on A is deposited in B. The kite grows by the amount needed each time to stay ahead of the float. At the point of collapse the apparent balance, perhaps hundreds of thousands of dollars, vanishes and the banks hold the loss. The statements show check #101 deposited on day 1 but not cleared until day 3, and the equal-amount cross-deposits are the fingerprint.

Criminal exposure arises mainly under 18 U.S.C. 1344 (bank fraud) and the wire and mail fraud statutes. Banks themselves monitor for kiting using “uncollected funds” and large-item reports, so the bank’s own investigation file is a useful source.

6 Lapping and skimming

Skimming is theft of receipts before they are recorded. Lapping is the cover-up method for stealing a customer's payment in an accounts-receivable system: the thief pockets customer A's payment, then applies customer B's later payment to A's account to keep A current, then applies customer C's payment to B, and so on. The “lap” must be sustained indefinitely, since stopping reveals the shortfall.

Detection procedure.

  1. Match deposits to remittances. For a sample of days, compare the deposit slip, the lockbox or mail log and the postings in the receivables ledger by customer name and amount. In lapping, the name on the check (customer B) differs from the account credited (A).
  2. Check dating. Compare the date of the check with the date it was deposited and the date it was posted. Lapping produces a growing delay between receipt and posting.
  3. Run an aging analysis by clerk. Accounts handled by the suspect show frequent short delays and late payments with partial aging; ones that are always “just current.”
  4. Send confirmations (positive, with the statement balance and the date of last payment) to a sample of customers, and have the replies go directly to the examiner, not to the clerk. A mismatch in last-payment date or amount is the best single indicator.
  5. Examine credit memos and write-offs approved or posted by the suspect: they may be used to clear a lapped balance.
  6. Look at the endorsement side of checks. Checks cashed or deposited into a non-company account carry a different bank stamp.

Worked numeric example. The suspect steals Customer A's $1,200 check on 3 March. On 12 March he applies Customer B's $1,500 check (actually owed on B's account) to A's account for $1,200 and records the other $300 as an unapplied credit. On 20 March he applies Customer C's $900 check to B's account, with a further $600 now needed from a later payment. Over months the amount of the lap, the sum of stolen receipts not yet covered, accumulates, so the number of “borrowed” payments climbs. A trace of March deposits shows B's remittance advice dated 12 March but B's account credited on 20 March, and customer B's confirmation shows a balance that disagrees with the ledger.

For skimming of cash sales, there is no ledger entry to trace; compare recorded sales volume to independent measures (inventory depletion, customer counts, utility use, industry gross margin) and run a proof of cash (section 3), looking at a drop in the ratio of cash-to-credit receipts. The ACFE classifies skimming as an “off-book” scheme, which is why its detection depends on indirect evidence.[3]

7 Check-tampering examination

Check tampering is a fraudulent disbursement in which an employee forges or alters a check to pay himself or an accomplice. The ACFE identifies five principal forms:[3]

FormMethodWhat to look for on the paid-check image
Forged makerEmployee signs the authorized signer’s nameSignature differing from the signature card; hesitation, tremor; “traced” look; signature stamp used by an unauthorized person
Forged endorsementEmployee intercepts a legitimate check to a third party and endorses itEndorsement not matching payee; deposited to an account not belonging to the payee; second endorsement by an unknown person
Altered payeePayee changed (often to the employee) after signingDifferent ink or pen pressure; payee line spaced irregularly; residue from chemical removal; payee inconsistent with the vendor master
Authorized makerAn employee with signing authority writes checks for personal usePayees not in the vendor file; round amounts; documentation missing; approvals missing
Concealed checkA check is slipped into a stack the signer approves with an invoice bundleCheck without supporting invoice or purchase order; payee unfamiliar to the signer

Examination procedure.

  1. Obtain the paid-check images (front and back) in the highest available resolution; the original instrument if litigation is likely, since images lose ink and indentation detail.
  2. Sort the population by payee, amount, signer and endorsement. Flag payees that are the employee’s name, near matches, or that appear nowhere in the vendor master or purchase-order system.
  3. Check the endorsement chain. Trace the depositary bank’s routing number and account stamp on the back of each suspect check, and request the deposit account’s signature card and statements through legal process.
  4. Compare check numbers to the check register. Gaps, out-of-sequence numbers, voided checks that nonetheless cleared, and checks cleared but not recorded are all indicators.
  5. Refer questioned documents to a qualified document examiner for handwriting, ink and alteration analysis. See Document Examination and Daubert Standard for the reliability standards to which such testimony is held.
  6. Quantify. Total the fraudulent checks by month; this is the loss figure for the report.

Legal timing. Under UCC § 4-406(f), a customer who fails to discover and report an unauthorized signature or alteration within one year after the statement or items are made available loses the right to assert the claim against the bank.[4] The practical consequence is that account statements should be reviewed promptly, and that an investigation which finds forged items must preserve the claim by notifying the bank in writing well inside that window; shorter periods can be fixed by account agreement. The “positive pay” service, in which the company transmits its issued-check file and the bank matches presented items, is the leading preventive control.

8 Source and application of funds; expenditures method

When books are missing, destroyed or untrustworthy, the examiner reconstructs income indirectly from how money was spent. The source and application of funds analysis (also called cash-flow analysis) lists every identified source of cash and every identified use over a period, and treats the difference as unexplained.

Formula.

Unexplained funds  =  Total applications of funds  −  Total identified sources of funds
Applications  =  living expenses + purchases of assets + debt repayments + deposits to savings
Sources       =  known (reported) income + loan proceeds + asset sales + decrease in cash on hand + gifts

The expenditures method is the same logic applied to a person: if expenditures exceed known sources of funds, the excess is attributed to unreported income. It is the cash-based sibling of the net worth method, which compares changes in net worth instead.

Worked example (illustrative).

ItemAmount
Living expenses (rent, utilities, food, travel, from bank and card records)$86,000
Vehicle purchased for cash$42,000
Mortgage principal repaid$18,000
Increase in savings and brokerage balances$30,000
Total applications$176,000
Reported salary after tax$95,000
Loan proceeds$10,000
Sale of old vehicle$8,000
Decrease in cash on hand (beginning less ending)$5,000
Total identified sources$118,000
Unexplained funds (possible unreported income)$58,000

Because the result is an inference, the examiner must (1) establish an opening position (cash on hand and net worth at the start; in tax prosecutions, the courts have required the government to establish an opening net worth with reasonable certainty and to investigate leads offered by the taxpayer), (2) rule out non-income sources, such as gifts, inheritances, loans and prior savings, and (3) show a likely source, such as the business. Without this, the figure proves only that spending exceeded recorded income. For large cases see Asset Tracing, and for laundering-related uses of the same logic, Money Laundering.

For a business, the equivalent is a cash-flow reconstruction: total bank deposits less transfers, loan proceeds and other non-income deposits gives net business receipts; compare it with reported revenue. Bank deposits method is the common name when the reconstruction starts from deposits. Adjustments needed: remove inter-account transfers (double-counting), refunds, redeposited items (a returned check redeposited), and add cash expenses paid from receipts before deposit.

9 Pitfalls and documentation

  • Double-counting transfers. Failing to eliminate transfers between the entity’s own accounts is the most common error and inflates apparent receipts.
  • Incomplete account coverage. A missing account breaks the proof of cash and makes the unexplained amount meaningless.
  • Cut-off drift. Unless beginning DIT and outstanding checks are carried across, a proof of cash will always show a difference.
  • Treating anomalies as proof. A mismatch is a lead. Interview the preparer (see Forensic Interviewing and Statement Analysis) before concluding that it is fraud; legitimate causes include timing, bank errors and foreign-exchange.
  • Confirmation bias. Run the tests on months you do not suspect as a control; a method that flags every month is measuring noise.
  • Documentation. Keep a working-paper trail: source documents, who obtained them and when, formulas used, reconciling items traced and the conclusion. Reproducible work is what survives cross-examination (see Evidence and Testimony and Forensic Accountant Ethics).

See also: Net Worth Method, Occupational Fraud, Journal Entry and Ledger Testing, Link and Network Analysis, Red Flags.

References

  1. Crain, M., Hopwood, W., Pacini, C. & Young, G. Essentials of Forensic Accounting (AICPA), 2015; Wells, J. T. Principles of Fraud Examination (Wiley), proof-of-cash and reconciliation procedures.
  2. Securities Historical Society. “Hutton Guilty” (1985 news record of E.F. Hutton’s plea).
  3. Association of Certified Fraud Examiners. Occupational Fraud 2024: A Report to the Nations (scheme definitions: skimming, check tampering). acfe.com
  4. Uniform Commercial Code § 4-406, “Customer’s Duty to Discover and Report Unauthorized Signature or Alteration.” Cornell Legal Information Institute. law.cornell.edu

Journal Entry and Ledger Testing

Journal Entry and Ledger Testing
PurposeDetect management override and fraudulent postings in the general ledger
Audit basisPCAOB AS 2401; ISA 240; AU-C 240
Core testsRound-amount, weekend/holiday, after-close, duplicate, gap, rare-user, Benford
ToolsSQL, Excel, Python (pandas), audit analytics packages
Key riskIncomplete or altered data extract

Journal entry testing is the examination of the general ledger’s postings to find entries that are unusual in timing, amount, preparer or account combination, and therefore more likely to be fraudulent or erroneous. It is a required response to the risk of management override of controls in financial-statement audits: PCAOB Auditing Standard 2401 notes that fraud often involves recording inappropriate or unauthorized journal entries throughout the year or at period end, and requires the auditor to test journal entries and other adjustments.[1] For a forensic examiner the same techniques apply at larger scale and with more freedom: the ledger is the place where financial-statement fraud must eventually be recorded and where many occupational-fraud schemes leave a trace. This article is a hands-on guide; for the statistical foundation, see Benford’s Law and Analytical Methods.

1 Data acquisition and completeness

PCAOB inspections have repeatedly found that auditors failed to test the completeness of the population of journal entries.[2] A flawless analysis of an incomplete extract is worthless, so validate before testing.

  1. Define the sources. The population should include the general ledger, subledgers that post by interface (AR, AP, payroll, fixed assets, inventory), manual top-side entries, consolidation and elimination entries, and post-closing adjustments. Fraudulent entries are frequently made in the last category, outside the ERP.
  2. Obtain the extract yourself or witness it. Have IT run the query under your direction, record the query text, server, run time and user, and take a hash of the output file (for example, SHA-256). Preserve it as evidence (see Chain of Custody).
  3. Required fields. Journal ID, line number, posting date, entry (document) date, period, account, amount debit/credit, description, preparer user ID, approver user ID, source/module, manual versus automated flag, reversal flag, and timestamp.
  4. Control totals. Verify (a) total debits equal total credits for every journal and for the file; (b) record count equals the count reported by the system; (c) the opening balance of each account plus the net activity equals the closing balance on the trial balance; (d) the trial balance agrees to the financial statements. Any unreconciled difference means missing or altered data.
  5. Sequence check. Entry numbers should run without gaps (see section 5); gaps may mean deleted or unextracted entries.
  6. Cross-source tie-out. Reconcile subledger totals to control accounts, and sample entries from the source documents to the ledger, to test whether entries outside the extract exist (a “reverse” completeness test).
  7. Document everything so the work is reproducible (see Report Writing).

2 Selection criteria

AS 2401 and the ACFE both list characteristics of entries associated with override. A practical criteria set, with the logic for each, is below.[1][2]

TestCriterionRationale / typical false positives
Round amountsAmount divisible by 1,000 (or ends in 000); entries ending in 999Estimates and plugs are round; genuine invoices rarely are. Rent, loan payments and accruals are legitimate.
Weekend / holidayPosting date on Saturday, Sunday or a company holidayOverride usually avoids supervision. Batch jobs and overseas offices are false positives.
After closeEntry date after period end but posted to the closed period; entries in the last 3 days of the period or the first days after closeUsed to meet targets. Normal close adjustments create many hits.
Rare usersPosted by an executive, an IT/administrator ID, or a user who posts fewer than N entries per yearManagement should rarely post directly.
Unusual account pairsDebit to expense and credit to revenue; debit to cash and credit to an unusual liability; entries to seldom-used, suspense or intercompany accountsRevenue overstatement often debits receivables and credits revenue with an unusual offset.
Missing or vague descriptionBlank, “adjustment,” “per CFO”Concealment.
Large and manualManual entry above materiality thresholdHigh-value manual entries have the greatest impact.
Round-trip / reversalsEntry reversed in the next periodWindow dressing across the period end.
ApprovalPreparer = approver; no approver; approval after postingSegregation of duties failure.
Near-thresholdAmounts just below an approval limit (for example, $9,900 with a $10,000 limit)Avoiding review.

No single criterion is conclusive. The skill is to combine them: an entry that is manual, round, posted on a Sunday by an executive and described as “adjustment” deserves attention in a way that any one of those features does not. A simple scoring approach assigns one point to each criterion met and sorts by score and amount; see also Fraud Detection Analytics and ML Forensics Explainability for model-based ranking.

3 SQL recipes

Assume a table gl_lines(je_id, line_no, post_date, entry_date, period_end, account, debit, credit, descr, preparer, approver, source). Standard SQL (adapt date functions to your engine).

-- Control total: every journal must balance
SELECT je_id, SUM(debit) - SUM(credit) AS diff
FROM gl_lines GROUP BY je_id HAVING ROUND(SUM(debit) - SUM(credit), 2) <> 0;

-- Round-amount entries (divisible by 1,000, nonzero)
SELECT * FROM gl_lines
WHERE (debit > 0 AND MOD(debit, 1000) = 0) OR (credit > 0 AND MOD(credit, 1000) = 0);

-- Weekend postings (SQL Server style: Saturday=7, Sunday=1 under default DATEFIRST)
SELECT * FROM gl_lines WHERE DATEPART(weekday, post_date) IN (1, 7);

-- Entries posted after period end
SELECT * FROM gl_lines WHERE post_date > period_end;

-- Self-approved entries
SELECT * FROM gl_lines WHERE preparer = approver OR approver IS NULL;

-- Rare posters
SELECT preparer, COUNT(DISTINCT je_id) AS n FROM gl_lines
GROUP BY preparer HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT je_id) < 10;

4 Excel and Python recipes

Excel. With dates in column B and amounts in column C: round amounts, =IF(AND(C2<>0, MOD(ABS(C2),1000)=0),1,0); weekend, =IF(WEEKDAY(B2,2)>5,1,0); second digit of the amount, =MID(TEXT(ABS(C2),"0.00"),2,1) (use with care for amounts with a leading zero or decimal point; a more robust approach is to strip the decimal and read characters 1–2); duplicates, =COUNTIFS(D:D,D2,C:C,C2)>1. Sort by a composite score column and filter.

Python (pandas).

import pandas as pd
gl = pd.read_csv("gl_lines.csv", parse_dates=["post_date"])
gl["amt"] = gl["debit"].fillna(0) + gl["credit"].fillna(0)
gl["round"]   = (gl["amt"] % 1000 == 0) & (gl["amt"] > 0)
gl["weekend"] = gl["post_date"].dt.dayofweek >= 5
gl["selfappr"]= gl["preparer"] == gl["approver"]
gl["score"]   = gl[["round","weekend","selfappr"]].sum(axis=1)
flag = gl[gl["score"] >= 2].sort_values(["score","amt"], ascending=False)

Keep the script and the input file hash with the working papers so a second analyst can reproduce the result.

5 Duplicate and gap tests

Duplicates. Duplicate payments and duplicated journal lines are a common error and a common fraud (a paid-twice invoice where the second refund goes to the employee). Run three levels of test, from strict to loose:

  • Exact: same vendor, invoice number and amount.
  • Near: same vendor and amount, different invoice number or dates within 30 days; or same invoice number and different amount.
  • Transposed or formatted variants: invoice numbers differing only by leading zeros, dashes or case (“INV-0045” versus “INV45”); amounts with transposed digits (for example, $4,580 versus $4,850, a difference divisible by 9).
SELECT vendor_id, invoice_no, amount, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM ap_payments GROUP BY vendor_id, invoice_no, amount HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Gaps. A sequence of document numbers, such as journal IDs or check numbers, should be continuous. In SQL, find the missing ranges with a window function:

SELECT je_id AS gap_after, next_id AS gap_before
FROM (SELECT je_id, LEAD(je_id) OVER (ORDER BY je_id) AS next_id
      FROM (SELECT DISTINCT je_id FROM gl_lines) t) s
WHERE next_id - je_id > 1;

Gaps are explained by voided entries, system-reserved numbers or skipped batches, but each needs an explanation from the preparer or the IT audit log. Conversely, a gap that falls inside a period end, or a sudden block of consecutive entries by one user, are leads.

6 Benford first- and second-digit tests

Benford’s Law gives the expected frequency of leading digits in many naturally occurring financial data sets (see Benford’s Law). The first-digit test reads the leading digit, expected frequencies running from 30.1% for digit 1 down to 4.6% for digit 9. The second-digit test uses the second digit, whose distribution is much flatter but still non-uniform:

Second digit0123456789
Expected %11.9711.3910.8810.4310.039.679.349.048.768.50

The second-digit test is more sensitive to rounding and to numbers invented by people (who tend to favour 0 and 5) than the first-digit test, because a made-up number tends to have a plausible first digit but a patterned second.

Procedure.

  1. Extract the field (for example, invoice amounts for one account) and drop zeros, negatives (or analyse separately) and amounts under a floor of, say, $10.
  2. Count the observed frequency of each digit; compute the observed proportion po.
  3. For each digit compute the z-statistic with the continuity correction: 
    z = ( |p_o − p_e| − 1/(2n) ) / sqrt( p_e (1 − p_e) / n )
    A z above 1.96 is significant at 5%, and above 2.58 at 1% (two-sided).
  4. Compute the overall chi-square (9 degrees of freedom for the second digit; critical value 16.92 at 5%) and the mean absolute deviation (MAD).
  5. Drill into any digit that deviates. Do not stop at the chart.

Worked example. A population of n = 2,000 payments shows a second digit of 0 in 15.5% of cases, against an expected 11.97%.
z = (0.155 − 0.1197 − 0.00025) / sqrt(0.1197 × 0.8803 / 2000) = 0.03505 / 0.00726 ≈ 4.83, well above 2.58. The excess is about 71 payments (310 observed versus about 239 expected). Extracting the amounts whose second digit is 0 reveals what they share: for example, many payments between $1,000 and $1,099 clustering to one approver, where a $1,000 approval threshold is being targeted.

Nigrini’s MAD conformity bands for the first-digit test are about 0.006 or below for close conformity, 0.006 to 0.012 acceptable, 0.012 to 0.015 marginal, and above 0.015 nonconformity.[3] Remember that with very large n almost any data set rejects the null; use MAD and the digit-specific z, and use judgment.

Limits. Benford tests are not appropriate for assigned numbers (check numbers, policy numbers), data with built-in minimums or maximums, small populations (n below about 300), or amounts set by price lists. A deviation shows where to look; it proves nothing about intent. See the literature review in Benford’s Law.

7 Sampling approaches

Journal-entry testing generates a large exception list and usually a sample is needed. There are three approaches:

  • Targeted (judgmental) selection. Select all entries meeting the highest-risk combination. This is the primary approach in fraud work, since the point is to look at the suspicious items, not to estimate a rate. The results cannot be extrapolated.
  • Monetary-unit sampling (MUS / PPS). Every dollar in the population has an equal chance of selection, so large entries are naturally more likely. Sampling interval = tolerable misstatement ÷ reliability factor. For example, population $50,000,000, tolerable misstatement $1,000,000, 95% confidence, expected zero errors (reliability factor 3.0): interval = $1,000,000 ÷ 3.0 = $333,333; sample size = $50,000,000 ÷ $333,333 = 150 items. Entries larger than the interval are selected with certainty.
  • Stratified random sampling. Divide the population into strata (for example, by size, user or source) and sample each, so that a rare high-risk stratum is not diluted. Useful when you want a statistically valid estimate of an error rate by group.

For a forensic engagement a discovery sample (to find at least one instance of a fraud when it is thought to exist at a stated rate) is also used: with an expected occurrence rate of 1% and a desired 95% chance of seeing at least one item, the required sample is about 299 items (ln 0.05 ÷ ln 0.99). Note that a clean discovery sample reduces, but does not eliminate, the likelihood of fraud.

8 Following up flagged entries

  1. Pull the support. For each flagged entry obtain the source document (invoice, contract, approval email), and the underlying business reason.
  2. Trace both sides. Follow the debit and the credit to subledgers, bank statements (see Bank Statement and Cash Analysis) and later reversals.
  3. Review the system audit trail. Login records, user-ID changes and edit logs show who actually keyed or changed an entry; shared or generic IDs are themselves a finding.
  4. Interview the preparer and approver using open questions (see Forensic Interviewing and Statement Analysis). Legitimate explanations are common and should be recorded.
  5. Quantify and conclude. Quantify confirmed misstatements by account and period and describe the evidence as confirmed, unexplained, or explained.

Pitfalls: analysing a sample of the data rather than the full population; ignoring reversed entries (a fraud that is booked and reversed leaves no net effect, but changes the interim numbers); testing only the ERP while top-side adjustments live in a spreadsheet; and reporting hit counts without a baseline (compare to prior years and peer entities).

See also: Benford’s Law, Financial Statement Fraud, Revenue and Earnings Manipulation Tests, Red Flags, Digital Forensics.

References

  1. Public Company Accounting Oversight Board. AS 2401, Consideration of Fraud in a Financial Statement Audit. pcaobus.org
  2. PCAOB. Audit Focus: Journal Entries (staff publication, January 2025). pcaobus.org
  3. Nigrini, M. J. Benford’s Law: Applications for Forensic Accounting, Auditing, and Fraud Detection (Wiley), 2012.

Link and Network Analysis

Link and Network Analysis
PurposeReveal relationships among people, companies, accounts and events
Core stepsCollect, standardize, resolve entities, link, visualize, measure, verify
Typical outputsLink chart, relationship (association) matrix, graph metrics, match report
Common toolsSpreadsheet/SQL joins, Python (networkx, rapidfuzz), Neo4j, Gephi, Maltego, i2 Analyst’s Notebook
Frequent useVendor-employee conflicts, shell vendors, bid rigging, beneficial ownership

Link and network analysis is the investigative discipline of turning scattered records into a structured map of who or what is connected to whom, and then reading the map for patterns that the individual records do not show. In fraud work it is the standard method for finding undisclosed conflicts of interest, corruption and fictitious-vendor schemes; in OSINT it connects public-record entities across registries. The method has three layers: (1) entity resolution, deciding that two records describe the same real-world person, company or account; (2) linking, recording relationships such as shared addresses, phone numbers, officers or payments; and (3) analysis, using charts, matrices and graph metrics to find clusters, bridges and anomalies. This article is a practical guide. The examples below use invented data; real investigations must confine analysis to lawful data sources (see OSINT Ethics).

1 The workflow

  1. Define the question. “Does any employee have a financial interest in a vendor?” or “Which shell companies share control with this contractor?” A defined question prevents an unreadable “hairball” chart.
  2. Collect structured data. Employee master, vendor master, accounts-payable history, bank account files, corporate registry extracts, procurement records, phone and email logs, public filings.
  3. Standardize fields (section 2).
  4. Resolve entities and create a link table with one row per relationship, including its source and the date it was observed.
  5. Visualize and measure (sections 6 and 7).
  6. Verify each link with an independent source, and grade confidence. A link is a lead until corroborated (the same discipline as the intelligence cycle).
  7. Report with the evidence trail, not just the picture.

2 Entity resolution

Entity resolution (also called record linkage or deduplication) decides whether records refer to the same entity. The standard pipeline has five stages:[1]

  1. Standardize. Uppercase; strip punctuation; expand or contract abbreviations consistently; split names into parts; drop legal suffixes (LLC, INC, CORP, LTD) into a separate field; normalize addresses to postal standards (for example, “1200 North Market Street, Suite 400” becomes “1200 N MARKET ST STE 400”); convert phone numbers to digits only, then to a single format (E.164); remove spaces and hyphens from bank account and tax identifier fields.
  2. Block. Comparing every record with every other is quadratic. Group candidate pairs by a cheap key (the first three letters of the name, postal code, last four digits of phone) so that only records in the same block are compared.
  3. Compare. For each candidate pair, compute similarity per field (section 3).
  4. Score and decide. Combine the field scores with weights (for example, tax ID 0.4, bank account 0.3, address 0.2, name 0.1), and classify as match, possible match or non-match using thresholds. The possible-match band goes to a human reviewer.
  5. Cluster. Link matched pairs transitively (if A=B and B=C then A=B=C) into entity clusters, with care: transitive closure can chain unrelated entities together through one false match.

Strong versus weak identifiers. Treat unique identifiers (government tax ID, bank account and routing number, registered company number) as strong; names and addresses are weak. A match on a strong identifier is much more probative than a name match: a name match can be a common surname, while a shared bank account number is extremely unlikely to be a coincidence between an employee and a vendor.

3 Fuzzy-matching techniques

TechniqueWhat it measuresBest forWeakness
Exact match after standardizationEqualityTax ID, account number, phoneMisses typos
Levenshtein (edit) distanceNumber of single-character insertions, deletions, substitutionsTypos in names and addressesSensitive to word order
Jaro-WinklerSimilarity weighted toward matching prefixes (0 to 1)Personal namesOver-scores short strings
Token set / JaccardOverlap of words, ignoring orderCompany names, addressesCommon words dominate
Phonetic (Soundex, Metaphone)Sound-alike codesSpelling variants of namesEnglish-centred; coarse
N-gram / TF-IDF cosineShared character sequences, weighted by rarityLarge-scale name searchNeeds tuning

Worked example. Vendor master lists “ACME CONSULTING LLC” (19 characters) and the employee’s spouse’s business registry entry reads “ACME CONSULTNG LLC” (18 characters). The Levenshtein distance is 1 (one missing letter), so normalized similarity = 1 − 1/19 = 0.947. After removing the legal suffix the strings are “ACME CONSULTING” and “ACME CONSULTNG”, with distance still 1, similarity 1 − 1/15 = 0.933. A token-set Jaccard score on {ACME, CONSULTING} and {ACME, CONSULTNG} is 1/3 = 0.33 because one token mismatches, which shows why character-level and token-level measures are combined. A reasonable rule: character similarity of 0.90 or higher on a name and an exact match on a second field goes to review.

In Python:

from rapidfuzz import fuzz
fuzz.ratio("ACME CONSULTING", "ACME CONSULTNG")         # ~96.6
fuzz.token_set_ratio("ACME CONSULTING", "CONSULTING ACME")  # 100

Remember that a high name similarity is common among legitimate businesses (“Smith & Sons Plumbing” appears across the country). Set the threshold from a labelled sample, not from a guess.

4 Vendor-employee matching

The classic internal-fraud application. The Association of Certified Fraud Examiners reports that billing schemes through shell or conflicted vendors are among the most common asset-misappropriation and corruption forms (see ACFE Report to the Nations). The test is a series of joins between the employee master and the vendor master (and the remit-to files):

Match fieldJoin ruleStrength
Bank account numberVendor account = employee payroll direct-deposit accountVery strong
Tax ID / SSN / EINVendor TIN = employee SSN or an employee-controlled EINVery strong
Street address (normalized)Vendor address = employee home address; including unit-less variantsStrong
Phone numberVendor phone = employee home or mobile, or the same number shared among several vendorsStrong
EmailSame email, or same domain registered to a personal addressMedium
Surname / nameFuzzy name match to vendor owner or officerWeak (relatives are named differently)
PO Box / mail dropVendor address = known mail-drop or registered-agent addressWeak; use in combination
-- Vendors whose address matches an employee address (after both are standardized)
SELECT v.vendor_id, v.vendor_name, e.employee_id
FROM vendor_master v
JOIN employee_master e ON v.addr_std = e.addr_std;

-- Vendors sharing a bank account with any other vendor or employee
SELECT acct_no, COUNT(DISTINCT payee_id) AS n_payees
FROM (SELECT acct_no, vendor_id AS payee_id FROM vendor_bank
      UNION SELECT acct_no, employee_id FROM payroll_bank) t
GROUP BY acct_no HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT payee_id) > 1;

Dates matter. A vendor created three days after an employee changed address, or paid only while the employee held an approval role, is a stronger indicator than a standing match. Also compare the vendor-creation user with the approver of the first payment. Matches should be tested against employee relationship-disclosure forms, since a disclosed and approved interest is a control success, not a fraud. Relatives often have different surnames, so extend to emergency-contact and beneficiary data only where lawful and permitted by the employer’s policy and local privacy law.

5 Shell vendor detection

A shell (fictitious) vendor is an entity created to receive payments for goods or services never delivered. The detection approach combines master-data attributes with payment behaviour:[2]

  • Master-data signals: PO box or residential address; no phone, or a phone that goes to a mobile or voice-over-IP number; missing tax ID or a TIN that fails validation; generic names with initials or sequential names (“ABC Services,” “ABD Services”); address shared with several vendors or with a registered-agent address; recently incorporated; no website or a template website; vendor name resembling a legitimate supplier with a minor change.
  • Payment signals: invoice numbers that are sequential with no gaps (a real vendor with other customers skips numbers); invoices just below the approval limit; round-dollar invoices; a single customer; vague service descriptions (“consulting,” “professional services”); invoices on weekends; payments approved by the same person, or sequenced right after vendor creation; no purchase order or receiving report.
  • Behaviour signals: payments drawn out quickly with the vendor account later closed; payments to a bank account in a different state or country from the vendor address; vendors with payments and no contact history.

Test procedure. (1) Run the master-data screens; (2) run Benford and duplicate screens on the vendor’s invoices (see Journal Entry and Ledger Testing); (3) check the vendor against corporate registry, tax authority status and sanctions lists; (4) site-visit or confirm the vendor’s existence by independent contact details (not those on the invoice); (5) trace payments to the receiving account and to the ultimate beneficiary (see Asset Tracing). Bid rigging yields analogous patterns: bidders sharing addresses, phone numbers, typos, or document metadata (see Anti-Corruption OSINT).

6 Relationship matrices and link charts

An association (relationship) matrix is a grid with entities on both axes; a cell records whether a link exists, or its type or strength. It is the oldest link-analysis tool and still the best for dense data because it shows every pair, including the absences. A link chart draws entities as nodes and relationships as lines; it communicates better but becomes unreadable above a few dozen nodes.

Vendor V1Vendor V2Vendor V3Employee E1
Vendor V1—Same phone—Same address
Vendor V2Same phone—Same bank acct—
Vendor V3—Same bank acct——
Employee E1Same address———

Read the matrix: V1 is tied to employee E1 by address, and to V2 by phone, while V2 is tied to V3 by bank account, so all three vendors are a single connected cluster reaching an employee, although no direct E1 to V3 link exists. That transitive chain is the finding a flat vendor-versus-employee join misses. Best practice for charts: use different edge types or colours for different link types, show confidence (solid for verified, dashed for inferred), keep a source reference on every edge, and filter to the cluster of interest.

7 Graph analysis

Once relationships are stored as a graph (a node table and an edge table), standard network measures give investigators a prioritized view:

  • Connected components. Groups of nodes reachable from one another. Each component with a mixture of employees and vendors is a lead.
  • Degree. The number of links of a node. A bank account used by 14 “different” vendors has degree 14.
  • Betweenness centrality. The share of shortest paths between other nodes that pass through a node; high values identify brokers, controllers or intermediaries.
  • Community detection (for example, the Louvain algorithm). Splits a large graph into densely connected groups, helpful in large data sets such as money-flow networks.
  • Shortest path. The minimum chain of links between two named entities, answering “how is X connected to Y?”
  • Bipartite projection. From a vendor-to-address graph, derive a vendor-to-vendor graph in which vendors sharing an address are linked.
import networkx as nx
G = nx.Graph()
G.add_edge("V1","E1", kind="address"); G.add_edge("V1","V2", kind="phone")
G.add_edge("V2","V3", kind="bank")
for comp in nx.connected_components(G):
    if any(n.startswith("E") for n in comp) and any(n.startswith("V") for n in comp):
        print("mixed cluster:", sorted(comp))
nx.betweenness_centrality(G)   # V1 and V2 score highest

Graph databases such as Neo4j make the same queries (for example, a path of up to four hops between an employee node and a vendor node) declarative, and are useful when the graph runs to millions of edges, as in money-laundering transaction analysis and cryptocurrency tracing. Machine-learning link prediction extends the approach; see AI Fraud Detection Platforms, but explainability requirements in court (see ML Forensics Explainability) mean the underlying links must always be shown.

8 Open-source data for links

External data lets an examiner extend links beyond internal records: corporate registries and their open aggregations (for example, OpenCorporates), securities filings on SEC EDGAR for officers and directors, court dockets, property and UCC filings, domain registration and archive data, and leaked-data collections such as the ICIJ Offshore Leaks Database, which links entities, officers, intermediaries and addresses from published investigations.[3] Treat leak-derived records as leads: appearing in a database does not itself show wrongdoing, and the ICIJ itself states this on the database. Methods and tool inventories are covered in OSINT Tools, OSINT Disciplines and Asset Tracing.

9 Pitfalls and verification

  • False positives from common values. Shared addresses at apartment buildings, shared registered-agent addresses, shared call-centre phone numbers and common surnames produce spurious links. Exclude high-frequency values (an address shared by hundreds of entities) or down-weight them.
  • Transitive chaining. One wrong merge can fuse two unrelated clusters. Review cluster merges and keep the pairwise evidence.
  • Stale data. Links must be dated; an address that matched in 2019 may not be current.
  • Confirmation bias and over-reading. A tidy chart feels like proof. Record confidence ratings and look actively for disconfirming links.
  • Privacy and legal limits. Restrict to lawful, authorized data; handle personal data of private individuals with care; follow employment and data-protection law (see OSINT Ethics).
  • Presentation. Courts and boards need the underlying records. Attach each edge to its source document (see Evidence and Testimony and Report Writing).

See also: Occupational Fraud, Red Flags, Bank Statement and Cash Analysis, Fraud Detection Analytics, Anti-Corruption OSINT.

References

  1. Christen, P. Data Matching: Concepts and Techniques for Record Linkage, Entity Resolution, and Duplicate Detection (Springer), 2012; Fellegi, I. & Sunter, A. “A Theory for Record Linkage,” Journal of the American Statistical Association 64 (1969).
  2. Association of Certified Fraud Examiners. Occupational Fraud 2024: A Report to the Nations (billing and corruption schemes). acfe.com
  3. International Consortium of Investigative Journalists. Offshore Leaks Database. offshoreleaks.icij.org

Revenue and Earnings Manipulation Tests

Revenue and Earnings Manipulation Tests
Quantitative modelsBeneish M-Score (1999); Altman Z-Score (1968)
M-Score threshold> −1.78 flags probable manipulator (Beneish’s 8-variable model)
Procedural testsCut-off, returns and credit memos, side-letter inquiry, percent-of-completion estimates, reserve rollforwards
Accounting frameworkASC 606 / IFRS 15 (five-step revenue model)
Named caseSunbeam Corp. (1996–1998)

Revenue and earnings manipulation tests are the quantitative and procedural techniques used to decide whether a company’s reported sales and profits have been inflated, smoothed or shifted between periods. Improper revenue recognition is the most common technique in financial statement fraud, and the ACFE reports that the median loss in such cases is far larger than in any other branch of the fraud tree. This article is a hands-on companion to the descriptive treatment in Financial Statement Fraud: it gives formulas, a fully worked numerical example, thresholds, and the sequence of audit-style tests for each scheme. Models are screening tools. They produce a probability or a flag that directs where to look and do not establish intent, which is a matter for evidence and interviews.

1 Beneish M-Score

Messod Beneish’s The Detection of Earnings Manipulation (Financial Analysts Journal, September/October 1999) estimated a probit model on 74 manipulating firms from 1982 to 1992 against a larger matched population, using eight variables that capture either distortions in financial statements caused by manipulation or the preconditions that prompt it. At a cut-off of −1.78 the model identified roughly half of the manipulators before public discovery.[1] The variables compare year t (the year under test) with year t−1.

IndexFormulaCoefficientMeaning of a high value
DSRI Days sales in receivables(Receivablest / Salest) ÷ (Receivablest−1 / Salest−1)+0.920Receivables growing faster than sales: possible revenue inflation
GMI Gross marginGross margint−1 ÷ Gross margint+0.528Margin deterioration (>1): incentive to manipulate
AQI Asset quality[1 − (current assets + PP&E) / total assets]t ÷ samet−1+0.404More assets in intangible or deferred costs: possible cost capitalization
SGI Sales growthSalest ÷ Salest−1+0.892High growth creates pressure to sustain it
DEPI Depreciation[Dep / (Dep + PP&E)]t−1 ÷ samet+0.115Slower depreciation rate: lengthened useful lives
SGAI SG&A expense(SG&A / Sales)t ÷ samet−1−0.172Rising overhead ratio (a negative coefficient in the model)
LVGI Leverage[(Current liabilities + total debt) / total assets]t ÷ samet−1−0.327Rising leverage
TATA Total accruals to total assets(Income from continuing operations − cash flow from operations) ÷ total assetst+4.679Earnings not backed by cash

The score is:

M = −4.84 + 0.920·DSRI + 0.528·GMI + 0.404·AQI + 0.892·SGI
        + 0.115·DEPI − 0.172·SGAI + 4.679·TATA − 0.327·LVGI

Thresholds. A score above −1.78 flags the firm as a probable manipulator under the cut-off Beneish used in the paper. Some practitioners use a more conservative cut-off such as −2.22, which catches more manipulators at the cost of more false alarms; this is a convention that varies by source, so state the threshold used and why. A neutral company has all indices near 1.0 and TATA near zero, which gives M of about −2.48 (see the worked example below for the arithmetic).

The model has a five-variable reduced form in later academic work; this article uses the original eight-variable version.

2 Worked M-Score example

The following data are fictitious, for one manufacturing company (in $ thousands).

ItemYear t−1Year t
Sales1,0001,300
Receivables120208
Cost of goods sold600830
Current assets400520
PP&E300310
Total assets1,0001,250
Depreciation4038
SG&A150182
Current liabilities200300
Long-term debt200260
Income from continuing ops—90
Cash flow from operations—10

Step 1: indices.

  • DSRI = (208/1,300) ÷ (120/1,000) = 0.16 ÷ 0.12 = 1.333
  • Gross margin: year t−1 = 1 − 600/1,000 = 0.400; year t = 1 − 830/1,300 = 0.3615; GMI = 0.400 ÷ 0.3615 = 1.106
  • AQI: t−1 = 1 − (400+300)/1,000 = 0.300; t = 1 − (520+310)/1,250 = 0.336; AQI = 1.120
  • SGI = 1,300 ÷ 1,000 = 1.300
  • DEPI: t−1 = 40/(300+40) = 0.1176; t = 38/(310+38) = 0.1092; DEPI = 1.077
  • SGAI = (182/1,300) ÷ (150/1,000) = 0.14 ÷ 0.15 = 0.933
  • LVGI: t−1 = (200+200)/1,000 = 0.400; t = (300+260)/1,250 = 0.448; LVGI = 1.120
  • TATA = (90 − 10) ÷ 1,250 = 0.064

Step 2: contributions. 0.920 × 1.333 = 1.227; 0.528 × 1.106 = 0.584; 0.404 × 1.120 = 0.452; 0.892 × 1.300 = 1.160; 0.115 × 1.077 = 0.124; −0.172 × 0.933 = −0.161; 4.679 × 0.064 = 0.299; −0.327 × 1.120 = −0.366.

Step 3: sum. M = −4.84 + 1.227 + 0.584 + 0.452 + 1.160 + 0.124 − 0.161 + 0.299 − 0.366 = −1.52. This exceeds both −1.78 and −2.22, so the company is flagged.

Step 4: interpret. The biggest drivers are DSRI (receivables up 73% on sales up 30%), SGI (30% growth) and the accruals term (net income of $90 versus cash from operations of only $10). Together these point the examiner to revenue recognition and receivables. The next steps are the procedural tests below: confirm the large receivables, test year-end cut-off, review post-period returns and credit memos, and read the sales contracts for side terms. For neutral comparison, if all indices equal 1.0 and TATA = 0, M = −4.84 + 0.92 + 0.528 + 0.404 + 0.892 + 0.115 − 0.172 − 0.327 = −2.48.

A spreadsheet implementation takes about a dozen formulas; keep each input traceable to the filed financial statements (for example, SEC EDGAR 10-K data) and recompute from restated figures where restatements exist. See Analytical Methods and Fraud Detection Analytics for the wider toolkit.

3 Altman Z-Score and pressure

Edward Altman’s Z-Score (1968) predicts financial distress, not manipulation, but distress is a classic pressure element of the fraud triangle, and firms near the grey zone have strong incentives to inflate earnings or avoid covenant breaches. For a public manufacturer:

Z = 1.2·X1 + 1.4·X2 + 3.3·X3 + 0.6·X4 + 1.0·X5
X1 = working capital / total assets        X2 = retained earnings / total assets
X3 = EBIT / total assets                   X4 = market value of equity / total liabilities
X5 = sales / total assets

Zones: Z above 2.99 is “safe,” 1.81 to 2.99 the grey zone, below 1.81 distress. Altman also published variants: Z′ for private firms (coefficients 0.717, 0.847, 3.107, 0.420, 0.998 with book value of equity in X4; cut-offs 2.9 and 1.23) and Z″ for non-manufacturers and emerging markets (6.56, 3.26, 6.72, 1.05 plus a constant of 3.25; cut-offs 2.6 and 1.1).

Example using the same fictitious company in year t with retained earnings of 300, EBIT of 110 and a market value of equity of 600: working capital = 520 − 300 = 220, so X1 = 0.176; X2 = 300/1,250 = 0.240; X3 = 110/1,250 = 0.088; total liabilities = 560, so X4 = 600/560 = 1.071; X5 = 1,300/1,250 = 1.040. Z = 0.211 + 0.336 + 0.290 + 0.643 + 1.040 = 2.52, in the grey zone. Combined with an M-Score above threshold, this profile (growth, rising leverage, weak cash conversion and a score that is not safely above 2.99) is the profile that most justifies a detailed look.

4 Revenue cut-off testing

Under ASC 606 (and IFRS 15) revenue is recognized when control of goods or services transfers to the customer, applying a five-step model: identify the contract, identify performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate it, and recognize revenue as obligations are satisfied. Cut-off testing checks that transactions are recorded in the right period. Procedure:

  1. Identify the period-end date and the control point for the product (shipment, delivery or acceptance, according to contract terms such as FOB shipping point or FOB destination).
  2. Select the last 10 to 20 shipments recorded before period end and the first 10 to 20 recorded after (or a stratified sample covering a window of several days either side).
  3. Trace each to the bill of lading, carrier record, proof of delivery and the invoice; compare shipment date and invoice date to the revenue-recognition date in the ledger.
  4. Flag revenue booked before shipment or delivery as required by the terms, shipments dated after year-end but invoiced before, and invoices backdated.
  5. Reverse-test: review shipments in the first weeks of the next period for revenue that belongs in the closing period (understatement), and for credit memos, returns and cancellations that reverse the sales recorded in the last days.
  6. Analyse the distribution of sales by day in the last month. A hockey-stick spike (for example, 40% of the quarter’s sales in the last three days) is a red flag; compare with prior periods and seasonality.
  7. Quantify cut-off error: error amount = sales recorded early × margin (for profit effect).

Related analytical tests: gross margin by month, DSO trend (DSO = receivables ÷ sales × days in period), and sales returns as a percentage of sales in the 30 to 60 days after period end.

5 Channel stuffing

Channel stuffing is shipping more product to distributors or retailers than end customers demand, often with discounts, extended payment terms or return rights, to pull sales into the current period. It is not necessarily illegal if sales are genuine and fully disclosed; it is fraud when the revenue is not properly recognized (for example, rights of return or side agreements negate the sale) or its effect on future results is concealed. In the SEC’s case against Sunbeam, executives were found to have used discounts and other inducements to pull merchandise sales into 1997 that otherwise would have occurred later, without disclosing that revenue growth was being achieved at the expense of future results; the SEC stated that at least $60 million of the $189 million in reported 1997 pre-tax earnings from continuing operations came from the accounting fraud.[2]

Detection tests.

  • DSO and DSRI jump in the stuffing quarter; receivables concentrated in a few distributors.
  • Sell-in versus sell-through. Compare shipments to distributors with the distributors’ sales to end customers (obtain third-party data or confirm directly). Channel inventory in days of sales rising well above prior levels is the core indicator.
  • Returns and credits spike in the next quarter; allowance for returns not increased in step with sales.
  • Unusual terms: extended payment terms, price protection, right-to-return, guaranteed sale, or consignment-like side letters. Read the contracts and email around quarter-end; ask sales staff, outside the manager’s presence, about oral promises (see Forensic Interviewing and Statement Analysis).
  • Customer confirmation asking explicitly about side agreements, return rights and payment contingencies.
  • Timing of shipments concentrated in the last days; carriers’ pick-up logs and freight bills are independent evidence.

6 Bill-and-hold

A bill-and-hold arrangement bills a customer for goods which the seller retains in its warehouse. Under ASC 606-10-55-83, revenue may be recognized only if all four criteria are met: the reason for the arrangement must be substantive (for example, the customer requested it); the product must be identified separately as belonging to the customer; the product must be ready for physical transfer to the customer; and the entity cannot have the ability to use the product or direct it to another customer.[3] The seller must also still evaluate whether it has other performance obligations, such as custodial services.

Tests. (1) Query the sales ledger for invoices with no shipping document, or with a carrier-pickup date after the invoice date. (2) Walk the warehouse (count and observe) and compare physical inventory with inventory records at year-end: finished goods that are on the books as sold but physically present. (3) Obtain the customer’s written request and acknowledgement and check that it pre-dates the sale. (4) Confirm with the customer that the goods were ordered, accepted and are owned by it. (5) Check whether the goods shipped shortly after period end and whether the customer paid or returned them. In Sunbeam, the SEC found that bill-and-hold sales were recognized in violation of the applicable accounting rules.[2]

7 Percent-of-completion and over-time revenue

For long-term contracts, revenue is recognized over time as work is performed. Under ASC 606 the typical measure is an input method such as cost-to-cost:

% complete = costs incurred to date ÷ total estimated costs at completion
Revenue to date = % complete × total contract price
Revenue this period = revenue to date − revenue recognised in prior periods

Worked example. A $10.0 million contract has estimated total costs of $8.0 million. At year-end, costs to date are $4.0 million, so completion is 50% and revenue to date is $5.0 million, giving a gross profit of $1.0 million. If management understates the estimated total cost at $7.0 million, completion becomes 4.0/7.0 = 57.1% and revenue to date is $5.71 million, so profit recognized rises to $5.71 − $4.0 = $1.71 million, an overstatement of $0.71 million from the estimate alone. The estimate is a judgment, which is why it is the favoured lever.

Tests. Compare the estimated cost to complete with actual cost-to-complete on finished similar contracts; analyse margin fade (profit recognized early, with margins declining as the contract closes); test whether claims and change orders were included in revenue before approval; examine whether costs were charged to the wrong contract to hit target percentages; inspect engineering and project-manager reports against the accounting estimate; and recalculate completion from independent physical progress measures. Large unbilled receivables (“costs and estimated earnings in excess of billings”) rising faster than billings point to over-recognition.

8 Cookie-jar reserves

A cookie-jar reserve is an over-accrued liability (restructuring, returns, warranty, bad debts, litigation) built in good years and released into income in weak years to smooth earnings. The SEC’s Sunbeam case also reported that executives used cookie-jar reserves among their earnings-management tactics.[2]

Tests.

  1. Reserve rollforward. Beginning balance + provisions − actual charges (utilization) ± releases = ending balance, for each reserve for several years. Persistent excess of provisions over charges, or a large release with no matching change in underlying exposure, is the indicator.
  2. Ratio trends. Allowance for doubtful accounts as % of receivables; warranty reserve as % of sales; returns reserve as % of sales. A fall in the ratio without a change in experience is a release in disguise.
  3. Timing. Releases in the quarter in which the company would otherwise miss analyst consensus; look at the effect on earnings per share relative to the miss.
  4. Restructuring charges that include costs of future operations, or reserves for plans never carried out.
  5. Compare to peers and to historical loss rates to see if the reserve at a given date was reasonable.

9 Limits and pitfalls

  • False positives. High-growth, acquisitive or restructuring firms often score high without any fraud; the M-Score was calibrated on a particular sample (manufacturers in 1982 to 1992), and misclassification of honest firms is substantial. Treat a flag as a reason to examine the specific accounts.
  • Data quality. Use as-originally-reported figures for detection and restated figures to validate; mismatched definitions across data providers change the indices.
  • Sector fit. Banks, insurers and firms without receivables or gross margin need modified models.
  • Accounting changes. The adoption of ASC 606 and changes in lease accounting alter ratios without any manipulation; adjust for them.
  • Intent. Error and aggressive-but-lawful accounting produce the same numbers as fraud. Establishing intent requires documents, communications and testimony (see Evidence and Testimony), and the scheme analysis in Case Studies and Major Fraud Case Studies.

Pair these tests with ledger-level analytics (Journal Entry and Ledger Testing) and with the red-flag catalogue in Red Flags.

See also: Financial Statement Fraud, Fraud Triangle, Benford’s Law, Forensic Accounting, Report Writing.

References

  1. Beneish, M. D. “The Detection of Earnings Manipulation.” Financial Analysts Journal 55(5), 24–36, 1999. cfainstitute.org
  2. U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Litigation Release No. 17710, SEC v. Sunbeam executives (Dunlap and Kersh settlement). sec.gov
  3. Financial Accounting Standards Board. ASC 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, including 606-10-55-83 (bill-and-hold arrangements).
  4. Altman, E. I. “Financial Ratios, Discriminant Analysis and the Prediction of Corporate Bankruptcy.” Journal of Finance 23(4), 1968.
