Forensic Interviewing and Statement Analysis

Forensic Interviewing and Statement Analysis
ScopeProcedures for planning, conducting, analysing and documenting interviews in fraud inquiries
Models coveredCognitive interview; PEACE; strategic use of evidence; admission-seeking sequence
Analysis toolsBaselines; CBCA and reality monitoring; verbal-content review
Legal limitsUpjohn warnings; Miranda; Garrity; Weingarten; recording-consent laws
Evidence baseAverage lie-detection accuracy about 54% (Bond & DePaulo, 2006)

Forensic interviewing is the structured questioning of witnesses, custodians, informants and suspects in a fraud or financial-crime inquiry, together with the analysis and documentation of what they say. The general principles (rapport, active listening, open questions) are set out in Investigative Interviewing. This article goes deeper into the how: the step-by-step structure of the main evidence-based methods, the practical use of baselines and verbal-content analysis, the admission-seeking sequence used in internal fraud cases, the written record, the legal limits on each step, and what the research says about the limits of detecting deception. The overarching message is that interviews are an evidence-gathering tool whose products must be tested against documents (see Evidence and Testimony), not a lie detector.

1 Planning an interview

  1. Sequence. Interview from the periphery to the centre: third-party witnesses and records custodians first, then process owners, then people with direct involvement, and last the principal subject. Each earlier interview yields facts and documents which narrow the subject’s room for manoeuvre.
  2. Know the documents. Prepare an exhibit binder with copies (not originals) of every document you may show, ordered by the interview agenda. Prepare a timeline and a list of points the subject can confirm, correct or explain.
  3. Define objectives. Write them as questions the interview should answer (“Who authorised vendor X?”, “What is the subject’s access to the payment system?”), not as the confession sought.
  4. Decide who attends and what status applies. Two interviewers (one leads, one records and watches); legal counsel involvement; whether the person is a witness, a subject or in custody, because the status determines the warnings and rights that apply (section 8).
  5. Logistics. Neutral, private room; no interruptions; a clear record plan (recording, notes). Agree on breaks, and do not hold interviews so long that they become coercive.

2 The cognitive interview

The cognitive interview (CI) was developed by Ronald Fisher and Edward Geiselman in the 1980s to improve witness recall using principles of memory research, and the “enhanced” version adds communication and rapport components. A meta-analysis of 57 articles (65 experiments) by Memon, Meissner and Fraser (2010) found a large and significant increase in correct details compared with standard interviews, with only a small increase in errors and no difference in confabulation rates.[1] It is the method of choice for cooperative witnesses, such as a clerk who watched the controller override a control, and for victims.

StepWhat the interviewer doesExample in a fraud inquiry
1. Build rapport and set the ground rulesExplain that the witness is the expert on what happened; instruct the witness to say “I don’t know” and to correct the interviewer; ask the witness not to guess“I wasn’t there, so I need you to tell me. If I get something wrong, tell me.”
2. Context reinstatementAsk the witness to mentally recreate the setting (place, mood, sounds, what they were doing) before recalling“Think back to the Friday close. Where were you sitting, who was around, what was on your screen?”
3. Open narrative / report everythingInvite a free account without interruption; encourage reporting of partial or trivial details“Tell me everything about how that invoice was approved, even small details.”
4. ProbingFollow up on images and details the witness mentioned, using the witness’s own words, and open questions“You mentioned a phone call. Tell me more about that call.”
5. Reverse order / change perspectiveAsk for the events in a different order or from another person’s point of view (use with caution; perspective-taking can raise error)“Start with the last thing that happened and walk backwards.”
6. Summary and closeSummarise the account and invite corrections; ask whether anything was left out; leave contact details“Is there anything I should have asked but did not?”

Pitfalls: leading or suggestive questions during probing contaminate memory; interrupting the narrative reduces the amount recalled; showing a document too early replaces recollection with recognition.

3 The PEACE model in practice

PEACE was introduced in England and Wales in 1992 to replace confession-oriented questioning following a series of miscarriages of justice, and is now the basis of non-accusatory interviewing in many jurisdictions.[2] It stands for Planning and preparation, Engage and explain, Account, Closure, and Evaluation. Its principle is that the interviewer’s job is to obtain an accurate and complete account, not a confession.

  1. Planning and preparation: aims, legal framework, evidence, topics, and a plan for each stage (section 1).
  2. Engage and explain: greet, build rapport, state the purpose, explain the process and the person’s status and rights, and explain the ground rules.
  3. Account: obtain the person’s own account using the cognitive interview (free recall first), then probe for detail and clarify, then challenge any inconsistency with evidence (“help me understand”), never with accusation or deception.
  4. Closure: summarise, check for corrections, give the person an opportunity to add anything, explain what happens next.
  5. Evaluation: assess what the interview achieved against the objectives and against other evidence; identify follow-up work; review the interviewer’s own performance.

The strength of the evidence for the information-gathering approach comes from comparative research. A meta-analytic review by Meissner and colleagues in the Journal of Experimental Criminology (2014) concluded that the available data support the effectiveness of an information-gathering style of interviewing suspects, while cautioning that the number of independent samples was small.[3] That is a more modest claim than that accusatorial methods always produce false confessions, but it supports a practical conclusion: where reliability matters more than speed, as in fraud cases that will be tested in court, the information-gathering approach is the safer default. The UN Special Rapporteur’s 2021 “Principles on Effective Interviewing for Investigations and Information Gathering” (the Mendez Principles) make the same recommendation a matter of international standards (see also International Forensic Standards).

4 Strategic use of evidence

The Strategic Use of Evidence (SUE) technique, developed by Par Anders Granhag and Maria Hartwig, manages when the interviewer discloses documents. Guilty and innocent subjects differ in how they respond to a question when they do not know what evidence exists: a person trying to hide something tends to avoid statements the evidence might contradict, whereas an innocent person tends to describe events freely.[4] The procedure:

  1. List the key pieces of evidence (an email, an access log, a bank record) and decide the order in which to disclose them.
  2. Ask open questions about the topic first (“Tell me about your dealings with Vendor X”) and commit the subject to a version of events without revealing the document.
  3. Ask specific, evidence-related questions that pin down details the document can test (“Did you ever visit their office? When was the last time you spoke with the owner?”).
  4. Disclose the evidence gradually, least incriminating first, and then ask the subject to explain any contradiction.
  5. Record the shifts in the account (admits, changes, denies) and compare them to the documents afterwards.

The value is in producing checkable statements. A subject who denies knowing a vendor and is later shown a phone log has produced a contradiction with physical evidence, which is worth far more than an impression of nervousness.

5 Baselines and verbal-content analysis

Behavioural baseline. At the start, spend five to ten minutes on neutral topics with known answers (job history, daily routine, how the department works). Note how the person speaks (fluency, detail, pace, directness) and behaves when relaxed. Later changes can mark topics for follow-up, but they are never evidence of lying by themselves, since a topic may simply be more stressful, embarrassing or complicated.

Verbal-content review (practical). A defensible review looks at what is in the account, not how it “sounds”:

  • Level of detail and verifiability: does the account contain checkable specifics (names, times, locations, documents) and are they correct when checked?
  • Consistency: within the account, across repeated tellings, and with the documents. Over-consistent (word-for-word) repetition can reflect rehearsal; ordinary memory varies in peripheral details but is stable on central ones.
  • Omissions and gaps: events that are skipped, time that is not accounted for, or sudden compression (“then I did the usual stuff”).
  • Changes in terms: shifts in how the subject refers to a person, thing or action (from “the vendor” to “my friend”).
  • Unsolicited information and spontaneous corrections, which are characteristic of genuine memory.

Two research-derived frameworks structure the review. Criteria-Based Content Analysis (CBCA), originally developed for statements by child witnesses, scores a statement against about 19 content criteria (logical structure, unstructured production, quantity of details, contextual embedding, reproduction of conversation, unexpected complications, and others). Reality monitoring assumes that memories of real events contain more sensory, contextual and spatial details than imagined ones. Both produce better-than-chance classification in laboratory settings, but neither is accurate enough to decide a case, and both are affected by the narrator’s verbal ability and the type of event.

Cautions about “statement analysis” systems. Popular schemes that rely on pronoun use, changes in tense or hedging words (such as Scientific Content Analysis, SCAN) have been tested and have not performed. In one controlled study of 117 participants who each wrote a true and a fabricated statement, SCAN criteria did not distinguish the two, leading the authors to say that its use in its current form should be discouraged.[5] A fair statement is that such indicators can prompt a question but cannot be reported as findings. Cognitive-load approaches (asking for a reverse-order account, or for unexpected questions, or asking the subject to draw a scene) are more promising because they increase the difference in the information that truthful and deceptive people produce.

6 The admission-seeking sequence

In internal fraud investigations the ACFE’s Fraud Examiners Manual teaches a graduated sequence in which the examiner moves from general questions to an admission-seeking stage only after the evidence has been gathered. The version below is summarised from that general approach; it is distinct from the confrontational Reid nine-step method discussed in Investigative Interviewing, but its final stage is still accusatory, so it carries more false-confession risk than information-gathering and requires safeguards.

StagePurposeTypical content
1. IntroductorySet tone, explain purpose, establish identity and baselineNon-threatening questions; the interviewer’s role; confidentiality limits
2. InformationalObtain facts about the process, controls and peopleOpen questions about the process, who has access, what changed
3. AssessmentTest whether the person is likely to be involved; separate witnesses from suspectsQuestions about control awareness, willingness to cooperate, who might have done it; observation against baseline
4. ClosingObtain the final account; rule in or outSummary; “is there anything else?”
5. Admission-seeking (only for a probable perpetrator)Obtain a truthful admission and the detailsPresent the evidence; minimise the moral gravity without promising leniency; seek the admission; then obtain details only the culprit would know; scope (other involvement, others, amounts); then a written statement

Safeguards. (1) Never present fabricated evidence; courts in some jurisdictions tolerate limited police deception, but in a corporate setting it creates legal and credibility risks and is incompatible with the PEACE model. (2) Never promise leniency, threaten, or imply a promise of non-prosecution which the organization cannot grant. (3) Avoid lengthy sessions, sleep or food deprivation, and take extra care with juveniles, persons with intellectual disability, and people under the influence. (4) Get corroborating detail: a reliable admission contains information that was not given to the subject and that checks against independent evidence (the location of the cash, the account number). Research on false confessions shows that persuasion can yield confessions that are factually wrong, which is why the admission must be tested, not simply recorded.

7 Documentation and written statements

  • Record or note-take. Where lawful and appropriate, audio-record the entire interview with the subject informed; otherwise, a second interviewer takes verbatim notes. Keep original notes (see Chain of Custody); a clean typed memorandum should be written as soon as possible and be reviewed against the notes.
  • Memorandum of interview. Contains date, time start and end, location, those present, status and warnings given, a summary of what was said (not a verbatim claim unless it is a transcript), the documents shown, any statements offered by the subject, and breaks. State the facts; leave out interviewer conclusions about credibility and personal opinions.
  • Written statement (if taken). In the subject’s own words, in first person, covering who, what, when, where and how; each page initialled; corrections initialled; a closing line stating that it is voluntary and that it has been read and is true; signature and date, with the interviewer as a witness. Do not draft it for the subject unless needed, and have the subject read it aloud or silently in full.
  • Preserve exhibits shown to the subject, marked with an exhibit number and the subject’s own comments.
  • Report. Feed the results into the report with the interview as one source among others, stating where the account was corroborated, where it was contradicted, and where it was not tested.

8 Legal limits

RuleWhen it mattersPractical consequence
Upjohn warning (Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U.S. 383 (1981))Company counsel (or investigators acting for counsel) interviewing employeesThe Supreme Court held that a company’s privilege can cover communications between company counsel and non-management employees made to enable counsel to give legal advice; it is the company’s privilege, not the employee’s.[6] The interviewer should state that counsel represents the company and not the employee, that the interview is privileged but the privilege belongs to the company, which may waive it and disclose it to authorities, and that the employee must keep the discussion confidential. Record that the warning was given.
Miranda warningsCustodial interrogation by government officersPrivate investigators are generally not bound, but their conduct can be attributed to the state if they act at the direction of law enforcement.
Garrity / KalkinesPublic employees compelled to answer on pain of dismissalCompelled statements may not be used in a later criminal prosecution; interviewers must know which warning applies before the interview.
Weingarten rights (NLRB v. J. Weingarten, Inc., 1975)Unionised employees in interviews that may lead to disciplineThe employee may request union representation; ignoring the request creates labour-law exposure.
Recording-consent lawsAny recording of telephone or in-person interviewsSome U.S. states and many countries require consent of all parties; follow the strictest applicable rule.
Whistleblower and anti-retaliation provisionsInterviews of those who reported concernsDo not discourage or retaliate against a reporter or ask the employee to waive protected disclosure rights.
Data-protection and employment lawCross-border and employee interviewsNotice, proportionality and right-of-access rules can apply to notes and recordings.

Because these rules differ by jurisdiction and facts, engage counsel before interviewing in any matter that may lead to litigation or prosecution; see also Forensic Accountant Ethics.

9 What the research says about detecting deception

Large bodies of research find that people, including professionals, are poor at telling lies from truths by watching and listening.

  • Accuracy near chance. Bond and DePaulo’s 2006 meta-analysis of 206 documents and 24,483 judges found an average accuracy of 54%: lies were correctly classified as deceptive 47% of the time and truths as non-deceptive 61% of the time (a “truth bias”).[7]
  • Cues are weak. Hartwig and Bond (2011), in Psychological Bulletin, argued that lie-catchers fail because the behavioural cues that actually differ between liars and truth-tellers are few and weak, and the cues that people believe indicate lying (gaze aversion, fidgeting) do not.[8]
  • Confidence does not track accuracy, and experience in law enforcement or investigations does not reliably improve accuracy; training in cue-reading may increase confidence without improving it.
  • Context effects. Interviewers who expect guilt ask more guilt-presumptive questions, and then see confirming behaviour in the answers (“self-fulfilling prophecy”).
  • Polygraphs. They measure arousal and are not a direct measure of deception; U.S. courts largely exclude results, and a 2003 National Research Council review concluded that polygraph accuracy in screening is insufficient for security use (see Daubert Standard and Forensic Validity Crisis for the admissibility framework).

The implication for practice is to shift effort from detecting lies to eliciting verifiable information and then checking it. Methods that increase cognitive load, ask for detail and use evidence strategically give a better chance of identifying deception than demeanour does; the final test is always the document trail. For a discussion of cognitive and organizational biases in investigators themselves, see Forensic Validity Crisis and CSI Effect.

See also: Investigative Interviewing, Evidence and Testimony, Occupational Fraud, Report Writing, Forensic Practitioner Burnout.

Business Valuation and Damages Quantification

Valuation & Damages
ApproachesIncome, market, asset (cost)
Core income modelDiscounted cash flow (DCF)
Damages modelBut-for (actual versus counterfactual)
StandardsIVS (effective 31 Jan 2025); AICPA VS Section 100; Rev. Rul. 59-60
Standards of valueFair market value; fair value; investment value
RelatedLitigation Support and Damages

Business valuation estimates what a business or ownership interest is worth under a stated definition of value at a stated date; damages quantification estimates the monetary difference between what happened and what would have happened but for a wrongful act. The two disciplines share their tools: the lost profits of a business are often measured by comparing its value, or its cash flows, in the actual world with the same measures in a counterfactual world. For the forensic accountant they matter in fraud and commercial cases (what did the victim lose?), in divorce and bankruptcy (what is the business worth, and is the owner understating it?), in shareholder disputes and in insurance claims. This article concentrates on the valuation methods; the wider practice of expert work, discovery and testimony is in Litigation Support and Damages, and admissibility in Daubert Standard.

1 Standards and premises of value

A valuation is meaningless until the standard of value is fixed. In U.S. tax practice, fair market value is defined in Revenue Ruling 59-60 as the price at which property would change hands between a willing buyer and a willing seller, neither under compulsion and both having reasonable knowledge of relevant facts; the ruling lists eight factors to consider, including the nature and history of the business, the economic and industry outlook, book value and financial condition, earning capacity, dividend-paying capacity, goodwill and other intangibles, prior sales of the stock, and the market price of comparable public companies.[1] Fair value is a statutory or legal standard, used in shareholder appraisal and oppression statutes and in some divorce jurisdictions, and may exclude marketability or minority discounts. Investment value reflects the benefits to a particular buyer. Choosing the wrong standard is the most common source of disagreement between experts. The premise of value (going concern versus liquidation) and the level of value (controlling versus minority, marketable versus non-marketable) must also be stated.

Professional standards govern the work. The AICPA's Statement on Standards for Valuation Services (VS Section 100, issued 2007 and effective for engagements accepted on or after 1 January 2008) applies to CPA members performing engagements that estimate value, and distinguishes a valuation engagement, which results in a conclusion of value (a single amount or a range), from a calculation engagement, where the client and valuer agree in advance on limited procedures.[2] The International Valuation Standards Council's IVS, effective 31 January 2025, contain seven general standards (IVS 100 Valuation Framework, 101 Scope of Work, 102 Bases of Value, 103 Valuation Approaches, 104 Data and Inputs, 105 Valuation Models, 106 Documentation and Reporting) and asset-specific standards.[3] Other credentialing bodies publish their own standards, and courts weigh compliance with them when assessing an expert's reliability.

2 The three approaches

ApproachIdeaCommon methodsTypical weaknesses
IncomeValue equals the present value of future economic benefitsDCF; capitalisation of earnings or cash flowSensitive to forecasts and the discount rate; forecasts may be prepared by interested parties
MarketValue is inferred from prices of comparable businesses or transactionsGuideline public companies; precedent transactions; industry rules of thumbComparables rarely identical; private-company data thin; size and liquidity adjustments needed
Asset (cost)Value equals adjusted value of assets less liabilitiesAdjusted net asset value; replacement costPoor for earnings-driven businesses; may omit unrecorded intangibles

Valuers normally apply more than one approach and reconcile the results, with the reasoning for weighting disclosed. The normalisation of historical financial statements precedes all three: adjusting for owner compensation above or below market, one-off items, personal expenses run through the business, related-party transactions at non-market prices, and accounting-policy differences. In a dispute, normalisation adjustments are often the most contested part of the analysis, because each adjustment moves the earnings base on which the final value rests. For the quality-of-earnings review that precedes it, see Analytical Methods.

3 DCF and the discount rate

A discounted cash flow model projects free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) — operating profit after tax, plus non-cash charges, minus capital expenditure and increases in working capital — for an explicit forecast period (commonly five years), adds a terminal value capturing cash flows beyond that period, and discounts all amounts to the valuation date. The terminal value is usually calculated with the Gordon growth formula, TV = FCFn × (1 + g) / (r − g), where g is the long-run growth rate and r the discount rate. Because terminal value often supplies more than half of the enterprise value, the choice of g (normally bounded by long-run nominal growth in the economy) and of r drives the conclusion.

The discount rate must match the cash flow being discounted. For FCFF it is the weighted average cost of capital (WACC): the cost of equity weighted by the equity share of capital plus the after-tax cost of debt weighted by the debt share. The cost of equity for a private company is commonly estimated with a build-up or CAPM approach: risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium, plus a size premium and a company-specific risk premium for factors such as customer concentration, key-person dependence and forecast risk. Each premium requires documentary support; unsupported company-specific premiums are a standard target of cross-examination. The discount rate also has to be consistent with the forecast: an optimistic management forecast with a mid-range discount rate overstates value, while a haircut forecast with an additional risk premium double counts risk.

Capitalisation of earnings is a single-period shortcut: value equals normalised sustainable cash flow divided by (r − g). It suits stable businesses and is also the usual way damages experts convert a permanent loss of annual profit into a lump sum.

Discounts and premiums. A discount for lack of marketability (DLOM) reflects the difficulty of selling a private interest; a minority discount reflects lack of control; a control premium reflects the added value of control. Courts differ on their application. In Delaware statutory appraisal, for example, the Supreme Court has held in DFC Global Corp. v. Muirfield Value Partners (2017) and Dell, Inc. v. Magnetar Global Event Driven Master Fund (2017) that the deal price from a robust sale process in an efficient market deserves heavy, if not dispositive, weight in determining fair value, without creating a presumption in its favour.[4] Divorce courts in many states exclude marketability and minority discounts when valuing a spouse's interest in a business that will be retained, and some distinguish enterprise goodwill (attached to the business, divisible) from personal goodwill (attached to the individual, treated differently by state); both rules are jurisdiction-specific and should be checked locally.

4 But-for analysis and lost profits

The but-for (or before-and-after, yardstick) method compares the plaintiff's actual financial results with a reconstructed counterfactual: what would revenue, costs and profits have been without the wrongful act? The damages expert follows a disciplined sequence:

  1. Define the wrong and the period. Identify the breach, fraud or interference, its start date, the end of the loss period and the valuation date.
  2. Build the counterfactual revenue. Use pre-event trend, backlog and contracts, market growth, comparable firms (a yardstick or control group unaffected by the wrong), and customer-level evidence. Growth assumptions must be consistent with the company's capacity and the market.
  3. Measure the actual outcome from audited or reliably reconstructed accounts, and adjust for unrelated factors (recession, supply shocks) so that the model isolates the damage from the wrong.
  4. Deduct avoided costs. Lost profit, not lost revenue, is the usual measure: subtract the variable costs the plaintiff did not incur because the sales never occurred, and consider whether fixed costs are truly fixed.
  5. Mitigation. Credit amounts the plaintiff earned, or reasonably could have earned, by mitigating.
  6. Discount and add interest. Express past losses with prejudgment interest where permitted and future losses at present value using a rate that reflects the risk of the lost cash flows. Where the loss is permanent, a diminution-in-value approach (value before minus value after) may be used instead, taking care not to double count lost profits and lost value.

The model has to measure only the harm attributable to the liability theory. In Comcast Corp. v. Behrend, 569 U.S. 27 (2013), the Supreme Court refused class certification because the plaintiffs' damages model measured damages from four theories of antitrust impact when only one had survived, so it could not show damages were measurable on a class-wide basis for that theory.[5] The principle applies broadly: an expert whose counterfactual is not tied to the legal theory risks exclusion (see Daubert Standard).

In a fraud case, the loss of the victim is often measured differently: out-of-pocket loss (what was paid minus value received), benefit-of-the-bargain (value as represented minus value received) or, for the perpetrator's gain, disgorgement. Tracing and quantification of gain use the net worth method and asset tracing.

5 Business-interruption insurance claims

Business-interruption (BI) coverage indemnifies an insured for lost income following insured physical damage. Claims commonly turn on three policy concepts: the measure of loss (a "gross earnings" or "profits" form), the indemnity period (generally commencing on the date of the damage and ending when the property is repaired, rebuilt or replaced, or at the end of a stated maximum), and extra expense incurred to reduce the loss.[6] The forensic accountant's job is to quantify the difference between projected and actual sales during the indemnity period, deduct non-continuing (avoided) expenses, add covered continuing expenses and extra expenses, and test the claim against policy language.

The standard steps are:

  • Establish the baseline from at least two to three years of monthly history, adjusting for seasonality, trend and known pending contracts.
  • Project but-for sales over the indemnity period and subtract actual sales; where a recovery period (an "extended period of indemnity") is bought, estimate the ramp-up back to normal.
  • Apply the gross-profit margin or the policy's formula, then adjust for expenses that stopped.
  • Reconcile with mitigation: make-up production, alternative sites and sales recaptured after reopening reduce the loss.
  • Test the claim for fraud indicators: inflated pre-loss forecasts, growth stories that appear after the event, personal expenses claimed as continuing costs, backdated contracts, and customers that cannot be traced.

Disputes about proper baseline and about the point at which the loss ceased to be caused by the insured event are the most common causes of litigation. Insurers' fraud units apply the same red-flag logic used in other contexts.

6 Matrimonial and shareholder disputes

Divorce

Valuation of a closely held business in a divorce serves equitable or community-property distribution. The central contested questions are the standard of value (fair market value or fair value), the treatment of marketability and minority discounts, whether goodwill is personal or enterprise, the normalisation of owner compensation (a spouse who pays himself $80,000 when a replacement manager would cost $200,000 is increasing apparent profits, while the reverse understates them), and the avoidance of double dipping, where the same stream of earnings is counted once as business value and again as income for support. The valuer must also be alert to manipulation, discussed in Hidden Assets in Divorce and Bankruptcy: deferral of revenue, acceleration of expenses, and loans to related parties shortly before the valuation date.

Shareholder disputes

Minority shareholders may seek relief through statutory appraisal (dissenting shareholders in a merger), oppression or dissolution statutes, or derivative suits. Most of these use "fair value", typically defined by statute and case law rather than by the valuation profession. Statutory buy-out valuations require a valuer to separate the value of the company from the conduct complained of, to establish the correct valuation date (e.g. the date of the filing, or the date before the oppressive act), and to consider whether discounts apply. Evidence of manipulation of results by controlling shareholders, such as excessive compensation, related-party charges and diversion of opportunities, is quantified as an addback to normalised earnings, a step closely linked to occupational fraud and conflict-of-interest analysis (see the fraud tree).

7 Worked numeric example

The following illustrates mechanics only; every input is hypothetical.

A. Enterprise value by DCF

A services company has forecast free cash flow to the firm of $1.00M, $1.10M, $1.20M, $1.30M and $1.40M in years 1–5. The cost of equity is built up as 4.0% risk-free + (1.10 beta × 5.5% equity risk premium) + 3.0% size premium + 1.5% company-specific premium = 14.55%. After-tax cost of debt is 7.0% × (1 − 25%) = 5.25%. With 70% equity and 30% debt, WACC = 0.70 × 14.55% + 0.30 × 5.25% = 11.76%, rounded to 11.8%. Long-term growth is 3%.

YearFCFF ($M)Discount factor at 11.8%Present value ($M)
11.000.8940.894
21.100.8000.880
31.200.7160.859
41.300.6400.832
51.400.5730.802
Sum of explicit-period PV4.267
Terminal value = 1.40 × 1.03 / (0.118 − 0.03) = 16.386; PV = 16.386 × 0.5739.382
Enterprise value13.65

Terminal value contributes about 69% of enterprise value. Sensitivity (same cash flows): at 10.8% and 3% growth, EV is about $15.45M; at 12.8% and 3%, $12.21M; at 11.8% and 2% growth, $12.61M; and at 11.8% and 4%, $14.95M. A one-point movement in the discount rate or the growth rate therefore changes the answer by roughly $1.2M to $1.8M, which is why the support for those inputs matters more than the arithmetic.

B. From enterprise value to equity

If the company has $2.0M of debt net of cash, equity value is 13.65 − 2.00 = $11.65M for a controlling interest. If a 15% discount for lack of marketability is applicable under the governing standard, the non-marketable equity value is $11.65M × 0.85 ≈ $9.90M. Under a standard that excludes discounts, the figure stays at $11.65M. The $1.75M gap is entirely a legal question.

C. But-for lost profits

A manufacturer had $10.0M of revenue in the year before a supplier's breach. The but-for forecast grows revenue at 8% (the pre-breach trend, confirmed by industry growth): $10.80M, $11.66M and $12.60M over the three-year loss period. Actual revenue was $9.0M, $9.5M and $10.2M. Lost revenue is $1.80M, $2.16M and $2.40M, totalling $6.36M. Variable costs avoided equal 55% of revenue, so the incremental margin is 45% and lost profit is $0.81M, $0.97M and $1.08M, totalling $2.86M. Discounting at 10% at year-ends gives a present value of about $0.74M + $0.81M + $0.81M = $2.35M. If the defendant shows that a quarter of the shortfall resulted from an unrelated market downturn, the opposing expert would reduce the loss accordingly. This is the sort of adjustment that Comcast requires to be modelled explicitly.

8 Fraud-sensitive review of a valuation

Investigators reviewing another expert's valuation, or a party's financial statements for a valuation, check for these signs of manipulation or error:

  • Forecasts prepared by an interested party after the dispute began, with growth far from history and no backlog support.
  • Owner compensation, related-party rent or management fees changed shortly before the valuation date.
  • Unusual timing: revenue deferred, customer deposits increased, bonuses accelerated, large capital expenditures just before the date.
  • Terminal growth near or above the economy's long-run growth, or discount rates with large unsupported company-specific premiums.
  • Comparable companies of very different size or business mix, or a lone "rule of thumb" used without reconciliation.
  • Gaps between the tax returns, bank deposits and financial statements, tested with bank statement analysis and, where necessary, the net worth method.
  • Undisclosed entities or accounts, found through beneficial-ownership research.

A valuation report should also state its limiting conditions, the information relied on, and the extent of independent verification, consistent with Report Writing and ethical standards on objectivity.

See also: Litigation Support and Damages, Net Worth Method, Hidden Assets in Divorce and Bankruptcy, Daubert Standard, Evidence and Testimony, Forensic Accounting.

Litigation Support and Damages

Litigation Support & Damages
RolesConsulting expert; testifying expert; special master or receiver's accountant
Core questionWhat are the plaintiff's damages, caused by whom, and where did the money go?
Federal rulesFRCP 26(a)(2)(B), 26(b)(4)(D), 64; FRE 702
Key damages casesStory Parchment (1931); Comcast v. Behrend (2013)
Key remedies caseGrupo Mexicano v. Alliance Bond Fund (1999)
Tracing rulesLowest intermediate balance; pro rata; FIFO (Clayton's Case)

Litigation support is the application of accounting, financial and investigative skills to disputes. A forensic accountant may quantify damages (what the plaintiff lost), measure a fraud's size, trace misappropriated money, or evaluate another side's expert. The work sits where forensic accounting meets procedure: the numbers must be right, but they also must be admissible, explainable to a lay fact-finder, and tied to a legal theory. Admissibility standards are covered in Daubert Standard and courtroom practice in Evidence and Testimony; this article concentrates on the substantive methods.

1 Roles and engagement structure

A consulting expert advises counsel and is generally shielded from discovery by Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(b)(4)(D) absent exceptional circumstances; work product flows through the attorney (the Kovel structure, commonly used to protect accountants assisting lawyers). A testifying expert must serve a written report under Rule 26(a)(2)(B) containing a complete statement of all opinions and their basis, the facts or data considered, exhibits, qualifications including publications from the preceding ten years, a list of cases in which the expert testified in the previous four years, and compensation. Drafts and attorney communications are protected only in part (Rule 26(b)(4)(B)–(C)), so the expert's file must be organized on the assumption it will be read by an adversary. Ethical constraints, independence, and conflicts are discussed in Forensic Accountant Ethics, and report structure in Report Writing.

2 Damages concepts

  • But-for world. Damages compare the plaintiff's actual position to the position it would have occupied but for the wrongful act. Every method is a way of constructing that counterfactual.
  • Fact versus amount. Under Story Parchment Co. v. Paterson Parchment Paper Co., 282 U.S. 555 (1931), the fact of damage must be established with reasonable certainty, but the amount may be estimated with reasonable approximation once a wrong is shown, particularly where the defendant's conduct created the uncertainty.
  • Model fit. In class actions, Comcast Corp. v. Behrend, 569 U.S. 27 (2013), requires that a damages model measure only damages attributable to the theory of liability that survives. A model that cannot isolate the harm from the wrong is vulnerable.
  • Causation, foreseeability and mitigation. Damages must be caused by the defendant; the plaintiff must take reasonable steps to limit loss, and avoided costs are deducted.
  • Time value. Past losses may carry prejudgment interest (rate set by statute, contract or court discretion); future losses are discounted to present value at a rate reflecting risk.

3 Lost-profits methodologies with a worked example

MethodHow the but-for is builtTypical evidence
Before-and-afterPlaintiff's own pre-wrong performance projected forwardHistorical financials, trend analysis
Yardstick / benchmarkComparable firms or plaintiff's other unitsIndustry data, competitor filings
Market-shareShare of a growing or stable marketMarket studies, sales data
Direct (contract/customer)Specific lost orders or contractsBids, pipelines, customer testimony

Lost profit is lost revenue minus the incremental (avoided) costs, not net income and not revenue. Worked example (illustrative): a distributor's but-for revenue is $2,000,000 per year after a competitor's tortious interference, and actual revenue is $1,200,000. Lost revenue is $800,000. Costs that vary with sales are 55% ($440,000 avoided); fixed costs are unchanged. Annual lost profit is $800,000 − $440,000 = $360,000. Over three future years at an 8% discount rate, using an end-of-year convention, present value is $360,000 × [1 − 1.08−3] / 0.08 = $360,000 × 2.5771 = about $927,800. Sensitivities are then shown: if the variable-cost ratio were 65%, annual lost profit would be $280,000 and the present value about $721,600. The defence expert will test the growth assumption, the cost behavior, and whether other causes (a recession, a lost key employee) explain part of the revenue shortfall; the plaintiff's expert should regress or otherwise control for those factors. Business valuation overlaps when the wrong destroys enterprise value rather than income.

4 Quantifying fraud losses

4.1 Specific identification

Where records survive, the loss is the sum of identified fraudulent transactions. Procedure: (1) obtain the full ledger or bank population and confirm completeness; (2) code each suspect transaction to source documents (invoice, approval, receiving record, bank item); (3) separate fraudulent from legitimate transactions with the same payee; (4) deduct value actually received; (5) add consequential components the law allows. Example: payments to a sham vendor total $412,600 over 31 months; the company can document goods of $58,000 actually received. Gross diversion is $412,600, and net direct loss is $354,600; investigation cost (say $46,000), interest and any restitution received are then layered on in separate lines so the court can accept or reject each.

4.2 Sampling and extrapolation

When the population is large, test a statistical sample and extrapolate with a confidence interval. Suppose 10,000 invoices were paid to a suspect vendor group; a random sample of 200 shows 14 fraudulent ones (7.0%), averaging $3,100. The standard error is about √(0.07 × 0.93 / 200) = 1.8 percentage points, so a 95% interval for the rate is roughly 3.5% to 10.5%, or about 346 to 1,054 invoices; the point estimate is 700 invoices, or $2,170,000, and the interval runs from about $1.07 million to $3.27 million (ignoring a finite-population correction). Experts should disclose the sampling frame, randomization method and interval, since a bare point estimate invites a Daubert challenge.

4.3 Indirect methods

When books are destroyed or the fraudster controlled them, income can be reconstructed indirectly—the net worth method, cash-expenditure and bank-deposit methods—by comparing known income sources to assets accumulated and money spent. These establish unexplained wealth but need corroboration to attribute it to the defendant's fraud. Pattern evidence from data analytics (see Fraud Detection Analytics) can help define the scheme's boundaries, and occupational fraud loss statistics provide context but are not a substitute for case-specific calculations.

4.4 Reconstructing the scheme period

Determine the earliest and latest affected dates by testing before and after the first known fraudulent item: take the vendor's first invoice, the date of the control change, and the date of the last payment. Unexplained margins (for example gross margin falling from 41% to 33% in exactly the scheme period while sales are stable) can help cross-check the extrapolated loss.

5 Tracing in civil asset recovery

To recover specific property or impose a constructive trust, a claimant must identify the fraud proceeds in the defendant's hands, even after they have been transferred, commingled or converted. Tracing is an equitable exercise with several competing conventions when proceeds mix with the wrongdoer's own money:

  • Lowest intermediate balance rule (LIBR). The claimant's traceable interest can never exceed the lowest balance reached after the deposit, because money spent is presumed to be the wrongdoer's own first; later deposits of the wrongdoer's own funds do not replenish the trust. This is the most claimant-friendly of the common rules for what remains in the account, and it is reflected in the Restatement (Third) of Restitution and Unjust Enrichment § 59.
  • Pro rata (proportionate) tracing. Each withdrawal is treated as drawn proportionally from the account's mixed contents; used, for example, in English law in Barlow Clowes where multiple victims share a pooled fund.
  • First in, first out (FIFO). From Devaynes v Noble (Clayton's Case) (1816): withdrawals are treated as drawn from the earliest deposits. It is often used to allocate among innocent investors in a Ponzi scheme; see Cunningham v. Brown, 265 U.S. 1 (1924), the original Ponzi receivership.

Worked example (illustrative). An account holds $20,000 of the defendant's own money. On 1 March $100,000 of fraud proceeds is deposited (balance $120,000). On 10 March $90,000 is withdrawn for a vehicle (balance $30,000). On 20 March the defendant deposits $40,000 of salary (balance $70,000). On 25 March $50,000 is withdrawn for a down payment (balance $20,000).

RuleFraud funds remaining in accountReasoning
LIBR$20,000Lowest balance after 1 March is $20,000; later deposits do not restore the claim
FIFO$0First withdrawal consumes the $20,000 own money then $70,000 of fraud funds; the second consumes the remaining $30,000 of fraud funds plus $20,000 of salary
Pro rataabout $7,143Fraud share 83.3% on 10 March: $75,000 spent, $25,000 left; share of $70,000 balance is 35.7%; $17,857 spent on 25 March; $7,143 left

The same tracing also identifies the vehicle and the down payment as products of the fraud, which may give the claimant a proprietary claim in those assets (and any appreciation) rather than merely a personal claim. The forensic accountant produces a day-by-day ledger of the account, a source-and-application schedule, and a flow chart for each commingled account, with the rule applied stated explicitly because the court, not the accountant, chooses the legal rule. For the investigative side of finding accounts and assets see Asset Tracing, Cryptocurrency Tracing and Money Laundering.

6 Prejudgment remedies

Because defendants often dissipate assets before judgment, plaintiffs seek early security. Rule 64 of the Federal Rules lets a federal court use the state-law remedies available for seizing property to secure satisfaction of a judgment, such as attachment, garnishment and replevin. State statutes vary; some, like Connecticut's prejudgment remedy statute (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-278a et seq.), require a hearing and a finding of probable cause that the plaintiff will prevail. In contrast, a federal court's authority to issue a preliminary injunction freezing assets in a purely money-damages action is narrow after Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo, S.A. v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc., 527 U.S. 308 (1999), which held that such relief was not available in the traditional equity jurisdiction of the federal courts where the plaintiff claims no lien or equitable interest in the assets. The decision leaves room where the plaintiff asserts an equitable claim (constructive trust, or tracing of identifiable proceeds), which is one reason tracing evidence matters at the very start. Other tools include receiverships, lis pendens, and, in common-law jurisdictions outside the United States, freezing injunctions (Mareva orders). Government actions use parallel routes: civil and criminal forfeiture and restitution under statutes such as 18 U.S.C. §§ 981 and 3663A. The expert's declaration at this stage usually presents a preliminary tracing schedule and an estimate of dissipation risk (rapid transfers, offshore wires, conversions to crypto).

7 Critiquing the other side's expert

A rebuttal expert checks: whether the but-for scenario relies on unsupported growth rates; whether avoided costs were ignored; whether double counting occurred (lost profit and lost enterprise value for the same period); whether the discount rate matches the risk of the cash flows; whether the extrapolation sample was random; and whether data were cherry-picked. Under Federal Rule of Evidence 702 as amended in December 2023, the proponent must show it is more likely than not that the opinion meets the reliability requirements, strengthening such challenges. Cross-examination preparation is covered in Evidence and Testimony; the reliability problems of forensic disciplines more generally appear in Forensic Validity Crisis.

See also: Daubert Standard, Evidence and Testimony, Net Worth Method, Asset Tracing, Forensic Accountant Ethics, Public Sector Fraud and Improper Payments.

  3. Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo, S.A. v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc., 527 U.S. 308 (1999). justia.com

Hidden Assets in Divorce and Bankruptcy

Hidden Assets
SettingsDivorce (equitable distribution); bankruptcy; judgment enforcement
Core techniquesLifestyle analysis; net worth tie-in; tracing; discovery and third-party subpoenas
Criminal law18 U.S.C. §§ 152, 157 (up to 5 years each)
Civil recovery11 U.S.C. §§ 544, 548, 727; Uniform Voidable Transactions Act
Bankruptcy toolsRule 2004 examination; § 341 meeting; examiner (§ 1104(c))

Hidden assets are property, income or ownership interests that a party conceals from a court, a spouse, a trustee or creditors in order to reduce what they must pay or share. Concealment occurs wherever someone's financial disclosure decides an outcome: in divorce, where the marital estate is divided; in bankruptcy, where the estate is distributed to creditors; and in judgment enforcement, where a debtor moves assets beyond reach. The forensic accountant's task is to test the disclosed picture against independent evidence. The methods are those of Asset Tracing and the Net Worth Method, applied under the distinct legal rules summarised below. This article is general information about U.S. law and practice and is not legal advice; family-law rules in particular vary by state.

1 Common concealment methods

  • Understating income — unreported cash receipts, deferred bonuses and commissions, paying personal expenses through a business, or routing pay to a relative.
  • Moving assets — transfers to relatives or friends ("holding" arrangements), to new entities, trusts or foreign accounts, or conversion into hard-to-trace assets such as cash, jewellery, art, collectibles or cryptocurrency.
  • Inflating liabilities — fictitious or related-party loans, backdated notes and overpayment of friendly creditors, so that net worth looks smaller.
  • Prepaying or overpaying — large payments to tax authorities or lenders that will be refunded or returned after the case.
  • Business manipulation — delaying contracts and receivables, accelerating expenses, or diverting opportunities to a related entity (section 8).
  • Titling and nominee ownership — holding property in the name of another person or a shell company; the same techniques seen in money laundering.
  • Dissipation — spending marital funds on a paramour, gambling or extravagant items before or during the dispute, sometimes called marital waste.

2 Lifestyle analysis

A lifestyle analysis (also called a lifestyle or standard-of-living analysis) reconstructs what a household actually spends and compares it with its disclosed income. It tabulates income and expenses from bank, credit-card and brokerage statements, then examines the discrepancy: spending that exceeds known after-tax income points to unreported income, to withdrawals from undisclosed accounts, or to borrowing that should be visible as a liability.[1] Typical steps are:

  1. Define the baseline period, usually the two to five years before the filing, and a comparison period after separation or filing.
  2. Collect statements for every account, card and loan, including those in the names of children, parents or entities, as far as discovery permits.
  3. Categorise spending (housing, travel, education, gifts, cash withdrawals, luxury purchases) and annualise it.
  4. Compare with sources: pay stubs, tax returns, K-1s, distributions and loan proceeds. Spending in excess of sources equals the "unexplained" amount.
  5. Test the sudden changes: new accounts, higher cash use, large single purchases, changes in who pays for shared expenses, and a falling lifestyle that coincides with the dispute while real quality of life seems unaffected.

The analysis is persuasive in court because it uses the party's own financial footprint and, where the spouse shared household finances, the opposing party's own recollection of living standards. Its limit is that gifts, inheritances, prior savings and loans may legitimately explain gaps, so the unexplained amount is a lead and not a finding. See also Bank Statement and Cash Analysis.

3 The net worth tie-in

The net worth method, developed in tax-evasion prosecutions, supplies the arithmetic that lifestyle analysis lacks. The examiner computes a person's net worth (assets minus liabilities) at the beginning and end of a period, adds non-deductible living expenses, and subtracts known legitimate income. A remainder is unexplained income. In a divorce or bankruptcy context the "tie-in" is a reconciliation between the net worth statement or financial affidavit the party filed and the net worth implied by the records:

StepSourceQuestion
Opening net worthPrior loan applications, tax returns, financial statements given to banksDid the party claim assets to a lender that are absent from the court filing?
Closing net worthSworn disclosure (financial affidavit; bankruptcy schedules)Does it reconcile to account balances and public records?
IncomeTax returns, 1099s, W-2s, K-1s, depositsDo deposits equal reported income?
ExpendituresStatements, lifestyle analysisCan reported income fund observed spending?
DifferenceComputedWhat is the unexplained increase, and where could it be held?

One of the most useful sources is the party's own loan applications and personal financial statements. A person who told a bank a year ago that he owned an investment account or a stake in a company, and then fails to list it in a bankruptcy schedule or a divorce affidavit, has given two inconsistent sworn or signed statements. The inconsistency alone often satisfies the threshold for deeper discovery and, in bankruptcy, may support a false-oath finding (sections 6 and 7). The net worth approach requires a reliable opening balance and the elimination of alternative explanations; its weaknesses are discussed in Net Worth Method.

4 Tracing transfers

Tracing follows value from a source account to its current form. Two techniques are used. Direct tracing follows a specific payment or asset (a wire to a named recipient, the title history of a vehicle). Indirect tracing infers movement from changes in balances and flows when records are incomplete: monthly cash-flow reconstruction, comparison of deposits with known income, and identification of round-sum outflows with no counterpart in the schedules. When funds are commingled, courts apply tracing conventions such as the lowest-intermediate-balance rule or first-in-first-out; the choice of convention can change the result and should be agreed with counsel.

A practical workflow for transfers:

  1. Build a master ledger of all outflows above a threshold from every known account for the review period.
  2. Classify each by payee type: related party, new payee, individual, entity, financial institution, cash.
  3. For payees that are entities, check corporate registries and public records for ownership and filing dates; an entity formed shortly before the transfer is a red flag.
  4. For property, check deed, vehicle, vessel and aircraft registries, UCC filings, and recorded mortgages.
  5. Identify round-trip patterns (funds that leave and return from a friendly party after the case) and gift-then-loan patterns (the transferee "lends" the money back at no interest).
  6. Use third-party subpoenas (banks, brokers, accountants, payment processors, exchanges) to obtain what the party did not disclose; tax-return transcripts and preparer files supply income and depreciation information (Tax Fraud and Evasion).

International structures require cross-border requests and are slow; see the discussion of MLATs in Asset Tracing. Where the property has been converted to digital assets, blockchain analytics may be used (Cryptocurrency Tracing).

5 Fraudulent transfer law

When a debtor moves assets to avoid creditors, the law offers a remedy: the transfer can be unwound and the asset returned to reach creditors. Two overlapping regimes exist.

State law: the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act

Most states have enacted the Uniform Fraudulent Transfer Act (1984) or its 2014 update, the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act (UVTA); more than twenty states had adopted the UVTA amendments at the last count found (2020).[2] The statute recognises two grounds for avoidance: actual intent to hinder, delay or defraud a creditor, and constructive fraud, where the debtor received less than reasonably equivalent value and was insolvent, left with unreasonably small assets, or was about to incur debts beyond ability to pay. Because intent is rarely admitted, the act lists non-exclusive badges of fraud from which intent may be inferred, including transfer to an insider, retention of possession or control after the transfer, concealment, a transfer made after the debtor was sued or threatened with suit, a transfer of substantially all assets, removal or concealment of assets, insolvency at or shortly after the transfer, and a transfer shortly before or after a substantial debt was incurred. The limitations period for most claims is four years after the transfer, with a shorter alternative for some claims measured from discovery; check the enacted version for each state.

Bankruptcy Code

Section 548 of the Bankruptcy Code allows a trustee to avoid transfers made within two years before the petition if the debtor acted with actual intent to hinder, delay or defraud, or if the debtor received less than reasonably equivalent value and was insolvent, undercapitalised, intended to incur debts beyond ability to pay, or benefited an insider outside the ordinary course. Section 548(e) extends the look-back to ten years for transfers to a self-settled trust or similar device where the debtor is a beneficiary and the transfer was made with actual intent to defraud. A transferee who takes for value and in good faith keeps protection to the extent of value given (section 548(c)).[3] Through section 544(b), a trustee can also use state law, borrowing the longer state period such as a four-year window. In practice trustees plead both.

In divorce, equivalent remedies are found in state family-law statutes (reallocating property, awarding the innocent spouse a larger share to offset dissipation, adverse inferences, sanctions and fee awards), and a spouse may also bring a fraudulent-transfer claim against a third-party transferee. A judgment after a divorce that is later found to have been procured by concealed assets can be reopened in some states within time limits that vary widely.

6 Bankruptcy fraud and denial of discharge

Criminal law

18 U.S.C. § 152 contains nine separate offences, including knowingly and fraudulently concealing property from the trustee, custodian, marshal or other officer of the court or from creditors (§ 152(1)); making a false oath or account (§ 152(2)); making a false declaration, certification, verification or statement under penalty of perjury (§ 152(3)); presenting a false claim (§ 152(4)); fraudulently receiving property from a debtor after filing (§ 152(5)); transferring or concealing property in contemplation of bankruptcy or with intent to defeat the Code (§ 152(7)); and concealing, destroying or falsifying records relating to the debtor's property or affairs (§ 152(8)). The maximum penalty is imprisonment for not more than five years, a fine, or both.[4] 18 U.S.C. § 157 separately prohibits devising a scheme to defraud and, for the purpose of executing or concealing it, filing a petition, filing or making a document, or making a false or fraudulent representation, claim or promise in connection with a bankruptcy case; its penalty is also up to five years.[5] Typical prosecutions involve omitting accounts, income or property from schedules, false statements at the § 341 meeting and transfers to relatives before filing. Prosecutors require proof that the concealment was knowing and fraudulent, which is why documented inconsistencies between the debtor's earlier statements and the schedules are so valuable.

Civil consequences

Fraud also has civil bankruptcy consequences. Section 727(a) denies a discharge to a debtor who, with intent to hinder, delay or defraud, transferred, removed or concealed property within one year before filing or after filing (§ 727(a)(2)); who concealed, destroyed or failed to keep records from which the debtor's financial condition could be ascertained (§ 727(a)(3)); who knowingly and fraudulently made a false oath or withheld records (§ 727(a)(4)); or who failed to explain satisfactorily any loss or deficiency of assets (§ 727(a)(5)).[6] A debt incurred by fraud may also be declared non-dischargeable under section 523(a), and a concealed asset discovered later can usually be administered by reopening the case.

7 Trustee and examiner techniques

A bankruptcy trustee works under statutory duties to investigate the debtor's financial affairs and collect and liquidate estate property. The tools are formal and cheap relative to civil discovery:

  • Schedules and Statement of Financial Affairs. The debtor's sworn schedules and statements disclose assets, income, recent transfers (the individual form asks about transfers within a defined look-back), closed accounts and business interests. The trustee compares them with tax returns and the debtor's prior credit applications.
  • Section 341 meeting of creditors. The debtor is examined under oath by the trustee, and answers are used later as the foundation for false-oath claims.
  • Document turnover. The trustee can demand tax returns, bank statements, and business records, and a debtor's failure to produce them can support denial of discharge.
  • Rule 2004 examination. Bankruptcy Rule 2004 permits the court to order testimony and document production concerning the acts, conduct, property, liabilities and financial condition of the debtor, or any matter that may affect the administration of the estate or the debtor's right to a discharge, and the examination can reach third parties such as banks, accountants and relatives.[7] It is broader than ordinary discovery and is commonly described as a "fishing expedition" that courts nonetheless permit within limits (it generally cannot be used once an adversary proceeding is pending on the same matter).
  • Forensic accountants retained by the trustee reconstruct cash flows, run lifestyle and net worth analyses, and prepare the avoidance claims.
  • Examiner. In a larger reorganisation, section 1104(c) provides for an examiner to investigate the debtor's acts, conduct, assets, liabilities and financial condition, and the section requires appointment on request where the debtor's fixed, liquidated, unsecured debts (other than for goods, services or taxes, or owed to an insider) exceed $5,000,000.[8] The New Century examiner's 550-page report on that company's accounting is an example of the product (see Financial Fraud Case Studies in Detection).
  • Referral. Evidence of fraud is referred to the U.S. Trustee and the U.S. Attorney. The Trustee Program's audits of debtors' disclosures are one source of such referrals.

8 Business-valuation manipulation

Owners of closely held businesses have the most scope to depress apparent value. In a divorce, a spouse who runs the business controls the information, and the valuation expert depends on data supplied by that spouse. Typical manipulations, and the tests an examiner applies, are:

ManipulationEffect on valueTest
Deferring revenue or delaying contract signing until after the valuation dateLower earnings in the base periodCompare backlog and pipeline to post-date results; cutoff testing; sales-order dates versus invoices
Accelerating or prepaying expenses; stockpiling inventoryLower reported profitTrend analysis of expense ratios; subsequent-period reversals
Inflated owner or family compensation, bonuses and perquisitesLower normalised earningsCompare to market compensation for the role; look for family members with no function
Related-party loans, fees and rent at non-market pricesMoves profit to hidden recipientsRelated-party transaction schedule; registry check of landlords and lenders
Diverting customers or contracts to a new entityStrips goodwillCustomer-level revenue analysis; domain, phone and registry searches; see Web Archives and Domain Intelligence
Cash-intensive business: skimming and under-ringingLower reported revenueReconstruct revenue from purchases, markups, utilities, and capacity; deposits analysis
Writing down assets or recognising impairmentsLower asset valueIndependent appraisal; subsequent sale of the same assets
Reducing book value via personal-goodwill argumentsCharacterises value as the owner's personal assetTest customer and employee relationships for transferability (jurisdiction-specific law)

The valuation methods themselves are described in Business Valuation and Damages Quantification. For the investigator, a few cross-checks are especially productive: reconcile business bank deposits to reported revenue; compare the business's tax returns with the financial statements submitted to lenders and insurers (people usually present the best version to lenders); and compare the value a party asserts in litigation with the value declared in recent applications, insurance schedules or buy-sell agreements. A mismatch between a lender-facing valuation and a litigation valuation is classic impeachment material.

9 Red-flag checklist

  • Lifestyle spending that exceeds disclosed income, with no loans or savings to account for it.
  • Financial affidavit or schedules that are late, incomplete, or amended repeatedly after discovery requests.
  • Missing statements, accounts closed shortly before filing, or statements with pages omitted.
  • Sudden transfers to relatives, friends or new entities; "loans" with no repayment terms; real property deeded for nominal consideration.
  • Large cash withdrawals, safe-deposit box rentals, or purchase of portable valuables.
  • Tax returns that show repeated Schedule C losses or a business that does not appear to need the owner's full-time attention; refunds that exceed expectations.
  • Income that falls sharply at the start of the dispute and then recovers afterwards.
  • Refusal or delay in providing business records; claims that records were lost, destroyed or are held by a third party.
  • New digital-asset accounts, exchange activity or hardware wallets.
  • Foreign accounts or entities that appear in earlier records or on tax forms (for example, foreign-account reporting) but not in the filed disclosure.
  • Inconsistent statements across lenders, insurers, tax authorities and courts.

Examiners should record each flag with its source and should consider an innocent explanation before escalating. Documentation must withstand challenge in court, and expert methods must satisfy the reliability standard in Daubert Standard. The counterpart for tax-related concealment is covered in Tax Fraud and Evasion, and for victims of investment frauds seeking recovery see Ponzi and Investment Fraud.

See also: Asset Tracing, Net Worth Method, Bank Statement and Cash Analysis, Business Valuation and Damages Quantification, Litigation Support and Damages, Shell Companies and Beneficial Ownership, Fraudster Psychology and the Dark Triad.
