Ponzi and Investment Fraud

Ponzi and Investment Fraud
Core mechanismReturns paid to earlier investors from later investors' money, not from real profit
VariantsPonzi; pyramid; affinity; advance-fee; "pig-butchering" crypto investment scams
Key U.S. statutesSecurities Act §17(a); Exchange Act §10(b) / Rule 10b-5; 18 U.S.C. §§1341, 1343, 1348; Advisers Act §206
Landmark casesMadoff (2008); Stanford International Bank (2009)
Largest reported U.S. loss categoryInvestment fraud, $8.65 billion (FBI IC3, 2025)

A Ponzi scheme is an investment fraud in which purported profits are paid to existing investors out of money contributed by new investors, rather than from any genuine business or trading activity. It collapses when inflows can no longer cover redemptions and promised returns. Closely related are the pyramid scheme (participants are paid mainly for recruiting others), affinity fraud (the offender exploits trust within a religious, ethnic, professional or social group) and the modern crypto-investment scam, often called "pig butchering," in which a victim is groomed over weeks or months and steered to a fake trading platform.[1] In the ACFE fraud tree these sit outside the occupational branches: the victim is an outside investor, not the employer. They are nonetheless the staple of forensic accounting engagements for receivers, trustees, regulators and prosecutors, because proof rests almost entirely on reconstructing money flows.

1 Structure and typology

All Ponzi-type frauds share one arithmetic fact: liabilities (what investors believe they are owed) grow faster than any real assets. The scheme survives only while net new deposits remain positive. Three features recur: promised returns that are high, steady and unusually insensitive to markets; opacity about strategy and custody; and a trusted central figure who controls statements, custody or both.[1]

TypeWho is paid, from whatTypical evidence of the scheme
PonziEarlier investors, from later investors' principalNo external revenue; bank inflows match outflows; fabricated statements
PyramidParticipants, from recruitment fees or required purchasesCompensation tied to recruits, not retail sales to outsiders
Affinity fraudEither of the above, distributed through a communityReferral chains inside a church, club or diaspora network; reliance on trust instead of due diligence
Crypto-investment ("pig butchering")Scam operator, from victim transfers to fake platformsFunds routed to operator-controlled wallets; fake dashboards showing profit; withdrawal "taxes" or "fees"
Hybrid / "real but fraudulent"Some genuine trading, with losses hidden by new moneyMismatch between trade confirmations and statements; undisclosed losses

2 Landmark cases

Madoff (Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities). Madoff confessed in December 2008 and pleaded guilty in March 2009 to eleven felonies; he was sentenced to 150 years. The court-appointed trustee under the Securities Investor Protection Act (SIPA), Irving Picard, reports that as of late September 2026 about $15.494 billion has been recovered through litigation and settlements and about $14.799 billion distributed from the customer fund, with seventeen interim distributions made; the trustee describes this as the most successful Ponzi recovery by dollar value and percentage in history.[2] Secondary reporting puts customers' principal losses near $17.5 billion, so recoveries have reached roughly three quarters of principal. The scheme persisted for decades in part because the "split-strike conversion" strategy was never independently verified, trades were not confirmed through a third-party custodian, and the audit was performed by a tiny firm unsuited to the assets involved.

Stanford International Bank. R. Allen Stanford was convicted in 2012 of a roughly $7 billion fraud centered on high-yield certificates of deposit sold by an Antigua-based bank; he received a 110-year sentence. The case illustrates an offshore-affinity variant: marketing to Latin American investors, a claimed portfolio of liquid assets that was largely illiquid or related-party, and a regulator and auditors that did not look through the structure. A court-appointed receiver pursued asset recovery worldwide.

Both cases are treated alongside other major prosecutions in Major Fraud Case Studies; Madoff also appears in Case Studies.

3 Forensic techniques: proving the scheme

The examiner's central task is to show, with documents, that investor returns were funded by investor capital. The standard toolkit follows.

3.1 Source-and-application-of-funds (cash-flow) analysis

Obtain every bank, brokerage and payment-processor account the operator controlled, including accounts opened under affiliate or "nominee" names. Normalize each transaction into a ledger and classify it as investor inflow, investor outflow (returns or redemptions), third-party revenue (real trading proceeds, operating-business income), operator expense/transfer, or inter-account transfer. Then compute, month by month: (a) total investor inflows; (b) total payments to investors; (c) legitimate external income. If (c) is small or zero while (b) is large, the "returns" necessarily came from (a). The result is an exhibit showing the scheme was insolvent from a specific date. Evidence produced: a monthly sources-and-uses schedule, a dated insolvency opinion, and a list of tainted payees.

3.2 Tracing commingled funds

Because inflows and outflows share accounts, tracing rules are needed to decide whose money went where. Common conventions are FIFO (first-in, first-out), pro rata, and the lowest intermediate balance rule (LIBR): a claimant's traceable interest in a commingled account cannot exceed the lowest balance the account reached between deposit and the date of examination. LIBR is routinely used in receiverships to separate fraudulently obtained funds from the operator's own. See also Asset Tracing.

3.3 Reconciling statements to the custodian

Compare what investors were told with what third parties can confirm: obtain DTC or custodian records, trade blotters, clearing-firm confirmations and exchange data. A strategy that claims thousands of equity trades must leave a footprint in clearing records and in market volume. Absence of trades, trades outside the day's traded price range, or trade volumes exceeding the market's volume for the security are conclusive indicators of fabrication. Evidence produced: a reconciliation schedule listing claimed holdings versus confirmed holdings.

3.4 Return-pattern analytics

Fabricated return streams often look too smooth. Useful tests include the proportion of positive months, the correlation with the claimed benchmark (an equity strategy with near-zero or negative correlation to the market is suspicious), the Sharpe ratio, and digit-distribution tests on reported returns (see Benford's Law). Autocorrelation of monthly returns can reveal "return smoothing." These tests do not prove fraud, but they justify subpoenas and support a regulator's exam priority.[3]

3.5 Investor-level reconstruction

For each investor, tabulate cash in and cash out from the bank records (not the account statements issued by the scheme). This produces the net investment, the basis for customer claims and for identifying net winners subject to clawback.

3.6 Operator lifestyle and insider tracing

Apply the net-worth method to the operator and insiders to quantify personal diversion, and trace transfers to real estate, art, vehicles and family entities. Sales-agent compensation (commissions as a share of funds raised) frequently shows a disproportionate payout to "feeder" funds or finders, who are then examined for knowledge or willful blindness.

4 Worked examples

The figures below are illustrative, not drawn from a real case.

Example A: net investment versus statement balance. Investor 1 deposited $1,000,000 in 2015 and withdrew $400,000 in 2019. The scheme's final statement shows $1,800,000 (fictitious gains). Net investment is $1,000,000 − $400,000 = $600,000; that is the amount of any allowed customer claim under the "net investment" method used in the Madoff liquidation, not the $1.8 million on paper. Investor 2 deposited $500,000 and withdrew $700,000: net −$200,000, a net winner who received $200,000 of other investors' principal. That $200,000 is the starting point for a fraudulent-transfer (clawback) demand.

Example B: arithmetic of collapse. A fund promises 1.5% per month. If every investor reinvests and no new money arrives, liabilities grow by 1.01512 − 1 ≈ 19.6% per year. With $40 million of investor claims, interest owed in year one is about $7.8 million, while real assets (say $4 million) are not growing. The funding gap rises each month, so the scheme must raise ever more new capital; any slowdown, such as a redemption wave of 10% of balances ($4 million), exhausts the real assets.

Example C: LIBR. A commingled account holds $2,000,000 on March 1 including $1,500,000 of victim funds. By March 15 the balance falls to $300,000 after the operator pays personal expenses. A deposit of $900,000 of new victim funds follows on March 20, bringing the balance to $1,200,000. Under LIBR, the traceable victim interest at the end of the month cannot exceed the lowest balance, $300,000, plus any later deposits that remain, here the $900,000 deposit: $1,200,000 total. The earlier $1,200,000 of victim money dissipated before March 15 is not recoverable by tracing and falls to the general claims pool.

Example D: clearing-record test. A manager reports buying 40,000 shares of a stock at $50.00 on a day when the stock's high was $48.75 and total volume was 1.2 million shares. The price is outside the day's range, so the trade is impossible. If the same pattern appears on 30 of 100 sampled trade tickets, the sample supports an inference of fabricated confirmations, and evidence extrapolation can be documented with a sampling plan (see Analytical Methods).

5 Crypto-investment scams (pig butchering)

The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) 2025 report records investment fraud as the largest loss category in cyber-enabled crime: 72,984 complaints and $8.65 billion, of which cryptocurrency investment scams accounted for about $7.2 billion, the largest source of loss to Americans that year. The report attributes these scams largely to organized criminal enterprises in Southeast Asia, using trafficked workers as forced labor, and says the FBI-led Operation Level Up has reduced potential losses by more than $500 million since 2024.[4] On October 14, 2025 the Department of Justice announced an indictment of the chairman of Prince Holding Group, a Cambodia-based conglomerate, and a civil forfeiture action against approximately 127,271 bitcoin valued at about $15 billion, described as the largest forfeiture in the Department's history.[5]

Investigative method. (1) Collect the victim's transaction hashes, deposit addresses, platform URLs and chat logs; preserve them under chain-of-custody discipline. (2) Use blockchain analytics to cluster addresses and follow funds through mixers, bridges and exchanges to off-ramps that perform customer due diligence; see Cryptocurrency Tracing. (3) Identify the fake platform's hosting, domain registration and app-store footprint using OSINT tools. (4) Serve preservation and freeze requests quickly: the IC3 Recovery Asset Team's Financial Fraud Kill Chain froze about $679 million of $1.16 billion attempted theft (58%) in 3,900 incidents in 2025, but speed is decisive.[4] (5) Pool victim complaints by wallet cluster; this converts scattered small losses into a prosecutable aggregate. The forced-labor dimension links this work to Human Trafficking Finance and money laundering typologies.

6 Clawbacks, receiverships and distributions

Receiverships and trustees. The SEC commonly seeks an asset freeze and a court-appointed receiver in civil enforcement actions; broker-dealer failures like Madoff's may proceed under SIPA with a trustee. Both gather estate assets, marshal claims and sue recipients of fraudulent transfers.

Fraudulent-transfer theory. Under Bankruptcy Code §548 a trustee may avoid transfers made within two years before the filing with actual intent to hinder, delay or defraud creditors; state fraudulent-transfer statutes (often the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act) extend the look-back, commonly to four years, and are used through §544(b). Because a Ponzi operator is presumed to have actual intent, transfers of fictitious profits are recoverable from net winners even if they were innocent, while a good-faith investor generally may retain return of principal. Courts in the Madoff litigation applied this distinction to hold that "profits" paid from other investors' money were not value given in exchange for the investor's claim.

Forensic role in distribution. The forensic accountant prepares claims analysis (net-investment method versus "last statement" method), identifies net winners and net losers, computes pro rata or interim distribution percentages, and defends the methodology in court. In the Madoff case, interim distributions have ranged from small percentage tranches against allowed claims, for example 1.302% on a February 2026 distribution of $253.6 million, until the cumulative distribution is complete.[2]

7 Detection and red flags

  • Returns too consistent for the stated strategy; very few down months.
  • Secrecy about methodology ("proprietary") and no independent custodian or administrator.
  • Small or unknown auditor relative to the assets under management.
  • Payments from other investors' accounts or from a pooled account that investors do not recognize.
  • Redemption friction: delays, new fees, "lock-up" extensions, or pressure to roll over.
  • Unlicensed sellers and unregistered offerings; check the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure database and FINRA BrokerCheck.
  • Affinity-based marketing and referral rewards.
  • Online grooming: unsolicited contact by text or dating app, quick move to an encrypted messaging platform, and a "mentor" who shows early profits.

Analytics-based detection is discussed in Fraud Detection Analytics and AI Fraud Detection Platforms; seniors are a disproportionate target, covered in Elder Financial Exploitation. For general warning signs see Red Flags.

See also: Payment Fraud and BEC, Cryptocurrency Tracing, Asset Tracing, Money Laundering, Federal Enforcement Agencies.

Procurement and Contract Fraud

Procurement and Contract Fraud
Fraud-tree branchesCorruption (bribery, kickbacks, bid rigging); asset misappropriation (billing schemes)
U.S. statutesSherman Act §1; Anti-Kickback Act (41 U.S.C. §§8701–8707); False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. §§3729–3733); 18 U.S.C. §§201, 666, 1343, 371
EnforcementDOJ Antitrust Division; Procurement Collusion Strike Force (since Nov. 2019); agency Inspectors General
Core evidenceBid files, vendor master data, invoices, change orders, emails, bank records

Procurement fraud is any deliberate deception in the acquisition of goods, services or construction, whether by a supplier (false claims, defective pricing, substitution), by an insider (kickbacks, steering to a favored vendor, fictitious vendors), or by a group of suppliers acting together (bid rigging). It sits across two branches of the fraud tree: corruption, when an insider and a vendor collude, and asset misappropriation, when the "vendor" exists only to extract payments. Public procurement is a large and attractive target; the ACFE reports that corruption is present in nearly half of occupational-fraud cases and that billing schemes are among the most common asset-misappropriation methods.[1] This article emphasizes how examiners test purchasing records rather than recount individual cases.

1 Scheme typology

Procurement fraud is easiest to analyze by lifecycle phase.[2]

PhaseSchemeMechanism
Needs definitionTailored specifications; need creationAn insider writes requirements only one vendor can meet, or buys things that are not needed
SolicitationSplit purchases; sole-source abuse; leaked bid informationOrders divided to stay under approval or competition thresholds; "emergency" justification without emergency
BiddingBid rigging: bid suppression, complementary (cover) bids, bid rotation, market allocationCompetitors agree who wins; others bid higher, withdraw, or subcontract afterward
AwardBribery; conflict of interest; shell vendorInsider is paid by, or owns, the winning vendor
PerformanceChange-order abuse; "low-ball and amend"; product substitution; defective pricingWinner bids low, then recovers margin through approved scope changes; cheaper materials supplied than invoiced
PaymentDuplicate or inflated invoices; false billing for services not rendered; kickbacksPart of the overcharge is returned to the insider, in cash, goods, or payments to a relative's firm

2 Law and enforcement

Antitrust. Bid rigging is a per se criminal violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act (15 U.S.C. §1); the maximum penalty is imprisonment up to 10 years and criminal fines up to $100 million for corporations and $1 million for individuals, with an alternative fine of twice the gain or loss. In November 2019 the Antitrust Division launched the Procurement Collusion Strike Force (PCSF), an interagency partnership of Antitrust Division prosecutors, U.S. Attorneys' Offices, the FBI, the Department of Defense and Offices of Inspector General, to deter, detect, investigate and prosecute antitrust crimes in government procurement, grants and other public funding.[3] Reported PCSF-era outcomes include the Korean military fuel supply conspiracy (corporate guilty pleas, roughly $82 million in criminal fines and a $154 million civil settlement reported in connection with the matter) and the 2021 Contech Engineered Solutions plea (a $7 million criminal fine and more than $1.5 million restitution for bid rigging and conspiracy to commit mail and wire fraud).[3]

Kickbacks and bribery. The Anti-Kickback Act prohibits kickbacks to prime contractors or subcontractors to obtain favorable treatment under a federal contract. For public officials, 18 U.S.C. §201 criminalizes bribery and gratuities, and §666 reaches bribery involving programs receiving federal funds. Foreign-official payments are covered by the FCPA (see Anti-Bribery Statutes).

False claims. The civil False Claims Act imposes treble damages plus a per-claim penalty, adjusted annually for inflation, on those who knowingly submit or cause false claims; the qui tam provisions let private relators sue on behalf of the government. Federal contractors are also bound by the mandatory-disclosure rule at FAR 52.203-13, requiring timely disclosure of credible evidence of fraud, bribery or gratuities. See Federal Enforcement Agencies.

3 Forensic techniques

3.1 Document and file review

  1. Reconstruct the procurement file for each selected award: needs justification, specification drafts (with metadata and revision history), solicitation, bidder list, bids as received (with time stamps), evaluation sheets, award memo, contract, modifications, invoices and payment approvals. Missing items are findings in themselves.
  2. Compare the specification to the winner's literature. Phrases copied from a vendor brochure or product part numbers inside "generic" specifications indicate tailoring. Document metadata (author, creation date, tracked-change history) can show who drafted the spec; see Document Examination and Digital Forensics.
  3. Compare bid documents across bidders for common typographical errors, identical formatting, the same arithmetic mistake, shared fonts, matching handwriting, same fax/IP/metadata origin, or sequential bond or insurance certificate numbers. Handwriting and typography comparison belongs to the document examiner.
  4. Review evaluation scoring: scores changed after opening, unexplained re-scoring of a rival, or evaluators who scored only one bidder.
  5. Interview evaluators, contracting officers, and losing bidders using non-leading, sequenced questions; see Interviewing.

3.2 Data analytics on bids

Economists and competition agencies use bid-rigging screens that flag suspicious tenders for review (they are not proof). Common ones:

  • Coefficient of variation (CV) of bids in a tender = standard deviation divided by mean. Collusive tenders often show unusually low CV (cover bids bunched together).
  • Relative distance (RD) = (second-lowest bid − lowest bid) divided by the standard deviation of the losing bids. A winner far below tightly clustered losers yields a high RD.
  • Winner patterns: a fixed group of bidders always participates; winners rotate in a regular sequence; one firm wins in a region and others never bid there (market allocation); losers later appear as subcontractors to the winner.
  • Price relationships: bids that move together with no cost explanation, or winning bids that rise when a particular rival drops out.
  • Withdrawal and no-bid behavior: firms that qualify but do not bid, or withdraw after submission.

Screens should be calibrated against a baseline of known-competitive tenders from the same agency and product category, as thresholds are market-specific.[4]

3.3 Vendor master-file and accounts-payable analytics

  1. Vendor master to employee master match: compare vendor and employee addresses, phone numbers, bank accounts, tax ID, and emails. A match is a primary conflict-of-interest indicator and the classic test for a shell company.
  2. Vendor attributes: PO-box or residential addresses; no website or phone; incorporation shortly before the first award; registered-agent addresses shared with many entities; no physical capacity.
  3. Invoice patterns: sequential invoice numbers (suggesting the vendor has no other customers), round-dollar amounts, invoices just under an approval limit, duplicate invoice numbers or amounts across dates, and invoices without purchase orders or receiving reports. Digit analysis (Benford's Law) applied to a vendor's invoices exposes a cluster of leading or second digits near the limit.
  4. Three-way match failures: purchase order, receiving report and invoice that disagree on quantity or price.
  5. Price benchmarking: compare unit prices against contemporaneous competitive awards, GSA schedule prices, or index data. Persistent premiums indicate overcharge or kickback loading.
  6. Split-purchase test: group purchases by vendor and approver over a rolling window; flag clusters where individual amounts fall below a threshold but the aggregate exceeds it.

3.4 Following the money

Kickbacks are proven through bank and corporate records: subpoena the vendor's disbursements and the insider's accounts, then match amounts and dates. Payments are often routed through relatives, consulting firms, or offshore accounts; asset tracing and the net-worth method identify unexplained wealth. Typical patterns include a payment to the insider (or a related entity) within days after the government pays the vendor, and a recurring percentage of invoice value. Cash-deposit structuring around reporting thresholds can also surface in suspicious activity reports; see AML Law and Money Laundering.

4 Worked examples

All numbers are illustrative.

Example A: bid screens. Four bids are received for a road-resurfacing contract: $960,000 (Firm W), $1,042,000, $1,045,000 and $1,049,000. The mean of all bids is $1,024,000; the sample standard deviation is about $42,760, so CV = 42,760 / 1,024,000 ≈ 4.2%. The three losing bids have a mean of $1,045,333 and a sample standard deviation of $3,512. RD = (1,042,000 − 960,000) / 3,512 ≈ 23.4. The losing bids are packed within $7,000 of each other (0.7% of value) while the winner is $82,000 lower. If the agency's baseline tenders show typical CV of 10–15% and RD under 3, this tender is a statistical outlier worth a file review. The follow-up step is to examine whether the three losers share document metadata, addresses or subcontract relationships with Firm W.

Example B: low-ball and amend. Firm W's $960,000 bid undercut the next bid by $82,000. During performance, nine change orders totaling $120,000 are approved without competition. Revised contract value = $1,080,000, which is $38,000 higher than the second-place bid. Change-order growth = 120,000 / 960,000 = 12.5%. Reviewers test whether each change order was foreseeable from the original specification, whether the same approver signed all nine, and whether quantities were measured against field inspection records. The conclusion that the award would have gone elsewhere had the true price been known is the core "materiality" evidence.

Example C: shell vendor. An accounts-payable extract shows Vendor X with 24 invoices in a year, each between $9,000 and $9,950 against a $10,000 approval limit, totaling $230,400 (average $9,600). Invoice numbers run 1001 to 1024 with no gaps; the vendor's address matches a residential address in the employee master file; all invoices were approved by one manager and none has a receiving report. Four independent red flags support a referral. Quantified loss = $230,400 minus the value of any documented goods actually received. Corroboration: the vendor's bank statements, state corporate filing date, and the manager's deposit records.

Example D: kickback detection. A purchasing agent approves invoices from Supplier S. Unit price for a standard component is $41.80 against a competitive benchmark of $36.00, a 16.1% premium. On 52,000 units the overcharge is (41.80 − 36.00) × 52,000 = $301,600. If the supplier returns 50% of the overcharge, the expected kickback stream is about $150,800, which can be compared to deposits in the agent's accounts (for example, 11 deposits clustered within five days after each payment run) to test the hypothesis.

5 Open-source and relationship analysis

Public-contract portals (USAspending.gov, SAM.gov, state and municipal e-procurement sites) allow award histories to be built for any vendor: number and size of awards, awarding offices, and timing relative to incorporation. Corporate registries show officers and registered agents; campaign-finance and lobbying disclosures show donations to officials who control awards; property records and court dockets expose family links. Link-analysis charts that connect vendors, officers, agents and officials are standard working papers; see Anti-Corruption OSINT, OSINT Tools and OSINT. Limitations: names are often common, registries differ by jurisdiction, and a relationship is a lead, not proof of collusion.

6 Red flags and controls

  • Repeated awards to one vendor without competition, or frequent "emergency" or sole-source justifications.
  • Specifications that match one vendor; unusually short bid windows; amendments issued to only some bidders.
  • Bidders that win in rotation, share addresses or personnel, or subcontract to each other.
  • Winning price much lower than the field, followed by large change orders.
  • Insider lifestyle inconsistent with salary; refusal to take leave or delegate vendor contact (see Red Flags and Fraud Triangle).
  • Controls: segregation between requisitioner, approver and receiver; vendor onboarding verification (independent address and ownership check); periodic vendor-master clean-up; rotation of buyers; conflict-of-interest disclosures; hotline and whistleblower channels; use of the screens above on every competitive tender.

Procurement fraud in the context of other corruption schemes is also summarized in Occupational Fraud and ACFE Report to the Nations; the analytic methods connect to Fraud Detection Analytics and Analytical Methods.

See also: Fraud Tree, Anti-Bribery Statutes, Healthcare and Insurance Fraud, Evidence and Testimony.

Healthcare and Insurance Fraud

Healthcare and Insurance Fraud
Main statutesAnti-Kickback Statute (42 U.S.C. §1320a-7b(b)); Stark Law (42 U.S.C. §1395nn); False Claims Act; Health Care Fraud, 18 U.S.C. §1347
Largest takedown (by intended loss)2025: 324 defendants, $14.6 billion
Latest takedownJune 23, 2026: 455 defendants, $6.5 billion in false claims
Industry bodiesNHCAA (health); NICB (property/casualty); Coalition Against Insurance Fraud
Key datasetsCMS provider utilization files; HHS-OIG LEIE; Open Payments

Healthcare fraud is the knowing submission, or causing the submission, of false or misleading claims to a public or private health plan to obtain payment that is not due; insurance fraud is the broader family of deceptions against insurers, including property, casualty, life and workers' compensation lines. Healthcare is the most data-rich of the two: payers hold millions of structured claims, so statistical analysis of billing behavior is the front door of most investigations. The National Health Care Anti-Fraud Association (NHCAA) estimates that at least 3% of health spending is lost to fraud, and some law-enforcement agencies put the figure as high as 10%; these are estimates rather than measured totals.[1] This article concentrates on how examiners test billing records and provider behavior. It extends the occupational frameworks in the fraud tree to external (vendor and provider) fraud.

1 Common schemes

SchemeDescriptionTypical forensic signature
UpcodingBilling a higher-paying code than the service delivered (e.g., a level 5 office visit for a level 3 service)Skewed distribution of evaluation-and-management (E/M) levels versus peers
UnbundlingBilling separately for components covered by a single comprehensive codePairs of codes that payers' edits say should not be billed together; misuse of modifiers (e.g., modifier 25, 59)
Phantom / billed-not-renderedBilling for services never provided or to patients who never visitedImpossible schedules; services on dates of death, incarceration or hospitalization
Medical necessity abuseUnneeded tests, devices, genetic panels or wound productsHigh volume, uniform orders, no clinical record support
Kickbacks and referral buyingPayments for patient or order referrals (telemarketing, "marketing fees," lab-order purchases)Payments from billers to marketers that track referral volumes
Self-referralPhysicians referring to entities in which they or family hold a financial interestReferral concentration to a single owned entity; compensation tied to referrals
Identity-based billingStolen provider or beneficiary identifiers; sham clinicsMany beneficiaries sharing addresses; sudden volume from a new enrollment
Opioid and pill-mill diversionPrescriptions issued without legitimate medical purposeOutlier prescriber volume, cash payment, high morphine-milligram-equivalent doses

2 Legal framework

Anti-Kickback Statute (AKS). It makes it a felony to knowingly and willfully offer, pay, solicit or receive remuneration to induce or reward referrals of items or services payable by a federal health care program. Penalties are up to ten years' imprisonment and fines up to $100,000 per violation (as amended in 2018), plus exclusion from federal programs and civil monetary penalties. Since 2010 a claim "resulting from" an AKS violation is deemed false for False Claims Act purposes. Regulatory safe harbors (42 C.F.R. §1001.952) protect arrangements that meet all conditions, such as bona fide employment or fair-market-value personal services contracts; fitting within a safe harbor is not required but gives certainty.

Stark Law. The physician self-referral law prohibits a physician from referring Medicare patients for designated health services to an entity with which the physician (or an immediate family member) has a financial relationship, unless an exception applies, and bars the entity from billing for the resulting services. Stark is a strict-liability civil statute: intent is not required for repayment, in contrast to the AKS, which requires intent. Many recent cases plead both together.

False Claims Act (FCA) exposes violators to treble damages plus per-claim penalties adjusted annually for inflation; qui tam whistleblowers can file on the government's behalf and receive a share of recoveries. Criminal health care fraud (18 U.S.C. §1347) covers executing a scheme to defraud any health care benefit program; related counts include conspiracy, money laundering and aggravated identity theft. Federal agency roles are described in Federal Enforcement Agencies.

3 Enforcement scale: takedowns

The Department of Justice's annual National Health Care Fraud Takedown is a coordinated nationwide charging announcement and a useful snapshot of prevailing schemes. The 2025 takedown (announced June 30, 2025) charged 324 defendants, including 96 licensed medical professionals, across 50 federal districts and 12 state offices for schemes involving over $14.6 billion in intended loss, more than doubling the prior record of about $6 billion. It included about $245 million in seizures, CMS's prevention of an estimated $4 billion in payments and revocation or suspension of 205 providers; the largest component was an alleged transnational scheme, Operation Gold Rush, tied to $10.6 billion in medical-equipment claims. Other categories included opioid diversion (74 defendants), telemedicine and genetic testing (49 defendants, about $1.17 billion), and wound care (about $1.1 billion).[2]

The 2026 takedown (announced June 23, 2026) charged 455 defendants, including 90 doctors and other licensed professionals, in schemes involving over $6.5 billion in false claims, across 56 federal districts with 50 state Medicaid Fraud Control Units participating. Public summaries emphasize wound-care allografts (including a case alleging over $4 billion billed for relabeled products at a 2,000% mark-up), behavioral health (a $67 million Illinois Medicaid scheme with claims of 500 or more counseling hours in a single day) and data-driven detection; CMS reported suspending 1,079 providers, revoking 1,403, and stopping $10 billion in payments.[3] Note the difference in headline metric: 2025 reports intended loss, 2026 reports false claims, so the two totals are not directly comparable. Treat all takedown figures as allegations until proven.

4 Forensic techniques

4.1 Claims-data profiling

  1. Define the peer group by specialty, geography, patient mix and setting. Public CMS datasets (Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners; Part D prescriber files) provide benchmarks for provider-level volumes and mix.
  2. Compute outlier metrics: percentage of visits at each E/M level; services per beneficiary; average payment per beneficiary; share of beneficiaries receiving a given service; and drug or device volume. Express each as a z-score or percentile against peers.
  3. Test impossibility: sum billed time by provider and date; daily totals above 24 hours, or services overlapping in time and place, are objective red flags that need no statistical inference.
  4. Test patient plausibility: services after death, during an inpatient stay or incarceration, or multiple providers billing the same patient the same service on the same day; beneficiary clusters with identical addresses.
  5. Network analysis: link ordering physicians to billing labs, DME suppliers and marketers; unusual concentration or ring structures suggest referral arrangements. See Fraud Detection Analytics.
  6. Digit tests on charges and payment amounts and on units billed (see Benford's Law) to find rounding or fabricated entries.

4.2 Medical-record and document review

Data flags a provider; records prove or disprove the claim. Pull a sample of medical records and compare each billed code to documentation of history, examination, decision-making and time; test for cloned notes (identical text across patients), missing signatures, late entries, and templates auto-populated by the electronic health record. Audit-trail logs from the EHR show who created and edited a note and when, a form of digital forensics. Verify patient existence and service receipt by interview or mailed attestation; see Interviewing and Document Examination.

4.3 Statistical sampling and extrapolation

Because reviewing every claim is infeasible, auditors draw a probability sample, measure the overpayment in each sampled claim and extrapolate to the universe. CMS contractors commonly use the OIG's RAT-STATS software and, by convention, project from the lower limit of a 90% one-sided confidence interval, which is conservative for the provider. Documentation of the sampling frame, random-number seed, and handling of errors is essential for evidence admissibility under Daubert.

4.4 Financial tracing

To prove kickbacks, trace payments from the provider or biller to marketers, recruiters, or physicians and compare them against referral counts. Cross-reference the Open Payments database (manufacturer payments to physicians), corporate filings, and bank records; test whether compensation varies with referral volume, which is the legally critical fact. Use the net-worth method for beneficial owners and asset tracing to identify transfers abroad. Check HHS-OIG's List of Excluded Individuals/Entities (LEIE) and state Medicaid exclusion lists for excluded persons on payroll or enrollment records.

5 Worked examples

Figures are illustrative.

Example A: E/M level outlier. Among 200 internists in a region, the mean share of office visits billed at the highest level (CPT 99215) is 12% with a standard deviation of 5 points. Provider P bills 71% of visits at that level across 4,200 visits. z = (71 − 12) / 5 = 11.8, an extreme outlier. If the payment gap between 99215 and 99214 is, say, $45, and P had billed the peer-average 12% share at the top level (the excess visits being billed at the next level down), the difference is roughly 4,200 × (0.71 − 0.12) × $45 ≈ $111,500 per year of potential overpayment, to be validated by record review rather than assumed.

Example B: impossible day. A behavioral-health provider bills 62 individual psychotherapy units of 30 minutes on one date: 62 × 30 / 60 = 31 hours. No single clinician can deliver 31 hours of face-to-face service in a day, and the claim is facially false or reflects group billing mischaracterized as individual. A scan across 365 days finds 87 days above 16 hours; those 87 days become the first audit sample.

Example C: sampling. A universe of 10,000 paid claims totals $1.8 million. An auditor draws a random sample of 100 claims and finds total overpayments of $4,600, a mean of $46 per claim with a sample standard deviation of $120. Point estimate = 10,000 × $46 = $460,000. Standard error of the mean = 120 / √100 = $12 (the finite-population correction, about 0.995, is ignored here). The one-sided 90% lower bound is 46 − 1.282 × 12 ≈ $30.6 per claim, so the extrapolated demand is about 10,000 × 30.6 = $306,000. The wide gap between point estimate and lower bound shows why larger samples matter.

Example D: kickback proof. A lab pays a marketing company $400 for each patient specimen it delivers. The marketing company's 2025 monthly payments are $38,000, $41,200, $39,600 and $44,000 for 95, 103, 99 and 110 specimens. Dividing payment by specimens gives about $400 in each month (38,000/95 = 400; 41,200/103 = 400; 39,600/99 = 400; 44,000/110 = 400). Per-unit compensation that stays constant and scales with referrals is strong circumstantial evidence of payment for referrals, the central element of an AKS case; the intent evidence comes from emails, contracts and witness interviews.

6 Insurance fraud beyond health

Industry classification separates hard fraud (deliberately staged or fabricated events: arson, staged collisions, faked theft) from soft fraud (padding or exaggerating a genuine claim, or misstating information on an application). The Coalition Against Insurance Fraud has estimated total U.S. insurance fraud at about $308.6 billion a year across all lines, a widely cited but modeled estimate.[4] The National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB), a nonprofit funded by insurers, collects claim-index data and publishes indicators for auto theft, staged accidents, catastrophe-related contractor fraud and cargo theft.

  • Staged accidents: link analysis of claimants, attorneys, clinics, tow operators and body shops that recur across claims; vehicle telematics and event-data-recorder data; damage consistent with prior photographs.
  • Arson-for-profit: financial distress analysis of the insured, fire origin-and-cause reports (NFPA 921), accelerant detection, recent coverage increases.
  • Workers' compensation: premium fraud (underreported payroll or misclassified employees), claimant fraud (surveillance, social media), and provider fraud.
  • Life insurance: application misrepresentation, faked death (verify with death certificate source and registries), stranger-originated life insurance.
  • Claims-data tools: index searches across carriers, anomaly scoring, image forensics on submitted photos and invoices, and special investigation unit (SIU) referral thresholds. Many states require insurers to maintain SIUs and report suspected fraud to a state fraud bureau.

The elderly are particular targets of health-related scams and billing abuse, covered in Elder Financial Exploitation.

7 Red flags

  • Billing patterns far from peers (high-level E/M share, unusually high per-patient spend) or impossible volumes.
  • New enrollments that ramp quickly to high billing and then disappear (hit-and-run).
  • Marketing or "management" payments that scale with orders, and consulting contracts with referral sources.
  • Telemedicine encounters with no real clinician-patient relationship; brace, genetic test and allograft orders signed in bulk.
  • Records that are identical across patients, lack supporting results, or are missing audit trails.
  • Patients unaware of services billed in their name; compromised beneficiary numbers.
  • Providers or owners appearing on exclusion lists, or with shared addresses and bank accounts among multiple billing entities.

See also general guidance in Red Flags, Occupational Fraud and AI-based claims scoring in AI Fraud Detection Platforms.

See also: Procurement and Contract Fraud, Money Laundering, Evidence and Testimony, Report Writing.

Payment Fraud and BEC

Payment Fraud and Business Email Compromise
BEC losses (IC3)2023: $2.95B; 2024: $2.77B; 2025: $3.05B
BEC complaints (IC3)2024: 21,442; 2025: 24,768
All IC3 losses, 2025$20.877B on 1,008,597 complaints
Recovery mechanismFBI IC3 Recovery Asset Team / Financial Fraud Kill Chain (FFKC)
Related fraud typesCheck fraud; romance/confidence; authorized push payment; vendor-impersonation; deepfake CEO fraud

Business email compromise (BEC) is a scam targeting businesses and individuals who regularly make wire or other payments, in which the criminal compromises or impersonates a trusted email account, supplier, executive, attorney or title company to induce a payment to an account the criminal controls.[1] Payment fraud is the umbrella for losses arising from payment instruments and channels themselves: wires, ACH, checks, cards, peer-to-peer transfers and cryptocurrency. Unlike the internal frauds of the fraud tree, most of these schemes are committed by outsiders; the control failure is usually a verification step that was skipped. The FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) 2025 report records BEC as the second-highest-loss category in cyber-enabled crime after investment fraud.[1] This article stresses the examination techniques for reconstructing a payment fraud and recovering funds.

1 Scale and trends (FBI IC3)

IC3's 2025 Internet Crime Report records 1,008,597 complaints and $20.877 billion in reported losses, a 26% rise over 2024. Selected categories follow.[1]

Category2025 complaints2025 loss2024 loss2023 loss
Investment72,984$8.65B$6.57B$4.57B
Business email compromise24,768$3.05B$2.77B$2.95B
Tech/customer support47,794$2.13B——
Confidence/romance23,159$929M$672M$653M
Credit card/check fraud18,774$283M$200M$174M

Two points matter for interpretation. First, IC3 data are self-reported and include only complaints filed, so true totals are higher. Second, BEC losses are lumpy: a few large wires drive the annual total, so year-to-year changes should be read with caution. The report also records 22,364 complaints mentioning artificial intelligence, with adjusted losses above $893 million; businesses reported more than $30 million in BEC losses with a likely AI nexus, and victims reported over $19 million in romance-scam losses with a likely AI nexus.[1]

2 Typologies

  • Executive impersonation ("CEO fraud"): a spoofed or compromised executive account instructs finance to wire funds urgently and confidentially.
  • Vendor email compromise / invoice redirection: the criminal, often after compromising a supplier's mailbox, sends genuine-looking invoices with changed bank details.
  • Real-estate and escrow BEC: a buyer receives "wiring instructions" from a spoofed title company or attorney. IC3 describes a March 2025 case in which a senior citizen attempted to wire over $1.3 million to a fraudulent account before the Recovery Asset Team froze the funds.[1]
  • Payroll diversion: a fake employee request changes direct-deposit details.
  • Account takeover (ATO): criminals take over bank or payment-platform logins and move funds through many transactions; IC3 notes ATO cases can involve 50 or more simultaneous ACH transfers to different banks.[1]
  • Deepfake-enabled impersonation: synthetic voice or video in place of email; see section 7.

3 Forensic techniques: email and identity

  1. Preserve first. Take a forensic copy of the relevant mailboxes, mail-server logs and the originals of the fraudulent emails (as .eml or .msg with full headers), recording hash values and custodian; see Chain of Custody and Digital Forensics. Screenshots are not sufficient.
  2. Analyze message headers. Read the Received chain from the bottom up to find the originating server; compare From, Reply-To, Return-Path and Message-ID domains; read Authentication-Results for SPF, DKIM and DMARC outcomes. A critical caution: a lookalike domain registered by the criminal will often pass its own SPF, DKIM and DMARC checks, because authentication only proves that the sender controls the domain it claims, not that the domain is the one you expect.
  3. Detect lookalike domains. Compare sender domains to legitimate ones by edit distance, homoglyphs (the digit 1 for the letter l; Cyrillic characters), added hyphens and alternate top-level domains. Look up registration date and registrar with WHOIS/RDAP; domains registered days before the fraud are strong indicators. Use passive DNS and certificate-transparency logs to find sibling domains from the same infrastructure; see OSINT Tools.
  4. Hunt for mailbox compromise. In Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, review audit logs for: new inbox rules that forward, delete or move mail containing words such as "invoice," "payment" or "wire"; forwarding addresses; OAuth app consents; unusual sign-in IPs and impossible travel; legacy-protocol logins; and MFA changes. Mailbox rules that hide replies are a hallmark of a compromised account, as opposed to a mere spoof.
  5. Reconstruct the timeline. Build a minute-by-minute schedule: first malicious login, rule creation, lure email, payment instruction, bank release, and discovery. Time zones must be normalized to UTC.
  6. Verify identities out-of-band during the investigation: call known numbers (not those in the email), and interview the payer's employees (Interviewing) to establish who approved, what verification was attempted, and what policy was in force.

4 Forensic techniques: payment tracing and recall

Speed is the primary variable. The victim should contact its bank immediately, request a wire recall and any necessary indemnification documents, and file an IC3 complaint with full transaction details. The IC3 Recovery Asset Team (RAT), established in 2018, streamlines communications between financial institutions and FBI field offices to freeze funds through the Financial Fraud Kill Chain (FFKC). In 2025 it handled 3,900 incidents involving $1.164 billion in attempted theft and froze about $679 million, a 58% success rate; domestic incidents numbered 3,574 ($507 million frozen) and international 326 ($172 million frozen). For the 655 incidents involving critical-infrastructure organizations, $146.6 million of $261.5 million (56%) was frozen.[1] IC3 also describes a case in which an Oregon city government office lost over $6 million in a BEC attack and the originating bank was able to issue a recall after the recipient account had been flagged through an earlier FFKC freeze.[1]

4.1 Following the funds

  1. Obtain the wire confirmation: originator and beneficiary account numbers, routing numbers, Fedwire IMAD/OMAD or SWIFT UETR/reference, and timestamps.
  2. Send preservation letters and subpoenas or legal process to the beneficiary bank for account-opening documents, signature cards, IDs, KYC data, IP logs from online banking, and statements showing onward transfers (the "second hop").
  3. Build a flow chart of each hop: amount, date, destination, and what remains. Apply the same tracing rules used in Asset Tracing. Recipients are frequently money mules or victims of other scams (the FFKC case above found the recipient account owner had been told to send $1 million to a Hong Kong account in an overpayment scam).
  4. For funds converted to cryptocurrency, follow on-chain with Cryptocurrency Tracing to an exchange that can freeze.
  5. Pool complaints sharing the same beneficiary account or wallet: multiple victims strengthen probable cause and recovery claims (see Money Laundering).

4.2 Bank-side analytics

Financial institutions screen for BEC and mule activity with: (a) beneficiary-change analytics, flagging a payment to a vendor within a short window after a bank-detail change; (b) first-time payee and amount outlier tests; (c) name-to-account mismatch checks (confirmation-of-payee style); (d) pass-through ratio for recipient accounts (outflows divided by inflows within 24–48 hours); (e) velocity and fan-in patterns, where many unrelated payers send to one new account. See Fraud Detection Analytics and AI Fraud Detection Platforms.

5 Check fraud examination

Check fraud remains significant despite digital payments. FinCEN's alert FIN-2023-Alert003 (February 27, 2023) described a nationwide surge in mail-theft-related check fraud; in the six months to August 31, 2023 FinCEN received 15,417 Bank Secrecy Act reports on such activity associated with more than $688 million, and asked institutions to use the key term "FIN-2023-MAILTHEFT" in suspicious activity reports.[2] IC3's 2025 credit-card/check category shows 18,774 complaints and $282.7 million.[1]

TechniqueWhat the examiner doesEvidence produced
Image examinationCompare the presented item with the account's signature card, prior checks, paper stock; look for washing (chemical alteration of payee and amount), overwritten fields, mismatched ink and fontsDocument-examiner opinion; see Document Examination
MICR and routing dataVerify the MICR line, check number sequence, and routing numbers; test for counterfeit checks with valid account numbers but out-of-sequence numbersException report showing number gaps and duplicates
Positive pay / payee positive payMatch presented checks to the issued-check file by number, amount and payeeUnmatched-item report, issue file timestamps
Remote deposit reviewDetect duplicate deposits of the same check at different banks or through mobile and teller channels; compare deposit device IDsDuplicate presentment analysis
Kiting analysisChart deposits and withdrawals between two or more accounts to find circular check floatFloat schedule; ratio of checks drawn on affiliated accounts
Endorsement reviewStudy back-of-check endorsements for chain of custody and deposit-account owner mismatchesEndorsement chain exhibit

6 Worked examples

Illustrative figures; domain names are fictitious.

Example A: lookalike domain. The company's supplier domain is example-corp.com. The fraud emails come from ap@examp1e-corp.com (digit 1 replacing the letter l). Edit distance is 1 (one substitution). WHOIS shows registration 6 days before the first message, while the real domain has been registered for 14 years. Headers show spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=examp1e-corp.com and dmarc=pass header.from=examp1e-corp.com. The passes confirm only that the criminal controls the lookalike. The examiner reports that the sender was not the supplier, which defeats any argument that the payer's email-security tools should have blocked an "authenticated" message. A reply-to difference and a first-time sender flag are additional indicators.

Example B: vendor-change analytics. The accounts-payable system's change log shows a bank-detail change for Vendor V on May 3, submitted by an email request, with no callback recorded. The next payment run on May 8 pays Vendor V $184,300, versus a historical median payment of $41,000, so the payment is 4.5 times the median ($184,300 / $41,000 = 4.5) and the first to the new account. Rule: flag any payment released within 10 days of a bank-detail change that exceeds 2 times the vendor's median. This case triggers on both conditions. On May 9 the real vendor asks about its unpaid invoice; the loss is $184,300 and the clock on a recall request has already run for one day.

Example C: mule pass-through. Recipient account R receives three transfers totaling $18,500 from three unrelated payers over two days and sends out $17,950 within 24 hours of the last credit. Pass-through ratio = 17,950 / 18,500 = 97%; retained balance $550 (3%). The account was opened 11 days earlier with a deposit of $100. These indicators justify a freeze request and a review of other inflows to R for additional victims.

Example D: check kiting. Accounts A (Bank 1) and B (Bank 2) belong to the same owner. On day 1 a $50,000 check drawn on B is deposited to A; before it clears, on day 2 a $55,000 check drawn on A is deposited to B; day 3, $60,000 on B to A; day 4, $65,000 on A to B; and so on with each cycle $5,000 larger. By the sixth cycle the outstanding float is a $75,000 check. If 100% of deposits in the period are checks drawn on the owner's other account, and no external deposits fund either account, ledger balances are fictitious. The examiner charts deposits against collected balances by day; the pattern of rising, alternating amounts is the evidentiary signature.

7 Romance scams, APP fraud and deepfakes

Romance (confidence) scams. IC3 recorded 23,159 complaints and $929 million in 2025. The offender builds a relationship with a fabricated persona, then solicits funds for emergencies, travel or investments. Examination: reverse-image search of profile photos; metadata and account-creation analysis of social profiles; message-language analysis; payment-trail tracing to the beneficiary accounts or crypto wallets; and a victim interview that preserves the complete chat history. Many romance scams blend into investment fraud (see Ponzi and Investment Fraud) and target older adults (Elder Financial Exploitation).

Authorized push payment (APP) fraud. In APP fraud the victim themselves initiates a real payment but is deceived about its purpose or recipient. In the United Kingdom, from October 7, 2024 the Payment Systems Regulator's mandatory reimbursement requirement applies to faster payments: sending firms must reimburse in-scope victims within five business days (with a possible "stop the clock" investigation pause), reimbursement is capped at £85,000 per claim, and the cost is split 50:50 between the sending and receiving firms.[3] In the United States, Regulation E (12 C.F.R. part 1005) protects against unauthorized electronic fund transfers; a transfer the consumer was tricked into authorizing is generally treated differently, which is why recall and freeze mechanisms matter so much.

Deepfake-enabled CEO fraud. In the best-known reported case, Arup confirmed in 2024 that a Hong Kong employee was deceived by a video call in which fake versions of colleagues appeared, resulting in 15 transfers totaling HK$200 million (about US$25 million).[4] Forensic response: secure the meeting recording and platform logs; extract the participants' account identifiers and join IP addresses; analyze audio and video for synthesis artifacts and compression anomalies (see Video Forensics); and trace the payments as in section 4. Preventive controls are procedural, since detection of synthetic media is unreliable: out-of-band callback to a known number, dual authorization for payments above a threshold, pre-agreed code words for executives, and a rule that no video or voice instruction alone can change payee details. See Emerging Trends.

8 Red flags and controls

  • Urgent, confidential payment requests that bypass normal approval; requests to change bank details by email.
  • Sender domain subtly different from the correct one; reply-to that differs from sender.
  • First-time payee, new account in a different bank or country, or payee name that does not match the account.
  • Mailbox forwarding or deletion rules; sign-ins from unusual locations.
  • Checks presented out of sequence; payee or amount altered; duplicate deposits.
  • Controls: verified callback to a number on file; dual approval; vendor-master change control with independent verification; positive pay; DMARC enforcement and external-sender banners; MFA; immediate incident playbook (call bank, request recall, file IC3 complaint, preserve logs).

General warning signs are collected in Red Flags; legal reporting duties tie to AML Law and the AML Statutory Framework; agencies are described in Federal Enforcement Agencies.

See also: Ponzi and Investment Fraud, Healthcare and Insurance Fraud, Digital Forensics, Cryptocurrency Tracing.

Tax Fraud and Evasion

Tax Fraud and Evasion
Principal statutes26 U.S.C. §§ 7201 (evasion), 7202, 7203, 7206, 7212(a)
InvestigatorsIRS Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI)
ProsecutionDOJ Criminal Division Tax Section (since Dec 2025) and U.S. Attorneys
Tax gap (TY2022)$696 billion gross; $606 billion net
IRS-CI FY2025$10.59 billion financial crime identified; $4.5 billion tax fraud
Offshore reportingFBAR (FinCEN 114), Form 8938 (FATCA)

Tax evasion is the willful, illegal attempt to defeat the assessment or payment of tax, as distinct from tax avoidance, the lawful use of the Code to reduce liability. Tax fraud is the broader category of false returns, false documents, schemes to misuse the refund system and employment-tax non-payment. Tax crimes are rarely the lead offense of an investigation in the way that securities fraud is; they are frequently the charge that is easiest to prove, as in the prosecution of Al Capone in 1931. For forensic accountants, the tax return is both a target of fraud and a document that can show unreported income.[1]

1 Evasion versus avoidance; the statutes

The Internal Revenue Code's principal criminal provisions are:

SectionOffenseMaximum penalty
§ 7201Attempt to evade or defeat tax (felony)5 years; $100,000 individuals, $500,000 corporations
§ 7202Willful failure to collect or pay over tax5 years; $10,000 fine under the statute (higher under 18 U.S.C. § 3571)
§ 7203Willful failure to file, pay, keep records (misdemeanor)1 year
§ 7206(1)Fraud and false statements under penalty of perjury3 years
§ 7206(2)Aiding or assisting false returns (preparers, promoters)3 years
§ 7212(a)Corrupt interference with the administration of the Code3 years
18 U.S.C. § 371Conspiracy to defraud the United States (Klein conspiracy)5 years

Evasion requires three elements: a tax deficiency, an affirmative act of evasion or attempt, and willfulness. Spies v. United States (1943) lists affirmative acts such as keeping a double set of books, making false entries, concealing assets, covering up sources of income, and handling affairs to avoid usual records. Willfulness is the “voluntary, intentional violation of a known legal duty” (United States v. Pomponio, 1976), and under Cheek v. United States (1991) a good-faith misunderstanding of the law, even if unreasonable, negates it, though a disagreement with the law's validity does not. Civil fraud under § 6663 imposes a 75% penalty on the underpayment attributable to fraud, and there is no statute of limitations on assessment for a fraudulent return (§ 6501(c)); the criminal limitation period is generally six years (§ 6531).

2 Scale and enforcement landscape

The IRS estimated the gross tax gap for tax year 2022 at $696 billion, of which $539 billion (77%) was underreporting, $94 billion underpayment and $63 billion non-filing; about $90 billion is expected to be paid late, leaving a net gap of $606 billion and a voluntary compliance rate of 85%.[2] Individual income-tax underreporting is concentrated in business income that has little third-party reporting; wages, which are reported on W-2s, show compliance above 99%, while non-farm proprietor income is under-reported by a large share. This is the intellectual basis for the indirect methods below.

IRS-CI's FY2025 annual report records $10.59 billion in financial crime identified (up 15.7%), of which $4.5 billion was tax fraud (up 111.8% from FY2024), with nearly 64% of investigative time spent on tax crimes, a 25% increase in search warrants and a 14% increase in prosecution referrals; it seized more than $800 million in assets and about 2.35 petabytes of digital data.[3] Cases are typically developed with analytics and from referrals from IRS civil examination, the IRS Whistleblower Office (§ 7623(b): 15–30% of collected proceeds in cases where tax, penalties and interest exceed $2 million), banks' SARs and other agencies (see Federal Enforcement Agencies and Whistleblowers and the False Claims Act).

The DOJ Tax Division, the historic gatekeeper that had to authorize most criminal tax prosecutions, was eliminated as a standalone component: the proposal appeared in the June 2025 budget, its website was archived in September 2025, dissolution was finalized on 30 November 2025 and the implementing rule took effect on 9 December 2025. Roughly 300 attorneys moved to a Tax Litigation Branch in the Civil Division and about 100 to a Tax Section in the Criminal Division.[4] Further reorganizations followed in 2026; defense and investigative practitioners should check current authorization procedures.

3 Proof methods: direct and indirect

Specific-items method. Used when the government can identify particular unreported receipts or false deductions: deposits traced to unreported sources, checks from customers not entered in the books, and personal expenses deducted as business costs. It proves the deficiency item by item and is the preferred method where records exist.

Indirect methods are used when books are missing, unreliable, or the taxpayer deals in cash. All rely on the principle that income must equal what the taxpayer applied to expenditures or accumulated, and are upheld in Holland v. United States (1954) (net worth) and United States v. Johnson (1943) (expenditures). The three principal methods are:

  1. Net worth plus nondeductible expenditures: compare year-end net worth (assets minus liabilities, at cost) with the prior year, add living expenses and nondeductible outlays, subtract known nontaxable income, and compare to reported income. Foundations require an established opening net worth, a likely source of the income, and negation of reasonable explanations such as cash hoards, loans, gifts and inheritances (Holland).
  2. Sources and applications of funds (expenditures method): used when net worth is stable but spending is high. Total expenditures plus increases in assets and decreases in liabilities (applications) minus known sources (decreases in assets, increases in liabilities, nontaxable receipts) equals required income.
  3. Bank deposits method: compute total deposits to all accounts; subtract transfers between the taxpayer's accounts, redeposited items, loans, gifts and other nontaxable sources; add cash expenditures paid from undeposited receipts; the result is gross receipts.
  4. Markup and percentage methods for retail and service businesses: apply an industry markup to cost of goods sold, or a standard ratio (e.g., tips-to-sales or gallons per vehicle) to estimate sales.

Each method produces a schedule that becomes the core exhibit, supported by summary testimony under Federal Rule of Evidence 1006 and bank, title and third-party records (see Evidence and Testimony). Defense experts attack the opening net worth, undeposited cash and the thoroughness of leads followed. Good practice documents the leads run to ground, the taxpayer's explanations (typically through interview or the tax-return preparer file), and a sensitivity analysis showing the deficiency under a range of assumptions.

4 Worked examples

4.1 Bank deposits method (hypothetical restaurant owner)

LineAmount ($)
Total deposits, all accounts, year612,000
Less: transfers between own accounts(95,000)
Less: loan proceeds (documented bank loan)(40,000)
Less: redeposited returned check(2,000)
Add: cash expenditures from undeposited receipts (payroll, produce)71,000
Gross receipts546,000
Less: reported gross receipts(410,000)
Unreported receipts136,000
Less: additional deductible costs identified in the records (e.g., 30% food cost)(40,800)
Understated net income95,200

Tax shown at a hypothetical 24% marginal bracket would be about $22,850 before penalties; the criminal "tax due and owing" threshold in the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines (§ 2T4.1) increases the offense level with the amount of loss (for example, more than $250,000 raises the base level from 16 to 18; more than $550,000 to 20). The examiner confirms each reduction with documents; unsupported subtractions are the most common defense attack.

4.2 Net worth method (hypothetical individual)

ItemYear 0 ($)Year 1 ($)
Assets at cost (cash, real estate, vehicles, accounts)300,000720,000
Liabilities(180,000)(310,000)
Net worth120,000410,000

Increase in net worth = $290,000. Add non-deductible living expenses of $64,000 = $354,000. Less known nontaxable sources (documented inheritance $50,000, gifts $10,000) = $294,000 of corrected income. If the filed return reported $85,000 in income, the apparent understatement is $209,000, but the government must also dispose of the "cash hoard" defense, that is, show the opening net worth did not omit cash on hand, usually through bank cash-withdrawal histories, safe-deposit records, prior statements to lenders on credit applications, and the absence of prior hoard-like behavior.

5 Offshore accounts: FBAR and FATCA

U.S. persons with a financial interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts whose aggregate value exceeds $10,000 at any time in the year must file a Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FinCEN Form 114) under the Bank Secrecy Act (31 U.S.C. § 5314), due 15 April with an automatic extension to 15 October. Willful failure carries a civil penalty of the greater of about $100,000 (inflation-adjusted) or 50% of the account balance at the time of the violation, and criminal exposure of up to five years. Separately, the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA, 2010; IRC § 6038D) requires individuals with specified foreign financial assets above thresholds (for single U.S. residents, generally $50,000 at year-end or $75,000 at any time) to attach Form 8938 to the return, and requires foreign financial institutions to report U.S. account holders to the IRS, directly or through intergovernmental agreements. The OECD Common Reporting Standard supplies similar automatic exchange for non-U.S. residents of participating countries, which is useful for tax investigators abroad.

Enforcement history: the 2009 UBS deferred prosecution agreement ($780 million and disclosure of about 4,450 accounts) and the Department of Justice's Swiss Bank Program (2013–2016) broke bank secrecy for U.S. clients. Practical examination procedures include: (1) compare the foreign-account indicators on Schedule B and the return with the FBAR database and Form 8938; (2) review U.S. bank records for wires to or from foreign banks and for checks drawn on foreign institutions; (3) examine credit-card and ATM use abroad, cross-border travel, and foreign property ownership (see Asset Tracing); (4) search for offshore entities in leak data and registries (see Shell Companies and Beneficial Ownership); and (5) for crypto, trace exchange accounts and wallets (see Cryptocurrency Tracing).

6 Employment tax and refund fraud

Employment-tax evasion. Employers withhold income tax and the employee share of FICA from wages, and hold these funds in trust for the government. Failure to remit is a felony under § 7202, and responsible persons face a civil trust fund recovery penalty equal to 100% of the unpaid trust-fund taxes under § 6672. Schemes include pyramiding (filing but not paying, then closing the business and opening a new entity), paying workers off-book in cash, misclassifying employees as independent contractors, and use of professional employer organizations (PEOs) or payroll agents that collect and keep the tax. Detection tests: compare Forms 941 with W-2/W-3 totals and state unemployment wage reports; compare payroll deposits with bank outflows labelled as payroll; compare reported wages with industry ratios (revenue per employee); and check Form 1099-NEC payments to workers who function as employees.

Refund fraud. Typical schemes are stolen-identity refund fraud (filing early in the season with a victim's data and routing the refund to a prepaid card or bank account), inflated withholding credits, false Schedule C and Earned Income Tax Credit claims, fuel-tax-credit abuse, and Employee Retention Credit (ERC) claims for pandemic-era periods, which prompted an IRS moratorium on new claims in September 2023 and a wave of prosecutions of promoters. Data tests include duplicate bank accounts or addresses receiving many refunds, refunds routed to accounts not in the taxpayer's name, W-2 and withholding data that do not match employer filings, return preparers with abnormal refund-per-return profiles, and returns filed from the same device or IP address.

7 Red flags and data tests

  • Lifestyle inconsistent with reported income (compare a property, vehicle and tax-return profile against a net-worth estimate).
  • Cash-intensive business with margins that differ from industry norms, or with deposits that change after a competitor opens.
  • Deposits structured just below $10,000 (see Money Laundering).
  • Two sets of books; backdated or missing records; frequent changes of accountants.
  • Large, round or unsupported deductions; “consulting” fees to related shells (see Shell Companies and Beneficial Ownership).
  • Transfers to nominee entities or foreign accounts, particularly if followed by reacquisition of the asset or loans back (a “round trip”).
  • Payroll tax liabilities that grow while the owner draws personal expenses.
  • Preparer-specific anomalies: identical deductions across clients, EIC claims for most clients.

Analytics such as Benford's Law on Schedule C line items, ratio analysis, and the techniques in Fraud Detection Analytics identify candidates; they are not evidence of willfulness. Investigators must also respect the limits on use of tax return information (26 U.S.C. § 6103), under which private examiners generally cannot obtain returns without the taxpayer's consent or a court order, and professional standards covered in Forensic Accountant Ethics.

See also: Net Worth Method, Forensic Accounting, Money Laundering, AML Law, Asset Tracing, Whistleblowers and the False Claims Act.
