Public Sector Fraud and Improper Payments

Public Sector Fraud & Improper Payments
Federal improper payments, FY2025About $186 billion (15 agencies, 64 programs); about $3 trillion since FY2003
GAO fraud estimate$233–$521 billion per year (FY2018–2022 data)
SBA OIG pandemic loan estimateOver $200 billion potentially fraudulent (EIDL and PPP)
DOL OIG unemployment estimateAt least $191 billion potentially improper; over $76 billion fraud
Key bodiesGAO, OIGs, PRAC, Treasury Do Not Pay, DOJ COVID-19 Fraud Enforcement Task Force

Public sector fraud is the deliberate deception of a government to obtain payments, benefits or contracts to which the perpetrator is not entitled. It must be distinguished from improper payments, which are payments that should not have been made or were made in the wrong amount, including administrative error, missing documentation and eligibility mistakes. Improper payments include fraud but are mostly not fraud; treating the two as synonyms is the most common error in public discussion of the numbers. This article sets out the best available estimates, the major pandemic-era schemes, and the data techniques investigators use.

1 Improper payments versus fraud: the estimates

Under the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (PIIA), agencies must estimate improper payments in programs susceptible to significant error. GAO's April 2026 report (GAO-26-108694) states that 15 agencies reported about $186 billion in estimated improper payments for FY2025 across 64 programs, up about $24 billion from the prior year; about 82% ($153 billion) were overpayments. Five programs account for about 73% (roughly $136 billion): Medicare ($57 billion), Medicaid ($37 billion), the Earned Income Tax Credit ($21 billion), SNAP ($10 billion) and the SBA Shuttered Venue Operators Grant program ($10 billion). Cumulative agency estimates since FY2003 total about $3 trillion. The estimate omits some programs deemed susceptible, such as TANF.[1]

Fraud is harder to measure because undetected fraud is unobserved. In April 2024 GAO published its first government-wide estimate (GAO-24-105833): direct annual losses to fraud of roughly $233 billion to $521 billion for FY2018–2022, a 90% interval built from adjudicated cases, detected potential fraud, and modeled undetected fraud. The range reflects the heightened risk environment of the pandemic years.[2] Neither figure should be added to the other: they overlap and use different methods.

2 Pandemic relief fraud

Congress authorized the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) and the SBA's COVID-19 Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) program in 2020. Both relied heavily on applicant self-certification. The SBA Office of Inspector General's June 2023 report 23-09 estimated that SBA disbursed over $200 billion in potentially fraudulent COVID-19 EIDL and PPP funds—about $136 billion in EIDL and $64 billion in PPP—at least 17% of roughly $1.2 trillion disbursed, and attributed it to weakened controls and a "pay and chase" environment. Nearly $30 billion had been seized or returned at that time.[3] "Potentially fraudulent" was defined by indicators such as use of SSNs of the deceased or minors, duplicate bank accounts, and applications from addresses and IPs tied to multiple filings; it is a risk flag, not an adjudication.

Typical PPP schemes: fictitious businesses with fabricated payroll and tax documents; inflated headcount or payroll at real businesses; "loan mills" and third-party processors who file bulk applications for fees; and misuse of proceeds (luxury cars, real estate, crypto). A representative public conviction: a co-founder of the PPP lender service provider Blueacorn was sentenced in late 2025 to 10 years in prison and ordered to pay over $66 million in restitution for a scheme involving over 530 fraudulent loans and more than $65 million in losses; the prosecution alleged fabricated tax documents and bank statements.[4]

Limitation periods matter: Congress extended the criminal statute of limitations for PPP and for COVID-19 EIDL fraud to ten years in 2022 legislation, which in practice allows charging into 2030–2031. DOJ's COVID-19 Fraud Enforcement Task Force (created 2021) is reported to have charged more than 3,500 defendants and recovered more than $1.4 billion, and civil False Claims Act pandemic settlements continue.[5] Treat these as law-firm summaries of DOJ figures and check DOJ releases for current totals.

3 Unemployment insurance and benefits fraud

The Department of Labor OIG estimated that of more than $888 billion in pandemic-era unemployment insurance benefits, at least $191 billion could have been improperly paid, "with a significant portion attributable to fraud" (over $76 billion by an earlier estimate). The Pandemic Unemployment Assistance program's reliance on self-certification without verification of eligibility or wages in its first months made it especially susceptible.[6] Common patterns: identity theft with stolen PII; multi-state filing with one identity; claims by incarcerated persons; and organized rings routing benefits to prepaid cards and drop accounts.

Beyond pandemic programs, steady-state benefit fraud includes Medicare and Medicaid billing (the 2025 National Health Care Fraud Takedown charged 324 defendants involving $14.6 billion in alleged false claims), SNAP trafficking (selling EBT benefits for cash), Social Security and VA payments continued after death, and tax-credit fraud (see Elder Financial Exploitation for the overlap with beneficiary exploitation).[7]

4 Oversight and enforcement architecture

  • Offices of Inspector General investigate their agencies' programs and report semiannually; see Federal Enforcement Agencies for the criminal investigators (FBI, Secret Service, HSI, IRS-CI, postal inspectors).
  • Pandemic Response Accountability Committee (PRAC), created by the CARES Act, supports OIGs with a data analytics center. Originally scheduled to sunset in September 2025, it was extended to 30 September 2034 by Public Law 119-21 (July 2025), which also gave it $88 million and wider jurisdiction. Its reported support: over 1,200 investigations, over 24,000 subjects and over $2.5 billion in potential fraud loss as of November 2025.[8]
  • Treasury's Do Not Pay (DNP), authorized in PIIA, lets agencies check payees against sources such as the System for Award Management exclusion list and death data before paying. Full access to the Social Security Death Master File was temporary (three years from December 2023) until legislation in February 2026 (the Ending Improper Payments to Deceased People Act) reportedly made it permanent.[9]
  • DOJ brings criminal prosecutions and False Claims Act civil actions (treble damages plus per-claim penalties). Qui tam relators have driven many PPP FCA cases.

5 Forensic techniques: finding program fraud in data

5.1 Eligibility re-performance against independent records

For each application, recompute what the program formula permits from independently obtained data. PPP first-draw loans equalled 2.5 times average monthly payroll (capped at $10 million); self-employed applicants were capped at 2.5 times monthly Schedule C net profit with profit limited to $100,000, i.e. $20,833. Example: an applicant claims 40 employees and $480,000 monthly payroll, producing a $1,200,000 loan (2.5 × $480,000). The IRS Forms 941 show wages of $38,000 per quarter for 6 employees, or about $12,667 per month; 2.5 × $12,667 is about $31,700. The loan is about 38 times what the filings support. Evidence: the side-by-side recomputation, the 941 transcripts and state wage records.

5.2 Duplicate and shared-identifier clustering

Build a graph in which applications are nodes and shared attributes (bank account, phone, email, device or IP, mailing address, registered agent, loan processor) are edges, then look at connected components. Illustration for unemployment claims: if one account receives weekly deposits for 14 different claimants at $1,000 per week (the sum of a $400 state benefit and the $600 federal supplement in the first months of the pandemic), that is $14,000 per week, or $364,000 over 26 weeks, flowing to one account holder. A rule of thumb used in screening is to review any account tied to more than three unrelated claimants. See Fraud Detection Analytics.

5.3 Master-file matching

Match payee SSNs and EINs against death records, prisoner lists, SAM exclusions, state business registries (a firm incorporated after the program's eligibility date, such as 15 February 2020 for PPP payroll eligibility, is ineligible) and NAICS codes versus the stated business. Quantify match hits as an error rate on the population and drill into the top-dollar hits. Beware of false positives in death matches (SSN transposition, late reporting); verification should use secondary identifiers.

5.4 Statistical screens

Apply Benford's Law to loan amounts or claim totals by lender or processor. Fabricated applications often cluster at round numbers or at program ceilings; for instance, an excess of loans at exactly $20,833 or $20,832 for sole proprietors implies formula-driven filing. Compare each lender's or processor's loan-size distribution and average jobs per dollar with peers, and flag outliers beyond three standard deviations.

5.5 Document and metadata review

Examine submitted tax forms, bank statements and payroll reports for font and layout anomalies, identical templates across unrelated applicants, PDF creation metadata (creator software, timestamps after the purported document date), and arithmetic inconsistencies (see Document Examination). Evidence: side-by-side exhibits and metadata dumps.

5.6 Tracing proceeds

Follow loan proceeds through the receiving account in the first 10–30 days: transfers to personal accounts, vehicle and real-estate purchases, and crypto exchange deposits. Use the lowest-intermediate-balance and similar methods covered in Litigation Support and Damages, with Asset Tracing and Cryptocurrency Tracing for destinations, and Money Laundering typologies for structured withdrawals. Output: a flow-of-funds chart tying specific dollars to specific uses, supporting forfeiture and restitution.

6 Evidence and prosecution

Common charges include wire fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1343), bank fraud (§ 1344), false statements to SBA or a financial institution, aggravated identity theft (§ 1028A), money laundering (§§ 1956–1957) and, for benefits, theft of government funds (§ 641). Civil False Claims Act liability turns on knowing false claims and materiality. Loss is typically calculated as the amount of the loan or benefit less any legitimate portion, and sentencing under the Guidelines scales with loss. Experts frame these computations and their reliability under Daubert.

See also: Federal Enforcement Agencies, Fraud Detection Analytics, Elder Financial Exploitation, Internal Controls and Fraud Risk Assessment.

Fraudster Psychology and the Dark Triad

Fraudster Psychology
Core questionWho commits fraud, and what warning behaviours precede it?
Data sourceACFE Report to the Nations (2,402 cases in the 2026 edition)
Personality frameDark Triad (Paulhus & Williams, 2002)
Theory extensionsFraud diamond (2004); fraud pentagon; MICE
Key cautionProfiles describe detected populations and cannot identify individuals

The psychology of fraud perpetrators asks what kind of people commit fraud and which behaviours reveal them before the loss is complete. The fraud triangle explains the conditions for fraud (pressure, opportunity, rationalization) and its extensions section introduces the fraud diamond's fourth element, capability; this article does not repeat that material. It adds three things: the measured profile of perpetrators in large case databases, the personality research behind the so-called Dark Triad, and the behavioural indicators examiners use in practice. It ends with the limits of all of this, because the literature is frequently over-read in both directions: as proof that fraudsters are "different", and as a guide to singling out individuals.

1 The measured profile (ACFE data)

The largest public data set on perpetrators is the ACFE's biennial Report to the Nations, compiled from cases reported by Certified Fraud Examiners. The 2026 edition analysed 2,402 cases from 143 countries (about $3.4 billion in total losses; median loss $104,000; an estimated 5% of annual revenue lost to fraud), and found that longer-tenured, college-educated male employees were the most likely perpetrators, although the share of female perpetrators rose from 25% to 28%.[1] Reported breakdowns of that edition show managers and employees each accounting for 41% of perpetrators and owners or executives for 16%, with median loss rising steeply with rank: about $475,000 for owners and executives, $125,000 for managers and $50,000 for staff.[2] Median loss also increases with tenure, from $50,000 for those with under a year to $200,000 for those with ten or more years.[2] The 2024 edition (1,921 cases, 138 countries) is consistent with that picture and adds that 74% of perpetrators were male, 69% were aged 31 to 50, and 87% had never been charged with or convicted of a fraud-related offence.[3]

CharacteristicFindingEditionInterpretation
PositionOwners/executives 16% of cases but ~$475K median loss; staff $50K2026Authority and access scale losses
TenureMedian loss $50K (<1 year) to $200K (10+ years)2026Trust and knowledge of controls grow with time
Gender74% male (2024); female share 28% (2026)2024, 2026Reflects workforce composition by role as well as propensity
Age69% aged 31–502024Peak-career years with authority and obligations
Criminal history87% no prior fraud charge or conviction2024Background checks have limited predictive power
Red flags84% exhibited at least one behavioural red flag2024, 2026Behaviour is more informative than demographics

Two features stand out. First, the demographic profile is that of the trusted middle-aged professional, not of a social outsider. Second, the same person who is the most trusted may be the least supervised, which is why the occupational fraud literature stresses that tenure and authority raise both access and the cost of a breach. See also ACFE Report to the Nations.

2 The Dark Triad

The Dark Triad is a term from personality psychology for three socially aversive but non-clinical traits: Machiavellianism (strategic manipulation and cynicism), subclinical narcissism (grandiosity, entitlement, need for admiration) and subclinical psychopathy (callousness, impulsivity, low empathy and remorse). Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams, studying 245 students, showed in 2002 that the three constructs are moderately intercorrelated but not equivalent; their shared Big Five correlate is disagreeableness, while psychopathy is distinguished by low neuroticism and, with Machiavellianism, by low conscientiousness.[4] Short self-report instruments (such as the Short Dark Triad) are widely used in research. Psychopathy in the clinical sense is assessed with Robert Hare's Psychopathy Checklist-Revised by trained raters, never by a questionnaire alone.

Why the Dark Triad is of interest to fraud examiners:

  • Rationalization is easier. Entitlement (narcissism) and a calculating view of rules (Machiavellianism) reduce the internal cost of the "non-shareable" step that Cressey described.
  • Manipulation of controls and people. Charm, persuasion and the ability to lie convincingly are the capabilities identified in the fraud diamond, and they matter most in management-override frauds (financial statement fraud), where the perpetrator also needs to deceive auditors and subordinates.
  • Low remorse and escalation. Where the trait profile includes low empathy, a first small theft is less likely to be followed by guilt or confession, and sums tend to grow.

Evidence from organisational research is suggestive, not conclusive. Babiak, Neumann and Hare (2010) studied 203 corporate professionals nominated for management-development programmes and found psychopathic traits, measured with the PCL-R and a screening-version equivalent, at higher levels than in community samples (press summaries put the figure for scores in the psychopathic range at about 4%). Psychopathy was positively associated with ratings of charisma and presentation style and negatively associated with ratings of responsibility and performance.[5] That combination is relevant to fraud risk: a person who is rated highly for charisma but poorly for conscientious performance can win trust while evading accountability. It does not show that these individuals commit fraud at higher rates in every setting, and these studies were not drawn from fraud samples. A defensible summary is that dark traits may increase the probability of misconduct when pressure and opportunity are present, but the research does not allow an examiner to infer fraud from personality.

3 Theory extensions beyond the triangle

Several frameworks add to the triangle and diamond. They are best treated as checklists of hypotheses rather than validated predictive models.

FrameworkElementsContribution
Cressey (1953)Perceived non-shareable financial problem; perceived opportunity; verbal rationalizationBased on interviews with incarcerated embezzlers; origin of the triangle (see Fraud Triangle)
Fraud diamond (Wolfe & Hermanson, 2004)Incentive, opportunity, rationalization, capabilityCapability traits: position or function, intelligence, confidence or ego, coercion skills, effective lying and immunity to stress[6]
Fraud pentagonAdds arrogance (or competence) to the diamondHighlights entitlement and the belief that controls do not apply; popularised in practitioner literature
MICEMoney, Ideology, Coercion, EgoA motivation taxonomy used in forensic-accounting teaching; covers fraud for cause, under duress, or for status, not just financial need
Sociological/behavioural-forensics approachesIndividual predisposition, organisational climate, social contextRamamoorti (2008) argued that fraud curricula should integrate the psychology and sociology of fraud, recognising purposeful intent, intensity of desire, perceived risk of apprehension, violation of trust and rationalization[7]

The practical consequence is a wider net for motive. Not every perpetrator has a financial problem: the CEO who inflates earnings to protect his reputation (ego), the employee who diverts money to a cause (ideology) and the subordinate who falsifies at a superior's command (coercion) all fall outside Cressey's original profile. The Nortel and Computer Associates cases in Financial Fraud Case Studies in Detection involved bonus triggers and analyst expectations, a mix of money and ego.

4 Behavioural red flags

Behaviour has proved more useful than demographics. In both the 2024 and 2026 ACFE studies, 84% of perpetrators displayed at least one behavioural red flag while the fraud was under way, and those who displayed one tended to cause larger median losses than those who did not.[1][3] The most common flags in the 2024 edition were living beyond one's means (39% of cases), financial difficulties (27%) and unusually close association with a vendor or customer (20%); the 2026 breakdown reports 39%, 29% and 17% respectively, with 16% of cases showing no red flag.[2][3] Other categories the ACFE tracks include control issues or an unwillingness to share duties, a "wheeler-dealer" attitude, irritability, suspiciousness or defensiveness, recent divorce or family problems, addiction problems, complaints about inadequate pay, excessive pressure from within the organisation and a refusal to take vacation.

These are cues for inquiry and not proof. The standard way to use them:

  1. Pair behaviour with a transaction test. A manager who never takes leave is a prompt to test the transactions that only that manager touches; a buyer with a supplier who is a personal friend prompts a vendor-master and beneficial-ownership check (Shell Companies and Beneficial Ownership).
  2. Translate lifestyle into numbers. Where living beyond means is observed, the net worth method and the lifestyle analysis described in Hidden Assets in Divorce and Bankruptcy convert an impression into a quantified gap between spending and known income.
  3. Look for clusters. A single flag is common and weak; two or three occurring together with a control weakness are stronger (see Red Flags).
  4. Route concerns through the response plan. Observations should go through the channels in Forensic Investigation Planning, not into informal accusations.

In interviews, behavioural cues (changes in language, evasion, inconsistent timeline) are weak indicators of deception at best; the literature on lie detection by demeanour is poor, and Interviewing practice emphasises information gathering and verification against documents.

5 Rationalization, escalation and the "ordinary" fraudster

Large frauds rarely start large. A common trajectory is a small borrowing from the organisation that the person intends to repay ("temporary loan"), followed by the discovery that nobody noticed, then repetition, then concealment that requires more fraud. Each step makes confession more costly, so the scheme grows until a change in circumstances (an audit, departure on leave, a system migration) exposes it. The same pattern appears in Ponzi schemes, where the operator conceals trading losses with new investor money and cannot stop.

Typical rationalizations identified in the literature are "I deserve it" (unrecognised effort, underpayment), "I will pay it back", "the company can afford it", "everyone does it" and "it's for the company". The last is characteristic of financial-statement fraud, where perpetrators may not personally profit beyond bonuses and may believe they are protecting jobs or waiting for a recovery. Understanding the narrative a suspect tells is useful in planning an interview, but the examiner should keep to evidence. Organisational culture also contributes: tone at the top, unrealistic targets and a record of weak sanctions all lower the barrier to rationalization (see Internal Controls and Fraud Risk Assessment).

An important corollary: most fraudsters are not sociopaths. Many are otherwise law-abiding people responding to pressure and opportunity, which explains the 87% with no prior fraud history. Prevention therefore relies chiefly on controls, segregation of duties, mandatory leave, surprise audits and hotlines, not on trying to screen out bad actors.

6 Using psychology in investigations

  • Risk assessment. Position, authority and tenure define who can override controls; assess override risk for senior roles separately from transaction-level risk. See Auditing Standards and Fraud, which require the auditor to address management override in every audit.
  • Hypothesis generation. Motive categories (money, ideology, coercion, ego) suggest where evidence of motive would sit: debt records and gambling for money, communications and affiliations for ideology, reporting lines for coercion, performance targets and compensation for ego.
  • Interview planning. Anticipating the subject's likely rationalization allows an interviewer to prepare documentary questions that do not depend on admission.
  • Open-source indicators. Public records, litigation history, social-media displays of lifestyle and corporate affiliations can corroborate behavioural flags; ethical and legal limits apply (OSINT Ethics).
  • Prevention. Mandatory vacation, job rotation, rotation of auditors and relationship disclosure rules target the opportunity and the concealment, which matter more than the person's character.

Employers who consider psychological testing for screening should take legal advice. In some jurisdictions, including the United States, personality or psychological tests that identify a mental disorder can be treated as medical examinations subject to restrictions on pre-offer use under disability-discrimination law, and a low score on a trait scale is not a lawful basis for adverse action by itself.

7 Limits of profiling

Several structural problems make any profile unreliable as a screening tool.

  • Detected-fraud bias. ACFE data are drawn from frauds that were discovered, investigated and reported by examiners. Undetected frauds, and those handled quietly, are missing, as are the successful and the skilled. A "typical fraudster" is the typical caught fraudster in a sample of cases handled by examiners.
  • Base rates. Millions of middle-aged, tenured, educated employees exist; the vast majority never commit fraud. A characteristic found in many fraudsters but in many more non-fraudsters has little diagnostic value. Even a trait with a large effect size produces mostly false positives when the underlying event is rare.
  • Hindsight bias. Behaviours that look sinister after discovery were often explained innocently at the time: living beyond means may reflect inheritance, a spouse's income or debt.
  • Measurement. Dark Triad scales are self-reports subject to faking, and they measure continuous traits, not categories. Corporate samples are small and drawn from a few organisations.
  • Context dominates. Experimental and field evidence on misconduct shows that situational factors, such as targets, climate and visibility of controls, explain a good deal of variation. The triangle's own structure treats the person as one of three conditions.
  • Ethical and legal risk. Singling out a person on the basis of personality or demographics invites wrongful-accusation and discrimination claims and is incompatible with the objective, evidence-led approach set out in Forensic Accountant Ethics.

The appropriate role of this literature is therefore modest: it improves hypotheses, interview preparation and control design, and it supplies a vocabulary for reports. It is not a method of detecting fraud. Detection rests on data, documents and tips (43% of cases in the 2026 ACFE study were detected by tip), not on character assessment.[1]

See also: Fraud Triangle, Red Flags, Occupational Fraud, Fraud Tree, Interviewing, Forensic Investigation Planning, Elder Financial Exploitation.

Financial Fraud Case Studies in Detection

Detection Case Studies
CasesNortel; Green Mountain Coffee Roasters; Bausch & Lomb; Bristol-Myers Squibb; New Century; Sino-Forest; Diamond Foods; Computer Associates
Dominant schemesReserve manipulation, channel stuffing, premature revenue, cost deferral, fictitious assets
SourcesSEC releases and orders, DOJ, court and securities-commission decisions
Companion articleMajor Fraud Case Studies

This article examines eight financial-reporting cases from the perspective of an examiner: what the scheme was, which red flags were visible, how it came to light, which forensic technique would have caught it sooner, and how it ended. It deliberately avoids WorldCom and Enron, covered with Lehman, HealthSouth, Madoff, Wirecard and others in Major Fraud Case Studies, and the broader mechanics of earnings manipulation in Financial Statement Fraud. Facts below are taken from regulator and court sources cited in the references. The "technique that would have caught it" paragraphs are analytical judgements of this wiki, not findings of the regulators, and carry hindsight bias: the techniques are offered as practice points, not as proof that anyone should have seen the fraud at the time. Where a case ended without a finding of fraud, that is stated.

1 Summary table

2 Nortel (reserve "cookie jars")

Scheme. According to the SEC, Nortel Networks manipulated its accounts between 2000 and 2003 to close gaps between actual performance, internal targets and Wall Street expectations. The SEC alleged that Nortel accelerated revenue in 2000 (by about $1.4 billion), maintained more than $400 million of excess reserves in 2002 that suppressed reported profit, and released roughly $500 million of reserves in 2003 to fabricate a return to profitability, which triggered "return to profitability" bonuses worth tens of millions of dollars to senior executives.[1]

Red flags. Large provisions with no clear operational driver; reserve releases clustered in the quarter in which a bonus threshold would otherwise be missed; earnings that landed just above target; repeated restatements; weak controls over provisioning and revenue recognition.

Detection. After Nortel announced an initial restatement in October 2003, its audit committee commissioned an independent review with outside counsel; as it progressed, new management was directed to examine provisioning and provision releases in depth, and the later restatements followed.[2] Detection was thus internal, driven by the audit committee, rather than by the external auditor or a whistleblower.

Technique that would have caught it. A reserve roll-forward analysis: for each reserve account, opening balance plus provisions minus utilisations minus releases equals closing balance, by quarter. Releases not matched to a utilisation or a change in estimate, and reserve movements that correlate with the gap between pre-reserve earnings and target, are the signature of earnings management. Pairing the roll-forward with the incentive-plan terms (the context track of the investigation timeline) exposes the motive.

Outcome. Nortel paid a $35 million civil penalty in October 2007 without admitting or denying the allegations, with funds earmarked for harmed shareholders, and accepted injunctions and remedial undertakings.[1] The SEC separately sued the former CEO, CFO, controller and assistant controller. In Ontario, the former CEO, CFO and controller were tried on criminal fraud counts alleging they manipulated results to trigger $12.8 million in bonuses and stock; the judge acquitted them in January 2012, finding he was not satisfied that they had deliberately misrepresented the finances, and the Crown did not appeal.[3] The case is a reminder that regulatory and criminal standards of proof differ and that complex estimates are hard to prosecute as intentional misstatements.

3 Green Mountain Coffee Roasters (restatement and a closed inquiry)

What happened. In September 2010 Green Mountain Coffee Roasters disclosed an SEC Enforcement inquiry into "certain revenue recognition practices and the company's relationship with one of its fulfillment vendors" and announced a restatement. The company said the errors, identified while preparing the fiscal 2010 financial statements and during the audit, would reduce cumulative net income across fiscal 2007 to 2009 and the first three quarters of 2010 by roughly $6.1 to $6.5 million, and it stated that none of the errors related to its fulfillment vendor.[4] A later accounting summary listed six categories of error totalling about $11.5 million of cumulative pre-tax overstatement, the largest being a $7.6 million adjustment from applying an incorrect standard cost to intercompany K-Cup inventory in consolidation.[5]

Why it belongs in a detection study. This is a case in which the red flags were public but the end point was not a finding of fraud. Hypergrowth, a heavy reliance on a single fulfillment vendor, intercompany inventory, and complex customer-incentive accruals created classic risk areas, and the company was publicly questioned by investor David Einhorn. In October 2014 the SEC staff notified the company that it had concluded its four-year inquiry without recommending enforcement action against the company or any current or former employee.[6] A securities class action, In re Green Mountain Coffee Roasters, Inc. Securities Litigation, was settled for $36.5 million in cash under a stipulation dated June 2018, a private settlement that involved no regulator finding.[7]

Technique that would have caught the errors. Standard-cost reconciliation: recompute consolidated inventory at the group standard cost and reconcile to the sum of entity-level inventories, eliminating intercompany profit; accrual back-testing of marketing and incentive programmes (compare accrued versus subsequently paid); and vendor confirmation of inventory and sell-through held at third-party fulfilment centres. These procedures distinguish honest accounting error from intentional manipulation by looking at direction and pattern: errors that consistently increase profit across several periods warrant a deeper look, while random errors do not.

Lesson. Not every restatement is fraud, and an examiner should record both the evidence of intent and its absence. The Green Mountain file is a counterweight to the other cases here, where documents showed management directing the outcome.

4 Bausch & Lomb (sales falsification, 1993–94, and subsidiary misconduct, 2002–05)

1993–94 scheme. The SEC's 1997 administrative findings describe two separate divisions inflating sales. The Contact Lens Division ran a "December Program" in late 1993 that pushed distributors to take about 1.8 million units of traditional lenses far beyond their needs just before year-end, granted unauthorised return rights to roughly 59% of participants, extended credit without creditworthiness analysis, and recognised about $5.7 million of revenue on goods not shipped until after year-end. In the Asia-Pacific Division, Hong Kong management fabricated sunglass sales, shipped goods to warehouses or complicit customers who never paid, forged delivery notes with receipt acknowledgments, and used sham "exchange" transactions to mask growing receivables and avoid raising the bad-debt reserve. Together the practices produced $42.1 million of improperly recognised revenue and overstated 1993 net income by at least $17.6 million, or 11%.[8]

Red flags. Year-end spikes in distributor shipments; unusually generous return rights and credit terms; ageing receivables not matched by reserve increases; "exchange" transactions with no cash movement.

Detection. An internal audit team began investigating in June 1994, and an anonymous letter from employees in August 1994 exposed the Asia-Pacific scheme; management and outside auditors then identified both problems and restated 1993–94 results in early 1996.[8] The case is a clean illustration of the ACFE finding that tips are the most common route to detection.

Technique. Revenue cutoff testing (match shipping documents to invoice dates for the last and first weeks of the year), receivables confirmation and subsequent-receipts testing (customers who never pay are exposed when cash receipts after year-end are traced), and return-rate analysis by distributor. Forged delivery notes are a document-examination problem (see Document Examination).

Outcome. The SEC issued cease-and-desist orders against the company and three executives; the order text reviewed here does not specify monetary penalties.[8]

A second episode. In 2006 Bausch & Lomb again restated, after investigations into its Brazilian and Korean subsidiaries. In Korea the company found improper sales practices — improper return rights, unaccounted product exchanges between customers, unprocessed returns and excessive credit — and concluded that all vision-care transactions from 2002 to 2005 should be recorded on a consignment basis, recognising revenue only upon customer payment; it restated 2003 and 2004 and removed about $26.7 million of net sales dating back to 2001.[9] Recurrence in remote subsidiaries shows why entity-level controls and distributor-return testing must extend to foreign operations. This wiki has not located an SEC enforcement order for the 2006 episode.

5 Bristol-Myers Squibb (channel stuffing)

Scheme. From the first quarter of 2000 through the fourth quarter of 2001, Bristol-Myers Squibb sold more pharmaceutical product to wholesalers than end demand justified, particularly near quarter-end, and improperly recognised revenue on about $1.5 billion of such sales to its two largest wholesalers, because the company covered the wholesalers' carrying costs and guaranteed them a return on investment until the product was resold, which meant the sales were not final. When results still fell short of analyst estimates, the company tapped improperly created divestiture reserves and reversed parts of them into income.[10]

Red flags. Wholesaler inventory far above normal weeks of supply; receivables and revenue rising faster than prescriptions written; side agreements with customers; reserve releases to fill earnings gaps.

Technique that would have caught it. Sell-in versus sell-through reconciliation: compare the company's shipments to wholesalers with independent prescription or end-demand data and with the wholesalers' own inventory reports, expressed as days or weeks on hand. A sustained build above historical norms, concentrated in the last days of each quarter, is the channel-stuffing signature. A review of customer correspondence and contract files for guarantees, as well as a reserve roll-forward for the divestiture reserve, would have reached the other two mechanisms.

Outcome. In 2004 the company agreed to pay $150 million: a $100 million civil penalty and $50 million to a shareholder fund. It also accepted a permanent injunction and an independent adviser to monitor accounting, reporting and internal controls; the SEC said its investigation of individual responsibility continued.[10] The release does not describe how the practice was first detected.

6 New Century Financial (loan repurchase reserves)

Scheme. New Century was a major subprime mortgage originator that sold loans into securitisations and was obliged to repurchase loans that breached representations or defaulted early. The SEC alleged that in the second and third quarters of 2006 the controller changed the method of estimating the loan-repurchase obligation contrary to GAAP and failed to ensure the backlog of pending repurchase requests was properly accounted for, understating the repurchase reserve and materially overstating results; the CEO and CFO were charged with not ensuring that negative trends were disclosed in periodic reports and private offerings.[11]

Red flags. Rising early payment defaults and a growing repurchase-request backlog; reserves falling as a share of exposure while risk rose; a loan-quality standard defined by whether loans could be sold to Wall Street; reserve-method changes made late in the period.

Detection. The mechanism that revealed the full picture was a bankruptcy examiner. Michael Missal's report, dated 29 February 2008 and unsealed on 26 March 2008, ran to more than 550 pages, rested on voluminous document productions and 110 interviews of 85 fact witnesses, and found at least seven improper accounting practices in 2005 and 2006. It said management knew of an "alarming and steady increase in early payment defaults" no later than mid-2004, and criticised both senior management and the auditor, KPMG; the audit committee had not been told of the accounting changes.[12] See Hidden Assets in Divorce and Bankruptcy for the examiner's powers.

Technique. Roll-rate and early-payment-default analysis against the repurchase reserve; ageing of the repurchase-request backlog (every unprocessed request is a liability); sensitivity analysis on reserve assumptions; and a change-in-estimate review, since a method change that increases income in a deteriorating environment is a standard auditor trigger.

Outcome. In 2009 the SEC charged the CEO (Brad Morrice), CFO (Patti Dodge) and controller (David Kenneally). Each consented to a permanent injunction and a five-year officer-and-director bar; Morrice agreed to disgorgement of $541,345 and a $250,000 penalty, Dodge to $450,000 and $100,000, and Kenneally to $150,000 and $32,500.[11]

7 Sino-Forest (alleged phantom assets)

Scheme. Sino-Forest, a Toronto-listed forestry company with operations in China, reported growth that its later court judgment described as extraordinary: between 2003 and 2010 revenue grew 625% and assets 1,270%, and the company raised about $3 billion in debt and equity. In March 2018 the Ontario Superior Court (Justice Penny) found that former CEO Allen Chan had secretly controlled counterparties through nominees, used them to receive deposits and advances from the company, and that Sino-Forest lacked the documentation to establish ownership of its standing timber assets.[13]

Red flags. Very high margins and growth in a capital-intensive industry; reliance on intermediaries to buy and sell standing timber; assets in remote regions that were difficult to inspect; cash flow that lagged reported profit; opaque related-party relationships.

Detection. Short seller Muddy Waters Research published a report on 15 June 2011 alleging that Sino-Forest was a "multi-billion dollar Ponzi scheme" involving theft, overstated revenue and undisclosed related-party dealings. The Ontario Securities Commission issued an order in August 2011 and delivered a statement of allegations in May 2012; Sino-Forest sought creditor protection under the CCAA in March 2012.[13] The sequence shows how public-record research outside the company can precede formal audit findings. Short-seller reports are advocacy documents and are not evidence of fraud on their own; in this case the Ontario court and the OSC later made findings.

Technique that would have caught it. Independent verification of existence and ownership: confirmation of title with registries and forestry authorities, direct inspection or satellite verification of claimed plantations (Geolocation and Imagery OSINT), confirmation of bank balances directly with banks, and counterparty vetting through corporate registry filings and beneficial-ownership research (Shell Companies and Beneficial Ownership, Corporate Registries and Leak Databases). Comparing reported revenue with operating cash flow and with the financial capacity of the named suppliers would have shown whether the commercial story was plausible.

Outcome. The court awarded the SFC Litigation Trust US$2.6 billion for fraud and breach of fiduciary duty, plus C$5 million in punitive damages, described as the largest fraud judgment in Canadian history. On 9 July 2018 the OSC imposed sanctions on Chan and other former executives, including lifetime market bans, and reports put the total ordered at more than $80 million in penalties, costs and disgorgement, with Chan ordered to disgorge $60 million.[14]

8 Diamond Foods (cost deferral)

Scheme. Diamond Foods, a snack and nut company, bought walnuts from growers. The SEC alleged that its former CFO, Steven Neil, directed an effort to under-report amounts paid to growers by delaying the recording of payments into later periods; he described walnut costs internally as a "lever" for managing earnings. Special payments were made to growers but portions were excluded from year-end statements and characterised as "advances on crops that had not yet been delivered" rather than as costs of prior deliveries, which lifted net income and earnings per share above analysts' estimates in fiscal quarters of 2010 and 2011.[15]

Red flags. A key commodity cost that moved inconsistently with market prices; earnings that repeatedly met consensus; significant grower payments recorded as prepayments near period-end; acquisition-driven pressure on reported growth (not detailed in the SEC release; treat as context only).

Detection. The scheme was discovered through the company's restatement, announced in November 2012, which triggered the SEC investigation; the stock fell from a peak near $90 to about $17.[15]

Technique that would have caught it. Cutoff and accrual-completeness testing of the largest cost line: search for payments made after year-end that relate to deliveries before it (subsequent-disbursements testing), and compare accrued grower obligations with the contract terms and with volumes delivered. Email keyword review on terms like "lever" or "push to next quarter" supplies direct evidence of intent. A prepaid-asset analysis would have flagged unusual growth in advances.

Outcome. In January 2014 the company agreed to pay $5 million to settle SEC charges. The former CEO, Michael Mendes, who should have known the reported walnut cost was wrong when he certified the statements, paid a $125,000 penalty and had returned or forfeited more than $4 million in bonuses and other benefits; litigation against Neil continued at the time of the release.[15] Clawback of incentive pay is the operative remedy highlighted in Financial Statement Fraud.

9 Computer Associates (the "35-day month")

Scheme. From 1998 to 2000, Computer Associates routinely kept its books open after quarter-end to record revenue on software licence contracts executed after the quarter closed, to meet analyst estimates; the practice was internally referred to as the "35-day month". The SEC said the company prematurely recognised $2.2 billion of revenue in fiscal 2000 and 2001 and over $1.1 billion in prior quarters, more than $3.3 billion from at least 363 contracts in all, and that in fiscal 2000 the inflation of individual quarters ranged from 22% to 53% of properly recorded revenue. Executives allegedly approved backdated contracts and made false statements to the SEC and encouraged employees to give misleading testimony to investigators and outside counsel.[16]

Red flags. A pronounced spike in signed contracts on the first days after quarter-end; contract signature dates conflicting with customer or counsel records; revenue per quarter that always barely met estimates; large multi-year licence deals with heavy up-front recognition.

Technique that would have caught it. Contract-date cutoff testing with independent evidence of when agreements were executed: counterparty confirmations, signature metadata, email timestamps, and fax or courier logs. Pattern analysis of booking dates (a histogram of contract dates by day relative to quarter-end shows a cliff if the books were held open). This is a straightforward test on a full population and an application of Fraud Detection Analytics. Evidence tampering is also a digital-forensics issue: the sentencing court found the CEO tampered with a laptop to conceal its contents from the government and the audit committee (Digital Forensics).

Outcome. In September 2004 Computer Associates agreed to a deferred prosecution agreement with the U.S. Attorney's Office and to a settlement with the SEC, paying $225 million in restitution, with an 18-month period of independent-examiner oversight and governance reforms. Former general counsel Steven Woghin pleaded guilty. Former CEO Sanjay Kumar pleaded guilty in April 2006 to securities fraud and obstruction and was sentenced on 2 November 2006 to 12 years in prison and an $8 million fine; prosecutors said the scheme prematurely recognised over $2 billion of revenue and caused shareholder losses above $400 million.[16][17]

10 Patterns across the cases

  • Period-end concentration. Five of eight cases (Nortel, B&L, BMS, Diamond Foods, Computer Associates) involved moving results across period boundaries. Cutoff testing is the most productive single procedure in financial-reporting fraud.
  • Estimates as the soft target. Reserves and accruals (Nortel, BMS, New Century, Green Mountain) require judgement and are hard to prove intentional; the best evidence is the direction and timing of changes relative to earnings targets and bonus triggers.
  • Detection came from inside or from outside the ordinary audit. An audit-committee review (Nortel), an internal audit plus anonymous letter (B&L), a bankruptcy examiner (New Century), a short seller (Sino-Forest) and a restatement (Diamond Foods) did the work; none was a routine external-audit finding. This matches the ACFE finding that tips and internal sources detect most frauds (see ACFE Report to the Nations).
  • Incentives mattered. Bonus plans, analyst consensus and acquisitions are recurring pressures; see the fraud triangle and Fraudster Psychology and the Dark Triad.
  • Outcomes diverge. Companies often settle with the SEC without admitting wrongdoing; individual executives face varied results, from acquittal (Nortel executives) and no enforcement (Green Mountain) to multi-year prison terms (Computer Associates). Reporting must state which standard of proof was met.
  • Existence is an audit assertion. Sino-Forest shows that completeness and valuation tests do nothing if the asset does not exist or is not owned; verify existence with external evidence.

See also: Major Fraud Case Studies, Case Studies, Financial Statement Fraud, Red Flags, Forensic Investigation Planning, Auditing Standards and Fraud.

Internal Controls and Fraud Risk Assessment

Internal Controls & Fraud Risk Assessment
Core frameworksCOSO Internal Control — Integrated Framework (2013); COSO/ACFE Fraud Risk Management Guide (2016)
Structure5 components, 17 principles; 5 fraud-risk principles
Related standardISO 37001:2025 (anti-bribery management systems)
Benchmark dataACFE Occupational Fraud 2024 (1,921 cases)
Forensic useControl testing, segregation-of-duties analysis, scheme-by-scheme risk matrices

Internal control is the set of policies, procedures and structures that give management reasonable assurance an organization will meet its operating, reporting and compliance objectives. A fraud risk assessment applies that lens to deliberate wrongdoing: it identifies who could commit which scheme, which controls would stop or reveal it, and where residual exposure remains. For the forensic accountant, controls matter twice: before a loss, as the thing to be designed and tested; after a loss, as the map of what failed and who was positioned to exploit the gap.[1]

1 COSO 2013 and the Fraud Risk Management Guide

The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO) issued its original Internal Control — Integrated Framework in 1992 and an updated version in May 2013. The 2013 framework is the one most U.S. issuers use to evaluate internal control over financial reporting under SOX Section 404 (see Auditing Standards and Fraud). It organizes control into five components—control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring activities—supported by 17 principles.[2] Principle 8 explicitly requires the organization to "consider the potential for fraud in assessing risks to the achievement of objectives."

COSO and the ACFE jointly published the Fraud Risk Management Guide (first edition 2008; second edition 2016) to expand that single principle into a program. Its five fraud-risk principles map onto the five components:[3]

Fraud risk principlePractical contentArtifact an examiner requests
1. GovernanceBoard/management commitment, fraud risk policy, rolesCode of conduct, board minutes, policy sign-offs
2. Risk assessmentScheme inventory, likelihood/impact scoring, anti-fraud-control mappingRisk register, prior assessment workpapers
3. Control activitiesPreventive and detective controls tied to each schemeControl matrix, procedure manuals, access lists
4. Investigation and corrective actionIntake, triage, remediation, disciplineHotline log, case files, root-cause memos
5. MonitoringOngoing evaluation, metrics, reporting of deficienciesInternal audit reports, KPI dashboards

The framework treats the fraud triangle elements as drivers to be managed: controls reduce opportunity, tone at the top and fair compensation reduce pressure and rationalization. It also cross-references the fraud tree for scheme inventories.

2 Segregation of duties

Segregation of duties (SoD) divides a transaction cycle so that no single person can initiate, authorize, record and keep custody of the asset. The classic four incompatible functions are authorization, custody, recordkeeping and reconciliation. Typical incompatible pairs include:

  • Creating vendors in the vendor master file and approving or releasing payments (the root of fictitious-vendor billing schemes).
  • Receiving cash and posting receipts to accounts receivable (skimming and lapping).
  • Adding employees to payroll and approving timesheets or distributing paychecks (ghost employees).
  • Preparing bank reconciliations and having check-signing authority.

Small organizations cannot always staff separate roles; the substitutes are compensating controls such as owner review of bank statements delivered unopened, mandatory vacation or job rotation, and periodic surprise counts. Because a determined insider with two incompatible roles can override a design, SoD should be combined with detective controls.

3 What the ACFE data say about controls

The ACFE's Occupational Fraud 2024 study (see ACFE Report to the Nations) reports that the presence of each of 18 anti-fraud controls was associated with lower median losses (reductions of roughly 23% to 63%) and shorter fraud duration (roughly 14% to 50%). Four controls—surprise audits, external audit of financial statements, hotlines, and proactive data monitoring/analysis—were associated with reductions of at least 50% in both loss and duration. On the cause side, 32% of cases were attributed to a lack of internal controls and 19% to an override of existing controls. On detection, 43% of schemes were found by tips, 14% by internal audit and 13% by management review, while external audit detected about 3%.[4]

These are correlations from self-selected cases investigated by CFEs, not controlled experiments, and the ACFE itself cautions that the data cannot prove causation. Even so, the pattern is consistent across editions: the most effective controls are those that surface information (tips, analytics, surprise tests) rather than only those that document approval.

4 Fraud risk assessment: steps

  1. Scope and team. Include finance, operations, compliance, IT and legal; interview people who actually run the processes.
  2. Inventory schemes. Use the fraud tree to list what could happen in each business cycle (procure-to-pay, order-to-cash, payroll, treasury, financial close), including management override and bribery.
  3. Rate inherent risk. Score likelihood and impact (for example 1–5 each) before considering controls.
  4. Map existing controls to each scheme and judge whether they would prevent or detect it.
  5. Test the controls (section 5) to separate controls that exist on paper from those that operate.
  6. Rate residual risk, rank, and assign response: add controls, increase monitoring, transfer risk (insurance), or accept.
  7. Document and refresh at least annually and on triggers such as acquisitions, system migrations or restructurings.

Illustrative scoring: a fictitious-vendor scheme in a company with unrestricted vendor-master access might score likelihood 4 and impact 4 (inherent 16). If a monthly independent review of new vendors exists and operates, residual might fall to 2 × 4 = 8; if the review is only on paper, residual stays at 16. The test in step 5 decides which.

5 Forensic techniques: testing controls and finding their failures

5.1 Walkthroughs and design versus operating effectiveness

A walkthrough follows one transaction from initiation to the general ledger, inspecting each document, approval and system screen, and interviewing the person who performs each step. It tests design. Operating effectiveness is tested by sampling: a common attribute-sampling convention for a control performed daily is 25–40 items, with any deviation requiring analysis. The evidence produced is a deviation list that states precisely which approvals were missing, late, or by the wrong person.

5.2 User-access and SoD conflict analysis

Export user-role assignments and the audit log from the ERP and build a conflict matrix (roles as rows and columns, incompatible pairs flagged). Then go beyond permissions to actual use: join the vendor-creation log to the payment-approval log on user ID. Example: if user U117 created 22 vendors in the year and approved payments to 9 of them totaling $318,400, that is a documented SoD breach with a quantified exposure and a ready list of transactions to vouch.

5.3 Vendor master file analytics

  • Match vendor addresses, bank accounts and phone numbers to the employee master; any match is a conflict-of-interest lead.
  • Flag P.O. Box-only addresses, vendors with no tax ID, and vendors with sequential invoice numbers (a vendor billing $4,100, $4,350 and $4,600 under invoices 0001, 0002 and 0003 has no other customers).
  • Fuzzy-match names to catch near-duplicates ("Acme Supply" versus "ACME Suply Inc").

5.4 Duplicate and threshold testing

Duplicate-payment tests join on vendor, invoice number, amount and date in progressively looser combinations: same vendor and amount within 30 days; same invoice number with transposed digits. For approval limits, compare the count of invoices just under a limit with adjacent bands. Illustration with a $10,000 limit: if 410 invoices fall between $9,000.00 and $9,499.99 but 1,260 fall between $9,500.00 and $9,999.99, a roughly threefold excess immediately below the limit suggests splitting or limit-avoidance, and the examiner then inspects those 1,260 for common approvers and vendors. The same logic underlies Benford's Law digit tests (see Fraud Detection Analytics).

5.5 Three-way match and override exceptions

Compare purchase order, receiving report and invoice. Count payments released with no receiving record, quantity or price variances approved manually, and manual overrides of system holds. A rising override rate (for example 0.8% to 4.1% of invoices over two quarters) is itself a red flag (see Red Flags). Evidence: exception report, user IDs, and the approver comments justifying each override.

5.6 Reconciliation and timing review

Re-perform bank reconciliations for sample months, tracing every reconciling item to clearing; reconciling items outstanding more than 90 days, or reconciliations prepared and approved by the same person or signed weeks late, point to concealment. Proof-of-cash and deposit-lapping tests (matching customer remittance dates against posting dates) detect skimming that leaves no entry (see Net Worth Method for indirect methods when records are absent).

5.7 Behavioral and HR controls

Review leave records: employees who never take consecutive vacation in sensitive roles, or whose files show duplicate address or bank data with others. Surprise cash counts and inventory observations produce a first-hand count that can be compared with the book balance. Hotline logs should be analyzed for volume, time-to-triage and substantiation rate; a hotline that has received zero reports in several years is not evidence of honesty but of low awareness or low trust.

6 ISO 37001 and anti-bribery controls

ISO 37001, Anti-bribery management systems, is a certifiable management-system standard first issued in 2016. A second edition, ISO 37001:2025, was published in February 2025. Reported changes include requirements to consider climate-change effects on bribery risk, an explicit concept of anti-bribery culture, renaming the "anti-bribery compliance function" the "anti-bribery function" with clearer independence, a fuller treatment of conflicts of interest, and harmonization with ISO 37301 and ISO 37000.[5] It requires bribery risk assessment, due diligence on projects and business associates, financial and non-financial controls over gifts, hospitality and donations, and reporting and investigation procedures. Certification does not confer immunity under statutes such as the FCPA, but regulators have treated an effective program as relevant (see Anti-Bribery Statutes and Anti-Corruption OSINT). The forensic counterpart is testing third-party payments: agent commissions above benchmark percentages, payments to jurisdictions unrelated to services, and consultants with no deliverables.

7 Limits of controls

Controls reduce, but do not eliminate, fraud. Collusion defeats segregation; management override (19% of ACFE cases above) bypasses the control environment entirely, which is why auditing standards treat override as a presumed risk in every audit. Controls also decay: staff turnover, system upgrades and workarounds erode design over time. An assessment should therefore be paired with continuous monitoring and independent testing, and findings should be documented in a form that can support later reporting if an investigation follows.

See also: Auditing Standards and Fraud, Occupational Fraud, Fraud Triangle, Fraud Detection Analytics, Red Flags, Forensic Accounting.

Auditing Standards and Fraud

Auditing Standards & Fraud
U.S. (AICPA)AU-C Section 240
U.S. (issuers)PCAOB AS 2401, AS 2110, AS 2415; SOX §404
InternationalISA 240 (Revised), issued July 2025
ISA 240 (Revised) effectivePeriods beginning on or after 15 December 2026
Standard of assuranceReasonable, not absolute
Presumed risksRevenue recognition; management override of controls

Auditing standards on fraud define what an independent auditor must do to obtain reasonable assurance that financial statements are free of material misstatement, whether caused by error or fraud. They do not make the auditor a guarantor and they do not turn the audit into a forensic investigation; but they require a fraud-oriented mindset, specific procedures, and documentation. Large frauds that evaded audit—Enron, WorldCom, Wirecard, Luckin—repeatedly show the gap between what the public expects and what the standards require (see Major Fraud Case Studies and Financial Statement Fraud).

1 The standards

AU-C 240 (Consideration of Fraud in a Financial Statement Audit) governs U.S. private-company audits under AICPA standards. PCAOB AS 2401 (same title) and AS 2110 (Identifying and Assessing Risks of Material Misstatement) govern audits of SEC issuers. ISA 240 applies in the many jurisdictions that adopt IAASB standards. They share a common architecture:

  • Professional skepticism throughout, including setting aside past experience that management is honest.
  • A team brainstorming session on how and where the entity might be susceptible to fraud.
  • Inquiries of management, those charged with governance, internal audit and others about knowledge or suspicion of fraud.
  • Evaluation of fraud risk factors organized by the fraud triangle (incentive/pressure, opportunity, attitude/rationalization).
  • Two presumed fraud risks: improper revenue recognition (rebuttable, with documented reasons) and management override of controls (never rebuttable).
  • Mandatory responses to override: test journal entries and other adjustments, review accounting estimates for bias, and evaluate the business rationale for significant unusual transactions.
  • Communication of identified or suspected fraud to appropriate management levels, governance, and, where required, regulators.

For issuers, the PCAOB standards operate alongside SEC rules and the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (SOX), which created the PCAOB itself after Enron and Arthur Andersen (see Case Studies).

2 ISA 240 (Revised)

The IAASB issued a revised ISA 240 in July 2025. According to the IAASB, it clarifies the auditor's responsibilities, strengthens a "fraud lens" in risk identification, assessment and response, and increases transparency in auditor's reports of publicly traded entities. It is effective for audits of financial statements for periods beginning on or after 15 December 2026, with early adoption permitted and encouraged.[1] Individual jurisdictions must adopt it into local standards before it binds auditors there; for example, South Africa's regulator announced adoption in early 2026.[2] Practitioners should verify the status in their own jurisdiction, and note that U.S. AICPA and PCAOB standards are separate instruments whose own revision status is independent of the IAASB project.

3 Auditor versus forensic accountant; the expectation gap

DimensionFinancial statement auditForensic engagement
TriggerAnnual/periodic requirementAllegation, red flag, or litigation
ObjectiveOpinion on whether statements are materially fairly presentedDetermine whether fraud occurred, who, how, how much
MaterialityThreshold-driven; small items may be ignoredAny amount may matter; intent is key
ScopeSampling, risk-basedOften targeted and exhaustive on the suspected area
OutputAudit reportReport, workpapers, expert testimony (see Evidence and Testimony)
IndependenceRequired of auditorRequired for experts, differs for consultants

The expectation gap is the difference between what users believe auditors do (detect all fraud) and what standards require (reasonable assurance of detecting material misstatements). It has persisted for decades. ACFE data show that external audit is the initial detection method in only about 3% of occupational-fraud cases, versus 43% for tips.[3] That figure does not mean audits are valueless; the ACFE also associates the presence of an external audit with materially lower losses, perhaps through deterrence. Auditors who find indicators of fraud are expected to stop, escalate, and often refer to forensic specialists, whose role and ethics are covered in Forensic Accountant Ethics.

4 SOX 404, SAB 99 and materiality

SOX §302 requires the CEO and CFO of an issuer to certify the financial statements and the effectiveness of disclosure controls; §906 adds criminal penalties for knowingly false certifications. §404(a) requires management to assess internal control over financial reporting (ICFR), conventionally against the COSO framework (see Internal Controls and Fraud Risk Assessment). §404(b) requires the external auditor to attest to ICFR for accelerated and large accelerated filers; non-accelerated filers have been permanently exempted from 404(b) since the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010. A material weakness is a deficiency, or combination, such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be prevented or detected on a timely basis.

The SEC's Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 99 (1999) rejects purely numerical materiality. A common 5% of pre-tax income rule of thumb is only a starting point; qualitative factors can make small misstatements material, including those that mask a change in earnings trends, turn a loss into a profit, hide a failure to meet analyst expectations, affect compliance with loan covenants, or increase management compensation. SAB 108 (2006) requires evaluating misstatements under both the "rollover" and "iron curtain" approaches. For fraud work, SAB 99 matters because intentional misstatements are rarely "immaterial."

5 Forensic techniques in fraud-focused audit and examination

5.1 Journal-entry testing

Management override is most often executed through manual top-side entries. Procedure: (1) obtain the full general-ledger population and reconcile its total debits and credits to the trial balance (completeness); (2) filter on risk criteria; (3) vouch selected entries to support. Typical criteria: posted by users outside the finance function or by senior executives; posted in the last days of a period or after period close; round-number amounts (e.g. ending in 000); no description or unusual descriptions; unusual account pairings (debit cash/receivable, credit revenue, with a later reversal); weekend or holiday posting; entries to seldom-used accounts. Illustration: of 1,200,000 lines, 340 are posted by non-finance users, 9,800 fall in the last three days of the quarter, and 6,100 are round thousands; the intersection yields 112 lines, which are traced to approvals and source documents. The evidence is the filtered population with user IDs, timestamps and, ideally, system audit logs.

5.2 Analytical review and ratio trend tests

Compute days sales outstanding (DSO = receivables / revenue × days). Suppose Q1 revenue is $50.0M with receivables of $9.0M (DSO = 9.0/50.0 × 90 = 16.2 days) while Q4 revenue is $80.0M with receivables of $30.0M (DSO = 30.0/80.0 × 90 = 33.75 days). Revenue grew 60% but receivables more than tripled: a signal of fictitious or premature sales. Add gross margin by product, cash conversion (operating cash flow / net income), and inventory days. The Beneish M-score combines eight indices (DSRI, GMI, AQI, SGI, DEPI, SGAI, LVGI, TATA) into a probability-of-manipulation score; the original 1999 study used a cutoff near −1.78, and later users often apply −2.22.[4] It is a screening tool with false positives, not evidence of intent. See Fraud Detection Analytics and Analytical Methods.

5.3 External confirmations and independent evidence

Evidence obtained directly from third parties is stronger than evidence supplied by the client. Controls over confirmations: the auditor selects the respondent, sends the request, and receives the reply directly, verifying the respondent's address and contact independently (not from client-provided details). Red flags include replies from free-email domains, replies delivered through the client, balances "confirmed" by the client's own trustee or agent, and refusals to allow direct contact. Complement with bank statements obtained directly, customer-count and shipping-document tests, and physical inspection of inventory and, for retailers, store-level verification such as foot-traffic or point-of-sale data comparisons.

5.4 Revenue cut-off and side-agreement tests

Select shipments and invoices in the five days before and after period-end and trace to shipping documents and customer acceptance. Review credit memos and returns in the first weeks of the next period: a spike (for example, returns of 7% of prior-quarter sales versus a normal 1.5%) suggests channel stuffing. Inquire of sales, legal and operations personnel—not only finance—about side letters, bill-and-hold and extended payment terms (see Interviewing).

5.5 Related-party and unusual-transaction tracing

Search customer and vendor masters, contracts, and public registries (see OSINT and Asset Tracing) for undisclosed related parties. In the SEC's account of the Luckin scheme, sales were fabricated through related parties using three purchasing schemes; the test is to trace cash from the "customer" back to its source and see whether it originated with the reporting entity or its affiliates ("round-tripping").

5.6 Cash proof and bank-flow reconstruction

Reconstruct total receipts and disbursements from bank statements and compare with recorded revenue and expense. A gap between recorded revenue and bank deposits that is not explained by receivables is quantifiable evidence; the method is the same as the indirect proofs in Net Worth Method.

6 Going-concern red flags

PCAOB AS 2415 and AU-C 570 require the auditor to evaluate whether substantial doubt exists about the entity's ability to continue as a going concern for a reasonable period (generally one year after the financial statements are issued or available to be issued; management's own evaluation is under ASC 205-40). Indicators include recurring operating losses, negative operating cash flow alongside reported profits, working-capital deficiency, loan covenant violations, defaults, reliance on short-term borrowings to finance long-term assets, inability to pay suppliers on normal terms, loss of a key customer or licence, pending litigation, and unusually large related-party funding. In fraud cases, a mismatch between reported profit and persistent cash shortfalls is among the most reliable signals.

7 Audit failures: Wirecard and Luckin

Wirecard. The German payments company collapsed in June 2020 after admitting that €1.9 billion in balances supposedly held in trustee accounts in Asia did not exist. Auditor Ernst & Young (EY) had audited the company for years. Germany's audit oversight body (APAS) found violations of professional obligations in EY's audits for 2016–2019 and, per press reports, imposed a two-year ban on new listed-company audit clients and a €500,000 fine; investors have sought damages exceeding €700 million from EY.[5] The lesson for confirmation procedures is that evidence routed through third parties selected by the client is weak evidence. The criminal trial of former CEO Markus Braun and two co-defendants began in Munich in December 2022; reporting in autumn 2026 indicated closing arguments were planned for late October with a verdict to follow, so no outcome should be assumed here.[5]

Luckin Coffee. On 16 December 2020 the SEC announced that the China-based chain had fabricated more than $300 million of retail sales from at least April 2019 through January 2020, inflating expenses to conceal the fabrication, and that Luckin agreed to pay a $180 million penalty without admitting or denying the allegations.[6] The fraud became public after a short-seller report built on thousands of store-hours of video observation and receipt collection—an OSINT-style counting of actual customers—preceded the company's own disclosure. It illustrates a technique available outside the audit: independent physical verification of the revenue driver (see Anti-Corruption OSINT).

See also: Internal Controls and Fraud Risk Assessment, Financial Statement Fraud, International Forensic Standards, Red Flags, Litigation Support and Damages.
