Whistleblowers and the False Claims Act

Whistleblowers and the False Claims Act
Core statuteFalse Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. §§ 3729–3733
Relator share15–25% (intervened), 25–30% (declined)
FY2025 FCA recoveriesMore than $6.8 billion (record)
FY2025 qui tam filings1,297 (record)
SEC programDodd-Frank § 922; 10–30% of sanctions over $1 million
ACFE tip rate43% of occupational frauds detected by tips (2024)

A whistleblower is a person who reports suspected wrongdoing to an organization, regulator or prosecutor. In U.S. fraud enforcement, whistleblowing is both a legal status, which carries retaliation protection and sometimes a financial award, and the single most productive detection channel. The False Claims Act (FCA) lets private persons, called relators, sue on behalf of the government in qui tam actions against anyone who defrauds federal funds. Together with the SEC, CFTC, IRS, FinCEN and DOJ programs, it forms a bounty-based system that turns insiders into the principal source of evidence in many federal enforcement cases.[1]

1 Why tips matter

The ACFE's Occupational Fraud 2024 found that 43% of cases were detected by tip, more than internal audit, management review or external audit combined; employees supplied 52% of tips, customers 21% and vendors 11%, and web-based hotlines (40%) and email (37%) were the most common channels.[2] The share has been stable across editions of the Report to the Nations. For the examiner, this means that an anti-retaliation policy and credible follow-up are detection controls, not only legal compliance. Organizations with hotlines detected fraud faster and with lower median losses than those without (see Occupational Fraud).

2 The False Claims Act

The FCA, first enacted in 1863 to combat Civil War contractor fraud, imposes liability on any person who knowingly presents a false claim, makes a false record or statement material to a claim, conspires to do so, or knowingly conceals or avoids an obligation to pay the government (§ 3729(a)(1)). “Knowingly” includes actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance and reckless disregard; no specific intent to defraud is required. Remedies are treble damages plus a per-claim civil penalty that is adjusted annually for inflation. The Supreme Court tightened the materiality element in Universal Health Services v. Escobar (2016) and held in United States ex rel. Schutte v. SuperValu (2023) that liability turns on the defendant's actual subjective belief, not what an objectively reasonable person might have believed.

Qui tam mechanics. The relator files a complaint under seal in federal court and serves the government with a written disclosure of material evidence. The seal lasts at least 60 days and is routinely extended while DOJ and agency Offices of Inspector General investigate, often for years. DOJ then intervenes (takes over the case), declines (the relator may proceed alone) or moves to dismiss. A successful relator receives 15–25% of the recovery if the government intervenes, and 25–30% if it does not, plus attorneys' fees. The first-to-file bar, the public-disclosure bar and the original-source exception limit later or copycat relators. In United States ex rel. Zafirov v. Florida Medical Associates, a Florida district court held the qui tam mechanism unconstitutional under the Appointments Clause in 2024; on 1 September 2026 the Eleventh Circuit reversed, holding that relators are not officers of the United States and that the qui tam provisions satisfy the Appointments Clause; it remanded two further challenges (Vesting and Take Care Clauses) to the district court, so the provision stands but litigation over it continues.[7] Readers should check its current status.

Scale. DOJ reported more than $6.8 billion in FCA settlements and judgments in fiscal year 2025, the highest annual total in the statute's history, including more than $5.3 billion (77%) from qui tam suits. Relators filed a record 1,297 new qui tam actions that year, up from 980 in FY2024, and DOJ opened 401 matters on its own. Healthcare accounted for more than $5.7 billion.[3][4] Typical theories are upcoding and medically unnecessary services, kickbacks that render claims false (Anti-Kickback Statute), Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment, Paycheck Protection Program loan fraud, customs-duty evasion, defective pricing and small-business set-aside fraud, and, since 2021, cybersecurity non-compliance by contractors under DOJ's Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative.

3 Other federal programs

ProgramAuthorityAwardNotes
SEC WhistleblowerSecurities Exchange Act § 21F (Dodd-Frank § 922, 2010)10–30% of sanctions over $1 millionFY2025: about 27,000 tips; more than $60 million awarded to 48 individuals (down from over $255 million to 47 in FY2024)[5]
CFTC WhistleblowerCommodity Exchange Act § 2310–30% of sanctions over $1 millionFunded by Customer Protection Fund
IRS Whistleblower26 U.S.C. § 7623(b)15–30%, where tax, penalties and interest exceed $2 millionForm 211; see Tax Fraud and Evasion
FinCEN AML/sanctionsAML Act of 2020; 31 U.S.C. § 532310–30% of sanctions over $1 millionAlso covers sanctions violations; see Sanctions and Export Controls
DOJ Corporate Whistleblower Awards PilotCriminal Division program launched 1 Aug 2024; amended 12 May 2025Discretionary, tied to forfeitures over $1 millionAdded procurement, trade/tariff/customs, sanctions and immigration-related offenses to the original priority areas (financial institutions, corruption, healthcare fraud against private insurers)[6]

The SEC rules require voluntary, original information leading to a successful enforcement action; submissions are accepted anonymously through counsel. Under Digital Realty Trust v. Somers (2018), Dodd-Frank's anti-retaliation provision protects only those who have reported to the SEC, not those who reported solely internally. The AML Act's whistleblower provisions were extended in 2022 to cover sanctions violations, and a FinCEN program awards are funded from collected penalties.

4 Retaliation protections

  • FCA § 3730(h): reinstatement, two times back pay with interest, special damages and fees; three-year limitation period from the retaliatory act. Protects acts “in furtherance of” an FCA action and efforts to stop violations.
  • Sarbanes-Oxley § 806 (18 U.S.C. § 1514A): protects employees of public companies, and their contractors, who report mail, wire, bank or securities fraud, or violations of SEC rules, to a supervisor, federal agency or Congress. A complaint must be filed with OSHA within 180 days; the employee may go to federal court if no final decision issues within 180 days. Remedies include reinstatement, back pay with interest and special damages. The Supreme Court in Lawson v. FMR LLC (2014) extended coverage to employees of private contractors of public companies, and in Murray v. UBS Securities (2024) held that a SOX plaintiff need not prove retaliatory intent, only that protected activity was a contributing factor.
  • Dodd-Frank § 21F(h): two times back pay for SEC reporters; six-year limitations period.
  • SEC Rule 21F-17: prohibits agreements, including severance and NDAs, that impede communication with the SEC. The SEC has brought repeated settled actions against firms whose confidentiality clauses lacked a carve-out for regulator reports.
  • Anonymous reporting and confidentiality: most programs allow counsel-submitted anonymous tips, while the FCA seal and IRS rules protect identity until litigation.

5 Forensic evaluation of a tip or complaint

An examiner, in-house investigator or relator's counsel receives a narrative, perhaps with documents. The central task is to convert allegations into testable propositions and corroborate them with independent records before expending resources or making any accusation. The following protocol reflects common practice and professional guidance on interviewing and chain of custody.

5.1 Intake and triage

  1. Record the allegation verbatim (who, what, when, which system, which contract or claim numbers) and the channel and time of receipt. Do not ask leading questions that put names into the complainant's mouth.
  2. Classify against the Fraud Tree and the legal theory (false claim, kickback, revenue recognition, etc.) to determine the records that would prove or disprove it.
  3. Preserve before you probe. Issue or request a legal hold on email, ERP and billing data. Take forensic images of relevant devices where authorized, and hash the files. Avoid alerting the subject: access logs may be reviewed by the subject's IT staff.
  4. Score credibility without prejudging: firsthand versus secondhand knowledge, specificity, documents provided, motive (grievance, pending termination) and consistency. Motive does not negate truth, and a grievance-driven relator may still be right.

5.2 Corroboration tests

  • Claims-data analysis. For healthcare allegations, extract paid claims by billing code and provider. Compare the distribution of E/M levels (99213 vs 99215) to peer-specialty benchmarks; a provider billing the top level for 80% of visits when peers average 25% is an outlier worth examining. Test for impossible days (more than 24 hours of services in a day), unbundling, duplicate claims and services after patient death.
  • Contract and cost testing. For a government contractor, tie invoices to timesheets, labor-category qualifications and delivery receipts; test whether charged labor categories match the actual staff's credentials; re-perform indirect-rate allocations.
  • Kickback tracing. Map payments from the vendor or manufacturer to referral sources, including speaker fees, “consulting” and grants; compare the timing and amounts against referral volumes (see Anti-Bribery Statutes). Open Payments data (CMS) is a public cross-check for payments to U.S. physicians.
  • Timeline construction. Build a dated chronology from emails, calendar entries, system logs and document metadata to test the complainant's account and identify who knew what and when, which is the scienter evidence.
  • Interviews in sequence. Start with neutral process witnesses and end with the subject, using the funnel approach in Interviewing. Upjohn warnings are given to employees interviewed on behalf of the company.

5.3 What each technique yields

TechniqueEvidence producedElement proved
Claims-code outlier analysisExhibit comparing provider vs peer distribution, with sample claim listFalsity; supports extrapolation
Statistically valid sample (RAT-STATS) of medical recordsError rate with confidence interval, extrapolated overpaymentFalsity and damages
Email and chat review (keyword plus threading)Communications showing awarenessKnowledge (scienter)
Payment tracing to referral sourcesFlow-of-funds scheduleRemuneration, link to referrals
Metadata and log forensicsAuthorship, edits, access timesBackdating, alteration

6 Worked example: sizing FCA damages

This is a hypothetical illustration. Suppose a probe sample of 100 paid claims from a population of 20,000 claims (total paid $4.0 million) shows 22 claims were upcoded, with an average overpayment of $85 per error across the sample. The point estimate of overpayment per claim is 22 × $85 / 100 = $18.70, extrapolated to 20,000 claims = $374,000. Because that is a sample, the examiner reports a confidence interval; if the standard error gives a 90% lower limit of $290,000, that conservative figure is commonly used for repayment demands. Under the FCA, single damages of $374,000 may be trebled to $1.12 million, plus per-claim penalties (for example 22 sampled false claims, or all identified false claims if separately provable, multiplied by the current penalty range), before any settlement discount for cooperation. Statistical extrapolation is accepted in many courts but is contested; the underlying methods are covered in Analytical Methods and Fraud Detection Analytics, and testimony standards in Daubert Standard.

7 Pitfalls

  • A whistleblower who takes privileged documents or exceeds authorized access can create exposure for themselves and taint the evidence; counsel usually directs preservation rather than copying.
  • Public-source corroboration (federal spending data, court dockets, Open Payments, SEC filings) is permissible and often decisive, but see OSINT Ethics before contacting potential witnesses.
  • Many tips are wrong or incomplete. Examiners should state clearly when an allegation could not be corroborated.
  • Statutes, award percentages and agency policies change; verify current text before relying on this summary.

See also: Occupational Fraud, ACFE Report to the Nations, Federal Enforcement Agencies, Tax Fraud and Evasion, Sanctions and Export Controls.

Sanctions and Export Controls

Sanctions and Export Controls
Sanctions authorityIEEPA (50 U.S.C. § 1701 et seq.), TWEA, country statutes
AdministratorTreasury OFAC
Export controlsExport Control Reform Act 2018; Export Administration Regulations (EAR), Commerce BIS
Liability standardCivil: strict liability; criminal: willfulness
Max civil penalty (IEEPA)$377,700 per violation or twice transaction value, whichever is greater (2025 figure)
Key listSpecially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List

Economic sanctions are legal prohibitions on dealing with designated persons, sectors or jurisdictions, used as an instrument of foreign policy. Export controls restrict the transfer of specific goods, software and technology, regardless of the counterparty's identity. The two regimes overlap in practice: a front company that buys dual-use chips for a sanctioned military end-user will violate both, and the concealment methods are those described in Shell Companies and Beneficial Ownership. For financial investigators, sanctions evasion is also a predicate for money laundering, and the same tracing and OSINT techniques apply.

1 Legal framework

OFAC administers programs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), the Trading with the Enemy Act and program statutes (for example CAATSA for Russia, Iran and North Korea). Designated persons appear on the SDN List; U.S. persons, which include U.S. entities, U.S. citizens and permanent residents wherever located, and anyone in the United States, must block their property and generally may not deal with them. Liability is strict in civil matters: no knowledge is required for OFAC to assess a penalty, though knowledge, voluntary self-disclosure and an effective compliance program affect the amount under OFAC's Enforcement Guidelines. Criminal penalties under IEEPA require a willful violation (up to 20 years' imprisonment and $1 million per violation).

Secondary sanctions threaten non-U.S. persons who engage in specified transactions with designated targets, such as significant transactions with listed Russian or Iranian financial institutions, with exclusion from the U.S. financial system. Primary sanctions bind U.S. persons directly. Dollar clearing, U.S.-origin goods and U.S. correspondent accounts create jurisdiction over non-U.S. actors; several European banks have paid multi-billion-dollar settlements on that basis (for example BNP Paribas, which in 2014 pleaded guilty and forfeited $8.9 billion).

Export controls. The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) administers the EAR and the Commerce Control List, including the Entity List, Military End-User List and Unverified List. Items are classified by Export Control Classification Number (ECCN), and licence requirements depend on item, destination, end-user and end-use. Criminal violations of the Export Control Reform Act carry up to 20 years and $1 million per violation. The Department of Justice and BIS also run the Disruptive Technology Strike Force, and the DOJ Corporate Whistleblower Awards Pilot (see Whistleblowers and the False Claims Act) now lists sanctions offenses among its priority areas.[1]

2 The 50 percent rules

OFAC's 50 Percent Rule (revised guidance of 13 August 2014) holds that any entity owned, directly or indirectly, 50% or more in the aggregate by one or more blocked persons is itself blocked by operation of law, even if the entity does not appear on the SDN List. Three points matter in analysis:

  • Aggregation: ownership by multiple blocked persons adds together. Two SDNs each holding 25% make the company blocked; one SDN at 49% and a non-blocked party at 51% does not.
  • Ownership, not control: a blocked person who controls an entity without owning 50% does not automatically block it, but dealing with the entity may still be risky, since OFAC may treat it as acting for a blocked person, and non-ownership indicia can support a designation. OFAC advises caution with entities controlled by SDNs.
  • Indirect chains: A 50% owner of B, owner of 50% of C, results in C being blocked (each link is tested separately at 50%).

OFAC stresses that the 50 Percent Rule is a floor and not a ceiling for diligence. On 31 March 2026 it issued an advisory on sham transactions: transfers in which a blocked person gives up property on paper while keeping a continuing interest. Red flags include commercially unreasonable transfers, transfers to family members or close associates, unduly complex structures, and continued involvement of the blocked person in managing the property.[2] OFAC enforcement in 2025 shows the rule in action, including a $215,988,868 penalty (announced 12 June 2025) against GVA Capital Ltd. for managing investments for a designated Russian oligarch after his designation, and a $1,092,000 settlement (9 December 2025) with an individual who served as fiduciary of a U.S. trust tied to a sanctioned oligarch.[3]

BIS adopted a parallel Affiliates Rule on 29 September 2025 extending Entity List, Military End-User List and some SDN-related restrictions to entities 50% or more owned by listed parties. On 10 November 2025 BIS suspended it for one year, until 9 November 2026, after a U.S.–China trade arrangement; during the suspension the EAR reverts to the prior “legally distinct entity” approach.[4] Because that date falls three weeks after this article, readers should check whether it was extended or reinstated. Other regimes (the EU, UK) use a “control” test in addition to a more-than-50% ownership test, so one structure can be blocked in one jurisdiction and not another.

3 Evasion typologies

TypologyHow it worksFootprint
Front and shell companiesNewly formed third-country firms (Hong Kong, UAE, Turkey, Central Asia, Caucasus) buy for the sanctioned end-userRecent formation, nominee directors, thin staff, shared address
Ownership fragmentationSDN reduces stake below 50% or splits among relatives and associatesTransfers just before or after designation; same family names; sham transaction indicators
Transshipment and re-exportGoods routed through intermediary country with falsified end-user certificatesCustoms data showing sudden volume surges to neighbors of the target; HS codes of controlled items
Trade-based misinvoicingOver- or under-invoicing and phantom shipments to move valueUnit-price outliers vs. market benchmark
Maritime evasionAIS switch-off or spoofing, ship-to-ship transfers, flag hopping, falsified bills of lading, shadow fleetsAIS gaps near loading zones, vessel name/IMO changes, single-ship owners
Payment obfuscationThird-country payers, netting, cash couriers, informal value transfer, stablecoins and virtual-asset exchangesPayer not party to contract; payment in unusual currency; blockchain exposure to sanctioned addresses
Professional enablersTrust companies, lawyers, fiduciaries who hold property for designeesFee flows; trustee for multiple designees

Typologies are periodically updated in joint advisories from OFAC, BIS and FinCEN, and in guidance from the FATF on proliferation financing. FinCEN SAR filings reference these through key terms specified in its advisories.

4 Forensic and OSINT examination methods

4.1 Screening and name resolution

  1. Build the party list: every counterparty, bank, intermediary, vessel, beneficial owner, director and address in a transaction file.
  2. Screen against SDN, Consolidated Sanctions List, EU, UK OFSI, UN and Entity List data using fuzzy matching tuned for transliteration (e.g. Cyrillic to Latin variants), word-order inversion, and abbreviations. Document each hit as true match, false positive or unresolved, with the identifiers used (date of birth, passport, IMO number, address, registration number) that distinguish them.
  3. Resolve ownership upward using the procedures in Shell Companies and Beneficial Ownership, and apply the 50% aggregation arithmetic in a written schedule. List each owner, percentage, source document and date.
  4. Re-screen on a schedule. A clean screen on the date of onboarding says nothing about a designation next month; investigators examining historical transactions must screen as of the transaction date, not today.

4.2 Transaction and trade-data analytics

  • Unit-price testing: compute price per kilogram or per unit from customs and invoice data and compare with commodity benchmarks; deviations beyond, say, two standard deviations flag misinvoicing.
  • Mirror-statistics: compare exports reported by country A to country B with imports reported by B from A; large gaps suggest diversion.
  • Network analysis: link shippers, consignees, banks and notify parties through shared addresses, phones, and bank accounts (see Analytical Methods). Newly active consignees buying the same controlled HS codes as a previously designated buyer are a standard lead.
  • Payment-chain review: in SWIFT message data, check ordering and beneficiary fields, intermediary banks, and remittance text for references to listed parties or vessels; examine whether the payer is the contracting party.
  • Vessel tracking: reconstruct the voyage from AIS positions, flag and ownership history (IMO number persists when names change), and port-call records; look for AIS gaps exceeding 24 hours near terminals and ship-to-ship rendezvous.
  • Blockchain analysis: trace exposure to addresses attributed to designated persons or exchanges (see Cryptocurrency Tracing); OFAC has listed wallet addresses on SDN entries.

4.3 Documents and open sources

Examine end-user certificates, bills of lading, commercial invoices and packing lists for inconsistencies (end-user name or address differing across documents, ports inconsistent with route, signatures reused). Open sources include corporate registries, customs-data vendors, satellite imagery of premises, vessel registries, court filings and news (see OSINT, OSINT Tools). Findings must be recorded with source, access date and archive copy to preserve admissibility (Chain of Custody).

5 Worked example: ownership aggregation and trade-data test

This is a hypothetical case. A distributor, Company C, is owned 30% by an SDN, 25% by Company B and 45% by an unrelated investor. Company B is owned 60% by the same SDN. The test: the SDN's indirect interest in C through B is not 60% × 25%, because under OFAC's rule B is itself tested first. B is owned 60% by an SDN, so B is blocked (60% ≥ 50%). B's 25% of C therefore counts as blocked-person ownership. Aggregate blocked ownership of C = 30% (SDN) + 25% (B) = 55%, so C is blocked even though the SDN holds only 30% directly. A naive multiplication (30% + 0.6 × 25% = 45%) would wrongly clear it.

Now the trade-data screen. Company C imported 4,000 units of a controlled component at an invoice price of $12 per unit; customs and market benchmarks put the price at $48, so the invoices are 75% below benchmark (($48 − $12) / $48). Across the year the undervaluation totals 4,000 × ($48 − $12) = $144,000, and the examiner asks who settled the difference and where. Cross-checking, the supplier's country reports exporting 5,200 units to C's country while C's customs shows 4,000 received; the 1,200-unit gap is a lead for diversion. None of these is proof; they define document requests (contracts, payments, warehouse records) and interview topics.

6 Enforcement and screening

Compliance programs follow OFAC's Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments (2019): management commitment, risk assessment, internal controls, testing and training. Banks screen customers and payments; exporters screen end-users, review red flags in BIS's “Know Your Customer” guidance, and file voluntary self-disclosures. Violations are reported to OFAC within 10 business days for blocked property and annually for rejected transactions. Investigators should assume that penalties are driven by egregiousness, harm to program objectives, and compliance culture, and that willfulness is usually proven by concealment (altered fields, stripped references, shell intermediaries). Related frameworks include AML Law, AML Statutory Framework and Anti-Bribery Statutes.

See also: Money Laundering, Asset Tracing, Shell Companies and Beneficial Ownership, Cryptocurrency Tracing, Federal Enforcement Agencies.

Shell Companies and Beneficial Ownership

Shell Companies and Beneficial Ownership
ConceptLegal entities used to separate assets from their true controllers
Key standardFATF Recommendations 24 and 25 (transparency of legal persons and arrangements)
U.S. regimeCorporate Transparency Act (2021), narrowed by FinCEN final rule of Aug 2026
UK regimeCompanies House PSC register; ID verification under ECCTA 2023
EU regimeNational registers; AMLR (Reg. 2024/1624) applies from July 2027
Landmark leakPandora Papers (ICIJ, Oct 2021)

A shell company is a legal entity with no significant independent operations, employees, or assets of its own, used to hold property, move money, or sign contracts. Shells are lawful and common (holding vehicles, special-purpose entities, dormant companies), but they are also the standard building block of money laundering, sanctions evasion, bribery and billing fraud. A front company differs in that it has a real or apparent business that disguises illicit flows. Beneficial ownership is the question of who ultimately owns or controls the entity, as opposed to who is named on the registry. The gap between the two is what investigators work to close.[1]

1 How concealment is built

Concealment is usually achieved by stacking several features, each of which is legal alone:

  • Nominee directors and shareholders. A professional service provider's employee is listed as director or shareholder, often under a private side agreement (a declaration of trust or a signed-but-undated resignation letter) that preserves the real owner's control. A single nominee may sit on hundreds or thousands of boards, a pattern visible in registry data.
  • Registered-agent addresses. Thousands of entities share one street address. In the United States, formation in Delaware, Wyoming, Nevada and New Mexico has long been favored because member or manager names of an LLC need not appear in the public filing; only a registered agent and the formation date are disclosed.
  • Layering across jurisdictions. A Delaware LLC owned by a BVI company owned by a trust in a third jurisdiction forces an investigator to obtain records under three legal systems.
  • Bearer or unregistered instruments (largely abolished but still found in legacy structures) and trusts and foundations, which often sit outside company registers entirely.
  • Circular and cross-holdings that make the 25% ownership arithmetic hard to resolve.

The scale is documented by journalism. The ICIJ's Pandora Papers, published beginning 3 October 2021, drew on about 11.9 million files (roughly 2.9 TB) from 14 offshore service providers, and named dozens of current and former heads of state and government among thousands of beneficial owners.[2] The earlier Panama Papers (2016, Mossack Fonseca) established the same pattern: the provider, not the client, is the investigator's best document source. Leak datasets are searchable through the ICIJ Offshore Leaks Database, which is an OSINT lead generator, not proof of wrongdoing: holding an offshore entity is not itself unlawful.

2 Registers and legal regimes in 2026

United States. The Corporate Transparency Act (CTA), enacted in the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020, required reporting companies to file beneficial ownership information (BOI) with FinCEN. After litigation and a March 2025 interim rule that exempted domestic companies, FinCEN issued a final rule dated 11 August 2026, effective 14 August 2026, that removes the reporting and update obligation for U.S. companies and U.S. persons; only entities formed abroad and registered to do business in a U.S. state or tribal jurisdiction remain reporting companies, and they report only foreign beneficial owners. FinCEN said it will work with the National Archives on a one-time deletion of BOI received before 11 February 2027 that it reasonably believes was supplied by U.S. persons.[3][4] The practical effect for investigators is that there is no federal database of who owns a typical Delaware or Wyoming LLC, and the BOI database was never open to the public in any case (access was limited to law enforcement, certain regulators and financial institutions with consent). Customer due diligence (CDD) rules for banks, which require identifying owners of 25% or more and one controlling person at account opening, remain in force, so the bank's file is now the main U.S. repository of ownership data, reachable by subpoena or in civil discovery.

United Kingdom. Companies House has published a free, searchable register of People with Significant Control (PSC; over 25% of shares or votes, or control of the board) since 2016. The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 added identity verification for directors and PSCs: voluntary from 8 April 2025, mandatory from 18 November 2025 with a 12-month transition for existing officers.[5] Verification improves the reliability of the register but does not detect a verified person acting as a straw owner.

European Union. Each member state keeps a beneficial ownership register under the AML directives. In WM and Sovim SA v Luxembourg Business Registers (Joined Cases C-37/20 and C-601/20, 22 November 2022) the CJEU held that unrestricted public access was invalid, and many registers closed to the public.[6] The AML Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, applying from 10 July 2027, replaces this with access for persons who can show a legitimate interest, expressly including journalists and civil society organizations; the new Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) in Frankfurt begins direct supervision in 2028.[7] Until then, access depends on the country.

JurisdictionOwnership data heldWho can see it (Oct 2026)Verification
United States (federal)BOI for foreign-registered entities onlyLaw enforcement, some regulators, FIs with consentSelf-reported
United States (state)Name, agent, formation date; sometimes managersPublic (Secretary of State search)None
United KingdomDirectors, PSCs, shareholdersPublic, freeID verification phased in 2025–26
EU member statesBeneficial owners (25%+ or control)Varies; legitimate interest model emergingVaries

3 Forensic examination: piercing the structure

Piercing a shell involves two separate tasks: establishing who controls it (an identification problem) and establishing whether it is a sham (a legal and evidentiary problem). The following procedures are used in combination and are normally documented in the working papers described in Report Writing.

3.1 Registry and corporate-record pull

  1. Obtain the certified formation documents, annual reports, and every amendment from the state or registry. Record the formation date, agent, filer name, and any organizer signature. Organizers who are law-firm or formation-service staff identify the incorporator, which is a subpoena target.
  2. Pull all entities sharing the registered agent address, officers, phone, email domain or website host. Cluster analysis (see Analytical Methods) on those fields often exposes a family of shells created within days of each other.
  3. Build the ownership chart to the first natural person, applying the 25% rule multiplicatively: an individual holding 60% of A, which holds 50% of B, holds 30% of B indirectly. Flag any branch that terminates in a trust, foundation or nominee rather than a person.

3.2 Bank and payment records

The account-opening file (signature cards, CDD forms, source-of-wealth statements, IDs) is usually the first document naming a natural person. Examine: authorized signers versus listed officers; the address and IP used for online banking; the first deposits (whose money capitalized the account); and the beneficiary names on outgoing wires. Compare signatures and device identifiers across supposedly unrelated entities. Procedures for tracing flows are set out in Asset Tracing, and for crypto-funded entities in Cryptocurrency Tracing.

3.3 Document metadata and infrastructure

Invoices, contracts and incorporation papers submitted by a suspected shell should be examined for authorship metadata (PDF producer, author and creation dates), template reuse across different “vendors” (identical fonts, typos, layout), and WHOIS and hosting history for the company website (see Document Examination and Digital Forensics). Invoices from different shells created on the same machine within minutes are strong evidence of a common hand.

3.4 Substance tests

A real business leaves real footprints. Check for: employees (payroll filings, unemployment-insurance wage reports); a physical premises (site visit, lease, utility accounts); tax filings that match claimed revenue; licenses and insurance; independent customers or suppliers; web or marketplace presence predating the transaction; and sales-tax or VAT registrations. A vendor that billed $2 million but filed no payroll tax and has a virtual-office address fails most substance tests.

3.5 Leak and sanctions datasets, then court tools

Screen entity and officer names against the ICIJ Offshore Leaks Database, OpenCorporates, national registers, litigation dockets, and sanctions lists (see Sanctions and Export Controls). Where records are abroad, formal channels include mutual legal assistance treaty requests, letters rogatory and, in civil matters, Norwich Pharmacal and Mareva-type orders in common-law jurisdictions. U.S. courts may order disclosure of ownership and, in appropriate cases, apply alter-ego or veil-piercing doctrines (see section 6).

4 Worked example: vendor-side shell test

This is an illustrative, hypothetical analysis in the style of the vendor-file tests used for billing-scheme detection. A company's accounts-payable ledger shows 14 new vendors set up over 18 months. The examiner extracts, for each vendor: bank account, address, phone, tax ID, approver, and total paid.

TestResultInterpretation
Vendor address matches an employee address0 of 14No direct hit
Vendor address is a known registered-agent/virtual office5 of 14Consistent with shell; not proof
Same approver on all invoices5 of 5 agent-address vendors; approver is a manager with no purchasing authorityControl override
Invoice totals just below approval limit ($9,500 vs $10,000 limit)41 of 47 invoices to those 5 vendorsThreshold avoidance
Sequential invoice numbers (001, 002, 003 over 14 months)3 vendorsVendor has almost no other customers
Payments to a bank account that later pays a personal account$212,000 across 3 vendorsBeneficiary traced via subpoenaed bank records

The result is not a conclusion; it is a set of leads. Each pattern would be confirmed by bank-account-opening records (who signed), the vendor's tax filings, and delivery evidence. The output of the examination is typically (a) a flow-of-funds chart, (b) a vendor-profile exhibit, and (c) a schedule of payments with approver and date, admissible under the business-records rules discussed in Evidence and Testimony. The same logic applies to public procurement: when a bidder's registry data shows the same agent, phone and formation date as a competing bidder, bid-rigging analysis becomes appropriate.

5 Red flags

  • Entity formed shortly before the first transaction, with no operating history.
  • Same address, phone, email domain or director across many unrelated entities.
  • Nominee officers who hold dozens of directorships.
  • Payments to a company whose stated activity does not match its industry code, or round-dollar invoices for vague “consulting” or “management services.”
  • Ownership that terminates in a trust or foundation with no named settlor.
  • Rapid pass-through: funds in and out within days with a negligible balance retained.
  • Reluctance to supply source-of-wealth documents; frequent changes of registered agent or name.
  • Bank account in a jurisdiction unrelated to customers or suppliers.

See also the broader Red Flags catalogue.

6 Limits and legal pitfalls

Courts pierce the corporate veil only on a showing, typically, of unity of interest (commingling, undercapitalization, disregarded formalities) and injustice or fraud; an entity's mere lack of employees is not sufficient. An investigator must also separate legal privacy from illegality: forming an anonymous LLC is lawful, while concealing ownership from a bank or lying on a CDD form can be a crime (for example under 18 U.S.C. 1344 or 1956). Private investigators must not obtain bank records by pretexting (the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act prohibits it) and should follow the guidance in OSINT Ethics. After the August 2026 FinCEN rule, claims that a U.S. entity's owners “are in the FinCEN database” should be treated as unreliable.

See also: Asset Tracing, Money Laundering, AML Law, Sanctions and Export Controls, Tax Fraud and Evasion, Anti-Corruption OSINT.

Public Records and Court Dockets

Public Records and Court Dockets
FieldOpen-source investigation; litigation and asset research
Federal courtsPACER (fee-based); RECAP / CourtListener (free mirror)
Securities filingsSEC EDGAR (free, rate-limited to 10 requests/second)
Secured-debt filingsUCC-1 / UCC-3 at state filing offices
Request statutesFederal FOIA, 5 U.S.C. § 552; state open-records laws

Public records research is the use of government-maintained filings, docket sheets, registries and disclosed agency documents to establish facts about transactions, ownership, debts and disputes. It is the most evidentially durable branch of open-source intelligence, because the underlying documents were created by courts, regulators and registries rather than by the subject, and can often be obtained in certified form. For the fraud examiner, these records answer the questions a bank statement cannot: who sued whom and over what, who holds a security interest in which assets, who really owns a parcel of real estate, and what a public company told the SEC and when. The records feed directly into asset tracing, anti-corruption due diligence and forensic accounting engagements. This article describes sources and reading techniques; it is a methods guide and does not endorse research on private individuals beyond what a lawful engagement requires (see OSINT Ethics).

1 Federal court records: PACER, RECAP and CourtListener

PACER (Public Access to Court Electronic Records) is the federal judiciary's system for dockets and filings in district, bankruptcy and appellate courts. The published fee schedule is $0.10 per page, with the charge for any single document capped at $3.00 (30 pages); an account that accrues $30 or less in a quarter pays nothing for that quarter, which the judiciary says covers about three-quarters of users.[1] Because each court runs its own CM/ECF instance, the PACER Case Locator is the usual starting point: it searches party names, case numbers and nature-of-suit codes across courts, though its index is only as good as each court's data entry.

The free complement is the RECAP browser extension, created by the Free Law Project. When a user buys a document from PACER, RECAP automatically donates it to a public repository, and it alerts later users when the document they are about to pay for already exists there.[2] The repository is searchable on CourtListener, which also hosts opinions, oral-argument audio and docket alerts. Practical consequences for investigators: search CourtListener first; set alerts on dockets of interest; and remember that a RECAP copy is only as complete as whatever earlier users happened to buy, so an absence there says nothing about whether a filing exists. For evidentiary use, pull the document from PACER directly so that the source and retrieval date are unambiguous (see Chain of Custody).

Bankruptcy courts deserve special attention. A Chapter 11 or Chapter 7 petition forces the debtor to file schedules of assets and liabilities, a statement of financial affairs listing recent transfers, and a list of creditors, so a bankruptcy docket is often the single richest public document on a debtor's finances. Transfers to insiders in the year before filing are what trustees pursue as preferences and what examiners should flag as potential concealment of assets.

2 How to read a docket

A docket sheet is the court clerk's chronological index of everything filed in a case. Reading one efficiently is a skill separate from reading the filings themselves.

  1. Caption and header. Case number (the prefix typically encodes the district, year and case type, for example "1:24-cv-01234"), the presiding and referred judges, the filing date, the nature-of-suit code, and the jury demand. A criminal docket uses "cr" and lists charges and their disposition; a related-case notation points to companion proceedings.
  2. Parties and counsel. The party list identifies corporate defendants, third-party defendants, intervenors and amici. The names of counsel and their firms are themselves a signal of who is funding the litigation and whether the party is represented by the lawyers one would expect.
  3. Entry numbers. Docket entries are numbered sequentially. Gaps, or entries marked "sealed" or "restricted," show where material is withheld; the existence and timing of a sealed entry is itself information. Attachments are numbered as sub-entries.
  4. The pivotal entries. The complaint (allegations and exhibits), the answer (admissions and denials), motions to dismiss and for summary judgment (the parties' best evidence presented in compact form), protective-order motions, notices of settlement, consent judgments and the final judgment or dismissal order. A voluntary dismissal "with prejudice" soon after a sealing motion often signals a confidential settlement.
  5. Exhibits. Summary-judgment exhibits frequently attach contracts, emails and deposition excerpts that never appear anywhere else in the public record.

The rules on privacy shape what you will see. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 5.2 (and parallel rules for criminal and bankruptcy cases), filers must redact Social Security and taxpayer numbers to the last four digits, birth dates to the year, minors' names to initials and financial-account numbers to the last four digits; failure to redact is a recurring source of accidental exposure that investigators should handle responsibly rather than exploit.

Docket entry typeWhat it tells an investigatorFollow-up
Complaint / indictmentAlleged scheme, dates, amounts, named co-participantsCross-check amounts to net-worth and bank data
Motion to seal / protective orderConfidential commercial or financial material existsCheck whether a redacted public version was filed
Lis pendens or writ of attachmentPlaintiff is pursuing specific propertySearch deed records for the parcel
Judgment / abstract of judgmentAmount owed; basis for judgment liensSearch county and UCC records for recorded liens
Proof of claim (bankruptcy)Creditors and secured-collateral descriptionsCompare to UCC filings
Satisfaction of judgmentDebt was paid; timing may show source of fundsLook for corresponding asset sale

3 State and local court records

State courts handle the great majority of litigation, including contract disputes, foreclosures, landlord-tenant matters, family and probate cases, and most criminal prosecutions, but access is fragmented. There is no state-level equivalent of PACER: each state, and frequently each county, runs its own portal, some free (a docket search by name), some fee-based, and some requiring an in-person visit to the clerk. Common pitfalls include name-search systems that return only exact matches, portals that purge older cases from online access, and inconsistent treatment of sealed, expunged or juvenile matters. Civil suits against a company in the counties where it operates, and in the home county of its principals, are standard checks. A pattern of collection suits, mechanics' lien claims or vendor judgments is a classic early indicator of the cash distress that frequently precedes financial statement manipulation, a point developed in Red Flags.

Probate files, divorce financial affidavits, and foreclosure complaints can disclose asset values and transfer histories that appear nowhere else. Treat those involving private individuals with the proportionality required by OSINT Ethics: use them where a defined investigative purpose exists, and do not republish personal details.

4 UCC filings, liens and judgments

Under Article 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code, a lender perfects a security interest in most personal property (equipment, inventory, receivables, deposit accounts by control, and so on) by filing a UCC-1 financing statement with the state filing office, typically the secretary of state for the debtor's state of organization. A filed financing statement is effective for five years; a UCC-3 continuation may be filed only in the six months before lapse (UCC § 9-515), and a lapsed filing cannot be revived, only replaced by a new UCC-1.[3] Amendments, assignments and terminations are also recorded on UCC-3 forms.

For investigators a UCC search reveals: who lends to the entity; what collateral is pledged (a blanket lien on "all assets" or a specific description); whether collateral descriptions match assets the subject claims to own free and clear; and whether a lender has recently assigned or terminated its filing. A debtor that reports no borrowings but shows several UCC-1s, or that pledges the same receivables to multiple lenders, is a red flag for undisclosed liabilities and double-pledging schemes. Searches are by exact debtor name as it appears on the public organic record, so search variants and check the charter name first.

Other lien and judgment sources include federal tax liens (the IRS files a Notice of Federal Tax Lien in the county or state office designated by local law), state tax warrants, mechanics' liens on real property, judgment liens recorded after a money judgment, and Fed. R. Civ. P./state-court abstracts of judgment. Each is a recorded public claim against assets and a timeline marker for financial stress.

5 Property, deed and mortgage records

Real property records are maintained by county recorders, registers of deeds or equivalent offices and by assessors for tax purposes. The recorded instruments of interest are deeds (the chain of title shows grantor, grantee, consideration statement and date), mortgages and deeds of trust (lender and amount), assignments of mortgage, satisfactions, liens, and lis pendens notices. Assessor databases add parcel identifiers, assessed value and the mailing address for tax bills. Many counties now publish indexes online and sell images; some require a name or parcel search by subscription.

The analytical value is in the mismatches. A deed transferring a property to a family member or newly formed LLC for nominal consideration shortly before a lawsuit or regulatory action is a conventional badge of a fraudulent transfer, and a mortgage far larger than the purchase price may indicate inflated appraisal or cash-out refinancing. Purchases in the name of a limited liability company, trust or land-trust nominee are why real estate is a favored integration channel in money laundering; the public deed will usually show the entity but not the individual behind it, so the next step is the state corporate filing, then the registry and leak databases. In the United States, FinCEN's Residential Real Estate Rule targeting non-financed transfers to entities was a significant planned change in this area; its effective date has been postponed and its status should be confirmed against current FinCEN notices before relying on it.

6 SEC EDGAR and corporate filings

EDGAR, the SEC's Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval system, is free and covers registered securities offerings and periodic disclosure by public companies. The SEC's fair-access policy caps automated retrieval at 10 requests per second and expects automated tools to identify themselves with a name and contact email in the User-Agent header.[4] Key forms:

  • 10-K / 10-Q — annual and quarterly reports with audited or reviewed financial statements, risk factors, legal proceedings and related-party disclosures.
  • 8-K — current reports of material events; Item 4.02 (non-reliance on previously issued financial statements) and Item 4.01 (change of auditor) are among the most significant signals for restatement and audit risk.
  • DEF 14A — proxy statements disclosing executive pay, related-party transactions and beneficial owners of 5% or more.
  • Forms 3, 4 and 5 — insider holdings and trades; a pattern of insider selling ahead of bad news is a classic detection pivot.
  • Schedules 13D / 13G — large-holder positions.
  • Form D — notice of exempt private offerings, a useful source on startups and funds that are not otherwise registered.
  • Comment letters — SEC staff correspondence on a filer's disclosures, released after review, which often reveal accounting questions months before any restatement.

Beyond the federal system, the state corporate filing (articles of incorporation, annual report, registered agent, and sometimes officer names) establishes that an entity exists, its formation date, its status (active, dissolved, revoked) and its registered agent address. Mass-registration addresses shared by hundreds of entities are a standard shell-company indicator. For foreign registries see Corporate Registries and Leak Databases. SEC enforcement releases, litigation releases and administrative proceedings are published on sec.gov and are an authoritative source on named defendants and settled orders (see Federal Enforcement Agencies).

7 FOIA and state open-records requests

When the record is not already published, a statutory request can reach it. The federal Freedom of Information Act, 5 U.S.C. § 552, obliges agencies to determine within 20 working days whether to comply with a request, subject to exemptions (for example for personal privacy, law-enforcement records, confidential commercial information and deliberative material) and to extensions in unusual circumstances. FOIA applies to federal executive agencies, not to courts, Congress or private companies. Every state has its own open-records statute with its own deadlines and exemptions; Pennsylvania's Right-to-Know Law, for instance, requires an initial response within five business days, which an agency can extend by up to 30 calendar days.[5]

Effective requests share a few traits: they describe records, not questions; they identify a date range and custodian; they request electronic format; they ask for fee waiver where the public-interest test applies; and they are kept in a log with dates and tracking numbers, because appeal rights run from the agency's response or its failure to respond. Contracts, invoices, procurement files, inspection reports, grant files and meeting minutes held by public bodies are the usual targets in procurement and bribery inquiries, and make a natural source for anti-corruption OSINT. Released documents should be archived with the request, the cover letter and any redaction log as part of the file.

8 Forensic examination techniques

The preceding sections describe sources; this section describes the concrete procedures an examiner applies to them and the evidence each produces.

Technique 1: Lien-stack reconstruction. Pull every UCC-1, UCC-3, tax lien and judgment lien against the debtor and any name variants; order them by filing date; compute lapse dates (filing date plus five years; continuation window opens six months earlier); and compare collateral descriptions with the balance sheet. Worked example: a borrower reports $2.0 million of bank debt in its financial statements. The search shows three active filings: Lender A, blanket lien, filed 2022; Lender B, receivables, filed 2023; and a UCC-3 assignment of Lender B's filing to a factor in 2024. If the factor advanced $1.5 million against receivables and the financial statements show only the $2.0 million loan, a potential $1.5 million undisclosed liability exists, and the same receivables may be pledged twice. The work product is a dated lien schedule with certified search results, which supports a finding of non-disclosure, not a conclusion of intent.

Technique 2: Timeline correlation across record systems. Build one chronology merging docket entries, recording dates, corporate filings and SEC filings. Look for transfers inside the look-back windows used by avoidance law (commonly two years under 11 U.S.C. § 548 for fraudulent transfers and 90 days for preferences, or one year for insiders). Worked example: suit filed 3 March; deed of the debtor's $850,000 house to a new LLC for "$10 and other consideration" recorded 19 February; LLC formed 11 February. Three events in 20 days, all before service, is a classic badge-of-fraud cluster. Output: a dated exhibit with each source document attached, giving a trustee or counsel a basis to plead avoidance.

Technique 3: Consideration and valuation test. For each deed, compare stated consideration or transfer-tax stamps to the assessor's value and recent comparable sales. Example: assessed value $850,000, recorded consideration $10, no mortgage satisfaction: implied transfer below reasonable equivalent value, so the examiner then looks for the transfer-tax affidavit or a related loan.

Technique 4: Party and relationship mapping. Extract every party, attorney, registered agent, notary and signatory from the records and load them as nodes in a link-analysis table (entity, role, source, date). Recurrence is the signal: the same registered agent address on 40 entities, the same notary on deeds in a disputed chain, or the same officer appearing across failed companies. Output: a relationship table that points to beneficial-ownership work; each edge must cite a document.

Technique 5: Restatement and disclosure analytics on EDGAR. Use full-text search to compare risk-factor and legal-proceeding language across consecutive 10-Ks; track auditor changes (Item 4.01) and non-reliance notices (Item 4.02); and compute simple ratios across years. Worked example: revenue up 30% while operating cash flow fell from $12 million to $4 million and receivables rose from 18% to 31% of revenue: days sales outstanding (receivables divided by revenue times 365) lengthens from about 66 to about 113 days, a standard indicator of aggressive revenue recognition worth pairing with Benford testing of disclosed figures and the methods in Fraud Detection Analytics. Insider-sale clustering is checked by tallying Form 4 sales in the 90 days before an adverse 8-K.

Technique 6: Open-records request audit trail. For each request, log the date sent, tracking number, statutory deadline (20 working days federally), response, redaction exemptions cited and appeal outcome. Compare produced contract totals with vendor payments in the entity's ledger: a $1.2 million purchase-order series paid to a vendor while only $0.9 million of contracts is produced indicates either missing records or off-contract payments, a lead for billing-scheme testing.

Evidence produced and its weight. Certified court and recorder copies and SEC filings are self-authenticating or readily admissible public records; portal screenshots, third-party aggregators and uncertified printouts are leads that need corroboration. Record the portal, query terms, date and time, and hash saved files (see Chain of Custody).

9 Limits, verification and red flags

  • Name collisions. Court and registry searches return people and companies with the same or similar names. Confirm identity with at least two independent identifiers (middle name, address history, case-specific detail) before attributing a record to anyone, and say when you have not.
  • Allegation versus finding. A complaint is an allegation. Distinguish pleadings from findings, judgments, consent decrees and convictions, and record the disposition. Dismissed, expunged or sealed matters require extra care.
  • Currency. Portals lag; liens may be satisfied but not yet shown as released. Note the retrieval date on every item.
  • Completeness. An empty result is evidence of nothing without knowing the system's scope. A clean US federal search does not cover state courts, foreign jurisdictions or arbitration.
  • Authentication. For anything intended for court, obtain certified copies from the clerk or recorder; evidence rules treat certified public records as self-authenticating.

Detection patterns. Frequent changes of registered agent or counsel, repeated judgments paid just before a financing event, newly recorded liens on assets the borrower claims as unencumbered, entity names that mirror a dissolved predecessor, and serial small-claims or collection suits all merit follow-up. None is proof of wrongdoing; each is a lead to be tested against primary documents.

See also: Asset Tracing, OSINT Tools, Corporate Registries and Leak Databases, Web Archives and Domain Intelligence, Chain of Custody.

Corporate Registries and Leak Databases

Corporate Registries and Leak Databases
FieldBeneficial-ownership and corporate-structure research
AggregatorsOpenCorporates; OCCRP Aleph; OpenSanctions
Official registriesUK Companies House; US state filing offices; GLEIF (LEI)
Leak dataICIJ Offshore Leaks Database (810,000+ offshore entities)
Core riskName matching, stale data, nominee owners

Corporate registries are government-maintained records of legal entities, and leak databases are searchable collections of documents obtained from offshore service providers and similar sources and published by journalists. Used together they let an examiner move from a company name seen on an invoice, deed or wire to its directors, shareholders, addresses, affiliates and, with luck, ultimate beneficial owners. They are the main OSINT front end of asset tracing and anti-corruption due diligence. This article covers major sources, their limits, and the examination procedures built on them. It is a methods guide: legitimate subjects are entities, public officials in their official capacity, and sanctioned or convicted parties, not private individuals (see OSINT Ethics).

1 Official registries

The primary evidence of a company's existence is its official registry entry. In the United Kingdom, Companies House publishes free online records of incorporated companies, including officers, persons with significant control (PSCs), registered office, accounts and charges (secured borrowing). The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 expands the registrar's powers and introduces identity verification: from 18 November 2025 verification began to become mandatory for directors and LLP members, with other categories phased in during 2026.[1] The practical effect for investigators is that post-2025 officer records should be more reliable than historical ones, while pre-reform filings remain unverified self-declarations.

In the United States there is no national company registry; each state's secretary of state maintains formation records, which vary widely in what they disclose. Delaware, Wyoming and others permit minimal public information, often only the registered agent. Federal beneficial-ownership reporting under the Corporate Transparency Act has been sharply curtailed by a FinCEN rule of August 2026 (see Money Laundering), so U.S. investigators generally cannot rely on a national ownership register and instead assemble ownership from state filings, UCC and court records, and bank KYC files obtained in discovery. Many other jurisdictions (EU member states, with the post-2022 court ruling limiting public access to some registers, and offshore centres) have registers with differing public access, and the legal position changes often, so confirm access rules for the jurisdiction at the time of the search.

2 Aggregators: OpenCorporates, Aleph, OpenSanctions

OpenCorporates is a large open database of company records compiled from official registries, searchable across jurisdictions and useful for finding entities that share an officer name or address. Its value is breadth; its limitation is that each record is a copy of a registry entry of variable age, so findings must be re-verified at the source registry.

OCCRP Aleph is a search platform operated by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project that indexes company registries, leaked and public documents, court records, sanctions lists and journalist-contributed datasets. Access is tiered, with the public interface available to registered users and expanded access aimed at journalists and investigators. Searching it returns cross-referenced entities, which can reveal that a name in a leak also appears in a procurement record.

OpenSanctions aggregates sanctions lists, politically exposed persons (PEP) data and other watchlists into a unified, deduplicated dataset. Its data are released under CC BY-NC 4.0; non-commercial use is free, but any use within a for-profit business, including compliance screening, requires a licence, with exemptions for qualifying journalism and non-profits.[2] Anyone using it professionally must check the licence terms. A match against a sanctions or PEP list is a screening hit to be adjudicated, not a finding.

3 GLEIF and the Legal Entity Identifier

The Legal Entity Identifier (LEI), standardised as ISO 17442, is a 20-character code assigned to legal entities, mainly those transacting in financial markets. The Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation (GLEIF) publishes the Global LEI Index free of charge. By the second quarter of 2026 the active LEI population exceeded 3.1 million, and registrants representing 99% of the population reported direct and ultimate parent information (“Level 2” data, answering “who owns whom”).[3] Reporting exceptions are permitted, for example where disclosure is legally restricted, so an exception code is itself a datum. The LEI is useful because it is a persistent unique identifier that is independent of name spelling and can be matched to registry numbers, and because parent relationships are self-reported but validated by the issuing organisation. It does not reveal individuals; parent chains typically end at a corporate or fund entity.

4 Leak databases

The ICIJ Offshore Leaks Database is the best known leak resource. It consolidates the Offshore Leaks, Panama Papers, Bahamas Leaks, Paradise Papers and Pandora Papers investigations and holds information on more than 810,000 offshore entities, linked to people and companies in over 200 countries and territories.[4] It publishes structured data on officers, intermediaries, addresses and entities, not the underlying emails and documents, and ICIJ states that appearing in it is not evidence of wrongdoing; offshore structures can be lawful. The Pandora Papers additions (December 2021, April and May 2022) added beneficial-owner data from providers including Alcogal and Fidelity Corporate Services.

SourceTypeBest forMain limit
Official registryPrimaryLegal existence, officers, filingsSelf-declared; few show real owners
OpenCorporatesAggregatorCross-jurisdiction name and address searchLag; copies of registry data
OCCRP AlephAggregator / archiveLinking entities across records and leaksAccess tiers; coverage uneven
OpenSanctionsWatchlist aggregatorSanctions and PEP screeningLicence; false positives
GLEIFIdentifier registryEntity disambiguation, parent chainsSelf-reported parents; financial-sector bias
ICIJ Offshore LeaksLeak dataOffshore officers, intermediariesSnapshots through about 2020; not proof of wrongdoing

Leaked data raise their own legal and ethical issues: provenance is uncertain, material may include private data, and use in litigation requires authentication. Stay within the public, journalist-curated tables, and do not seek out or republish raw leaked personal data.

5 Forensic examination techniques

Technique 1: Ownership-chain reconstruction. Start from the target entity and record, per level: legal name, registry number, jurisdiction, status, formation date, officers, shareholders, registered agent and address. Proceed upward until you reach (a) a natural person, (b) a listed company or state body, (c) a nominee, trust or bearer structure, or (d) a registry that discloses nothing. Then compute effective ownership by multiplying percentages. Worked example: Target Ltd is 60% owned by Holdco A, which is 50% owned by Trust B and 50% by Holdco C; Holdco C is 80% owned by an individual. The individual's effective stake in Target is 0.60 × 0.50 × 0.80 = 24%, below a 25% PSC threshold, so a naive PSC screen could miss them. The examiner also tests control separate from ownership (voting agreements, board appointment rights). Output: an ownership diagram with every edge sourced to a registry extract, and each break in the chain stated explicitly.

Technique 2: Address and agent concentration analysis. Export all entities matching a registered address or agent from an aggregator. Compute the count and the share that were formed within 12 months, are dissolved, or have no filed accounts. Example: 212 entities at one suite address, of which 160 (75%) formed within two years and 140 show no officers: that address is a formation-agent location and is no evidence of common ownership; but if 6 of the 212 share an officer, those six are the lead. Over-reading shared addresses is the commonest error.

Technique 3: Officer-network pivot with disambiguation. For each officer, collect date of birth (month/year where published), nationality, service address and prior roles, then assess whether two records are the same person using at least two identifiers beyond the name. Record a confidence level (confirmed, probable, possible). Output: a person-to-company table that distinguishes confirmed links from name-only matches.

Technique 4: Timeline and lifecycle tests. Plot formation, name change, officer change, accounts, charge registration and dissolution dates against transaction dates. Shells commonly show formation shortly before first payment, officers resigning immediately after a payment or audit, and dissolution after receipt of funds. Example: an entity formed 4 January, invoicing from 20 January, three invoices totalling $480,000 paid by 28 February, officer resignation 3 March: a 48-day active life with no filed accounts.

Technique 5: Charges and filings as financial evidence. UK charge registers and US UCC filings show who lent to the company; accounts filed at Companies House show turnover bands, employee numbers and director loans. A company claiming $20 million of sales but filing micro-entity accounts with two employees is internally inconsistent and warrants a reasonableness test.

Technique 6: Screening protocol. Run entities and officers against sanctions and PEP datasets with documented fuzzy-matching thresholds. Adjudicate each hit using date of birth, nationality and role: a name hit with a mismatched birth year is closed as false positive with the reason recorded; unresolved hits are escalated. Keep the query log and dataset version/date. Example: 400 officers screened, 23 hits, 19 closed on mismatched identifiers, 3 confirmed PEP associations, 1 unresolved: the report states these numbers and the method rather than only the confirmed hits.

Technique 7: Leak cross-match. Search each target name, address and intermediary in the Offshore Leaks Database. A match establishes an appearance in a source dataset; to establish relevance, confirm identity through independent identifiers and ask whether the structure was disclosed to the relevant tax and regulatory authorities. Output: a documented match with source node ID and a statement of what the match does and does not show. Findings then feed tracing and net-worth work.

6 Limits and verification

  • Nominees. Nominee directors and shareholders sit on the register in place of real owners; look for professional nominees who hold hundreds of directorships.
  • Stale and self-declared data. Most registries accept filings without verifying them; note the filing date of every datum.
  • Transliteration and name matching. Names rendered from Cyrillic, Arabic or Chinese scripts vary; search variants and use identifiers instead of names.
  • Coverage bias. Leak and sanctions datasets reflect what was leaked or listed, not the universe of wrongdoing; absence of a name is not exoneration.
  • Licensing. Check terms for each dataset before using it commercially or republishing it.
  • Fairness. Present links as links; do not infer guilt from an offshore appearance or a PEP relationship.

See also: Asset Tracing, Anti-Corruption OSINT, Public Records and Court Dockets, OSINT Tools, AML Law.

Geolocation and Imagery OSINT

Geolocation and Imagery OSINT
DisciplineGEOINT / IMINT within open-source intelligence
Core questionsWhere was it taken? When? Is it authentic?
Reference casesBellingcat’s MH17 Buk investigation (2014–2015)
Typical toolsGoogle Earth, Sentinel Hub EO Browser, SunCalc, reverse image search
Key riskStripped metadata; AI-generated and recycled imagery

Geolocation is the process of determining where a photograph or video was captured, and chronolocation the process of determining when. Together with media verification they form the imagery branch of OSINT disciplines (GEOINT and IMINT). In financial-crime and trafficking work they are used to confirm that a facility exists and operates, that goods or assets are where documents say, that a claimed site visit or inspection occurred, and that images offered as evidence are what they claim to be. The approach is the one popularised by Bellingcat and by the Verification Handbook: treat every image as a claim, extract every observable clue, and corroborate with independent sources.[1] It is a methods discipline; locating private individuals' homes or movements is outside the scope of ethical OSINT, and the examples here involve public events, infrastructure and commercial sites.

1 Satellite and aerial imagery sources

Free sources include Google Earth (whose desktop version has a historical-imagery slider showing earlier captures), Sentinel Hub EO Browser with Copernicus Sentinel-2 imagery at roughly 10 metre resolution and a revisit of a few days, and mapping services with street-level coverage. Commercial providers such as Planet Labs and Maxar offer sub-metre to daily-revisit products at a cost. Resolution drives what is answerable: 10 m imagery shows a field or a large warehouse but not a vehicle; 30–50 cm imagery shows vehicles, shipping containers and building details. Bellingcat’s Online Investigations Toolkit catalogues these tools with their limitations.[2] Always record the capture date shown by the viewer, because map tiles blend imagery of different ages.

2 The Bellingcat approach

Bellingcat’s investigation of the Buk missile launcher linked to the downing of MH17 is the standard teaching case. Using videos and photographs shared on social media, the team matched distinctive features in the background, such as buildings, road layout and signage, to satellite imagery to fix where each image of the convoy was recorded, and used shadow analysis with SunCalc to estimate the time of day.[3] The method generalises to any chain of images: each geolocated and dated image becomes a point on a timeline, and the chain’s strength comes from many independent images that agree. Public sources of this kind later informed formal findings, but a reader should treat each open-source claim as only as strong as its documented steps, which is why the method emphasises showing the work.

3 Forensic examination techniques

Technique 1: Clue inventory and ranking. Before searching, list every observable feature and rank it by how location-specific it is: (1) unique landmarks and skyline; (2) road geometry, intersections, bridges; (3) signage, language, script, phone-number formats; (4) utility poles, bollards, road-marking style, driving side, licence-plate format; (5) vegetation, soil, climate; (6) vehicles and architecture style. Highly specific features are searched first. Output: a clue table that lets another analyst reproduce the reasoning.

Technique 2: Progressive narrowing. Country (driving side, language, plate style), then region (climate, architecture), then city or district (landmarks), then the exact vantage point (match skyline and building edges to satellite and street-level views). Confirm by matching at least three fixed features whose relative geometry agrees: a bend, a building footprint and a utility pole line, say. A single matching feature is only a candidate.

Technique 3: Shadow-based chronolocation. Measure an object’s height H and its shadow length L in the image, in the same plane. The sun’s elevation angle is arctan(H/L). Worked example: a 6.0 m pole casts a 9.0 m shadow, so elevation = arctan(0.667) ≈ 33.7 degrees. At a known location and date, a sun calculator such as SunCalc lists the times of day when the sun reaches that elevation, typically one morning and one afternoon time; shadow direction then selects which. Conversely, with a known time the date can be estimated, since at mid-latitudes elevation at the same clock time changes with season by tens of degrees. Uncertainty is substantial where height or the ground plane is estimated, so report a time window, not a minute.

Technique 4: Imagery-date bracketing. Compare historical satellite imagery to find when a feature appeared or disappeared (new construction, a cleared field, a vessel at a berth). If the feature is absent on 2 March and present on 18 April, the photograph showing it is no earlier than 2 March and the build occurred in that 47-day window. Cross-check with seasonal cues (leaf cover, snow, crops) and weather records for the claimed date.

Technique 5: Reverse image search and earliest-appearance analysis. Run the image through several engines (Google Images, Yandex, TinEye, Bing) and crop to distinctive regions. TinEye is useful for finding the earliest indexed instance; Yandex is often effective for places and faces, but searching for faces raises privacy questions that OSINT Ethics addresses. For video, extract keyframes and search those. If an image predates the claimed event, it is recycled. Output: a log of engines, queries, dates and earliest dated hit.

Technique 6: Metadata (EXIF) examination. Inspect Exchangeable Image File Format fields: capture timestamp, device make/model, software, GPS coordinates, lens and orientation, and thumbnail. Compare them with the visible content: a file claimed as phone photography whose software field shows an editor, a thumbnail that differs from the main image, or a capture time that conflicts with shadows are warning signs. Most social platforms and messaging apps strip or rewrite metadata on upload, so absent EXIF is normal, not suspicious, while intact EXIF on a file obtained directly from a source is high-value but also trivially editable. Treat metadata as a lead, never as proof, and hash the original file before examining a copy (see Digital Forensics Tools and Chain of Custody).

Technique 7: Image-integrity analysis. Look for inconsistent lighting and shadow directions, repeated texture (clone stamping), edge halos, and mismatched noise or compression between regions; error-level analysis and noise-residual views assist but produce false positives on recompressed images, so they support but do not decide. For video, see Video Forensics, which covers frame analysis and authentication in more depth.

Technique 8: Corroboration matrix. For each conclusion record location confidence, time confidence and authenticity confidence separately, with the independent items supporting each (satellite match, shadow estimate, second angle of the same event, local weather, eyewitness or official statement). A claim supported by one line of evidence is reported as unconfirmed.

4 AI-generated imagery and provenance

Generative models can produce photorealistic scenes, which means the question “is this real?” now comes before “where is this?”. Visual tells (malformed hands, garbled text, inconsistent reflections, implausible architecture) are unreliable as models improve. Provenance technologies help but have gaps: C2PA Content Credentials are cryptographically signed metadata recording a file’s origin and edits, while SynthID is an invisible watermark embedded in pixels at generation; in May 2026 OpenAI and Google jointly endorsed pairing the two because each alone is insufficient.[4] Platforms commonly strip embedded metadata on upload, so credentials usually survive only on files obtained from the source, and the absence of a credential or watermark proves nothing. Detection classifiers produce both false positives and false negatives and should not be cited as conclusive. The robust approach is to geolocate and chronolocate: a fabricated scene will usually fail to match real satellite and street-level geometry, and a real one will match in several independent respects. Authenticity findings for court use belong with a qualified examiner (see Evidence and Testimony and the Daubert standard).

5 Documentation, limits and ethics

  • Preserve first. Save the original file and the page it came from, hash it, and capture the URL and time; sources vanish (see Web Archives and Domain Intelligence).
  • Show the work. Annotated side-by-side comparisons, coordinates, imagery dates and calculation steps let others reproduce the finding.
  • State uncertainty. Use confidence levels and time windows.
  • Confirmation bias. Try to disprove the hypothesis; a peer reviewer should repeat the geolocation blind where possible.
  • Do not target individuals. Do not geolocate private residences or track private persons; blur faces and licence plates in anything published; consider that publication can place people in danger.
  • Imagery limits. Cloud cover, old tiles, seasonal change and low resolution can produce wrong matches; satellite imagery shows a surface, not intent.

See also: OSINT Disciplines, Video Forensics, Digital Forensics, OSINT Tools, Web Archives and Domain Intelligence.
